question: (a) Define public health, community health and community health nursing. (3 marks) (b) Trace the evolution of public health and community health nursing in the world and in India. (8 marks) (c) Explain the present status of community health nursing in India. (4 marks)
tags: history of public health in India
All India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health

diagram.caption: Milestones in public health and community health nursing in India
labels: Sushruta) – sanitary commissions (1864) – Plague Commission and Epidemic Diseases Act (1897) – Lady Dufferin Fund (1885) and health visitors – All India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health (1932) – Bhore Committee (1946) – Community Development Programme and PHCs (1952) – Kartar Singh Committee
multipurpose workers (1973) – Alma-Ata (1978) – NRHM (2005) – NHM (2013) – Ayushman Bharat
Health and Wellness Centres and Community Health Officers (2018)

answer_html:
(a) Definitions (3 marks)

  • Public health (C.-E. A. Winslow, 1920) – "the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting physical health and efficiency through organised community efforts for the sanitation of the environment, the control of community infections, the education of the individual in principles of personal hygiene, the organisation of medical and nursing services for the early diagnosis and preventive treatment of disease, and the development of the social machinery which will ensure to every individual a standard of living adequate for the maintenance of health."
  • Community health – the health status of a defined group of people (a village, town, school or workplace) and the actions and conditions – public and private – that promote, protect and maintain their health.
  • Community health nursing (WHO Expert Committee) – "a special field of nursing that combines the skills of nursing, public health and some phases of social assistance, and functions as part of the total public health programme for the promotion of health, the improvement of conditions in the social and physical environment, and the rehabilitation of illness and disability." It is population-focused, continuous and comprehensive, directed to individuals, families, groups and the whole community, mainly outside hospitals.

(b) Evolution of public health and community health nursing (8 marks) A. In the world

  1. Ancient period – planned drains and baths in the Indus Valley, Roman aqueducts and public baths; Hippocrates' "Airs, Waters and Places" linked disease with environment.
  2. Middle Ages – epidemics of plague, leprosy and cholera; quarantine (forty days) introduced in Venice; isolation of lepers.
  3. Sanitary awakening (19th century) – Edwin Chadwick's report on the sanitary conditions of the labouring population (1842) led to the Public Health Act (England, 1848); John Snow traced cholera to the Broad Street pump (1854) – the beginning of epidemiology.
  4. Germ theory and the bacteriological era – Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch identified microbes; vaccines and sanitation brought infectious diseases under control.
  5. Modern public health – WHO (1948); smallpox eradication (declared 1980); Alma-Ata Declaration (1978) – primary health care and "Health for All"; Ottawa Charter (1986) for health promotion; Millennium Development Goals (2000) and Sustainable Development Goals (2015).
  6. Community health nursing – Florence Nightingale and William Rathbone started district nursing in Liverpool (1859); Lillian Wald founded the Henry Street Settlement in New York (1893) and coined the term "public health nursing"; school nursing and maternal and child health nursing developed in the early 20th century.

B. In India

  1. Ancient and medieval India – Indus Valley sanitation; Ayurveda (Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas) described personal hygiene, diet and seasonal regimens; hospitals during the reign of Ashoka; the Unani system in the medieval period.
  2. British period
    • Sanitary commissions were set up in Bengal, Madras and Bombay in 1864 after the Royal Commission on the health of the army.
    • The Plague Commission (1896); Haffkine developed plague and cholera vaccines; the Epidemic Diseases Act (1897).
    • The Indian Research Fund Association (1911), later ICMR; the All India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health, Kolkata (1932).
    • Women's and child health – the Lady Dufferin Fund (1885) provided female medical aid; the Victoria Memorial Scholarship Fund (1903) trained dais; the Lady Chelmsford League (1920) and the Lady Reading Health School, Delhi trained the first health visitors; the Indian Red Cross Society (1920) and the Maternity and Child Welfare Bureau (1931).
    • Nursing – the Trained Nurses' Association of India (1908), with which the Health Visitors' League later merged; B.Sc. Nursing began in Delhi and Vellore in 1946 with public health content.
    • The Bhore Committee (1946) recommended integration of preventive and curative services and a network of primary health units.
  3. After independence
    • Constitution – health is a State subject; Article 47 makes improvement of public health and nutrition a duty of the State.
    • Community Development Programme and primary health centres (1952); national programmes for malaria (1953/1958), family planning (1952 – India was the first country to start one), leprosy, TB and smallpox (eradicated in 1977).
    • Indian Nursing Council Act (1947); training of ANMs, LHVs and public health nurses; community health nursing in GNM and B.Sc. Nursing curricula.
    • Kartar Singh Committee (1973) – multipurpose health workers; Rural Health Scheme (1977) – village health guides; Alma-Ata (1978) and the National Health Policy (1983) with the goal of Health for All by 2000.
    • Universal Immunisation Programme (1985), Child Survival and Safe Motherhood (1992), RCH (1997), National Rural Health Mission (2005) with ASHAs, National Urban Health Mission (2013) and National Health Mission.
    • Polio-free certification (2014), Mission Indradhanush and Swachh Bharat (2014), National Health Policy (2017).
    • Ayushman Bharat (2018) – Health and Wellness Centres (now Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) with Community Health Officers (mostly B.Sc. nurses) and PM-JAY insurance; the COVID-19 response and vaccination drive (2021); Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission.

(c) Present status of community health nursing in India (4 marks)

  • A network of community health nursing personnel
    • ASHA at the village level (about one per 1,000 population).
    • ANM / MPW (female) at the sub-centre (Ayushman Arogya Mandir – Sub Health Centre).
    • Community Health Officer (CHO) – a B.Sc. nurse or trained mid-level provider leading the AAM-SHC team for comprehensive primary health care.
    • Staff nurses and LHVs (health supervisors) at PHCs; public health nurses at CHCs and district level.
  • Expanded roles – NCD screening, mental health, elderly and palliative care, tele-consultation, digital records, school health, disaster response.
  • Education – community health nursing is a core subject in all nursing programmes; M.Sc. and Ph.D. programmes in community health nursing; nurse practitioner programmes.
  • Challenges – shortage and uneven distribution of staff, heavy workload and reporting burden, inadequate supervision and transport, limited career growth, and difficult working conditions in remote areas.
  • Opportunities – Ayushman Bharat, NHM, digital health and greater recognition of nurses as leaders of primary health care.

Lessons from history for community health nursing

  • Great improvements in health came from sanitation, safe water, nutrition and education, not only from hospitals – prevention remains the core of community health nursing.
  • Women health visitors and dais were the first community health workers in India; today's ANMs, ASHAs and CHOs continue their work of reaching mothers and children at home.
  • Success needs community participation, intersectoral coordination and political commitment, as shown by smallpox and polio eradication.
  • Equity matters – services must reach the poorest, rural, tribal and urban slum populations first.

Nursing importance

  • Knowing how public health developed – from sanitation and epidemic control to primary health care and universal health coverage – helps the community health nurse understand her place in the health system and the value of prevention, community participation and equity.

Conclusion Public health is the science and art of preventing disease and promoting health through organised community effort; community health refers to the health of a defined population; and community health nursing combines nursing, public health and social assistance for population health. From ancient sanitation, the sanitary awakening, germ theory and Alma-Ata worldwide, and from sanitary commissions, health visitors and the Bhore Committee to NHM and Ayushman Bharat in India, community health nursing has grown into a network of ASHAs, ANMs, CHOs, LHVs and public health nurses who form the backbone of primary health care.

question: (a) Define health indicators and state the characteristics of an ideal indicator. (3 marks) (b) Classify health indicators with examples. (8 marks) (c) Explain the uses of health indicators, with the current values of important indicators in India. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Classification of health indicators
labels: mortality; morbidity; disability; nutritional status; health care delivery; utilisation rates; social and mental health; environmental; socio-economic; health policy; quality of life (PQLI

answer_html:
(a) Definition and characteristics (3 marks) Definition – health indicators are variables that help to measure changes, directly or indirectly, in the health status of a community and in the factors affecting it (WHO). Health cannot be measured directly, so indicators are used to describe it, compare areas and times, and monitor programmes.

Characteristics of an ideal indicator

  1. Valid – actually measures what it is supposed to measure.
  2. Reliable – gives the same result when measured by different people at different times under similar conditions.
  3. Sensitive – reflects changes in the situation.
  4. Specific – reflects changes only in the situation concerned.
  5. Feasible – data are available or can be collected without undue cost.
  6. Relevant – contributes to understanding the problem and to decision-making.
  7. Objective and simple to calculate and interpret.

(b) Classification with examples (8 marks)

  1. Mortality indicators
    • Crude death rate, life expectancy at birth, infant mortality rate (IMR), neonatal mortality rate, under-five mortality rate, child mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio (MMR), disease-specific death rates, proportional mortality rate.
    • IMR is considered the most sensitive indicator of the health status of a community and its socio-economic development.
  2. Morbidity indicators – incidence and prevalence rates, notification rates, OPD attendance rates, admission and readmission rates, average duration of hospital stay, spells of sickness.
  3. Disability indicators
    • Event-type – days of restricted activity, bed-disability days, work-loss and school-loss days.
    • Person-type – limitation of mobility or activities of daily living.
    • Composite measures – DALYs (disability-adjusted life years) = years of life lost through premature death + years lived with disability; HALE (health-adjusted life expectancy).
  4. Nutritional status indicators – stunting, wasting and underweight in children under five, low birth weight, prevalence of anaemia, BMI of adults.
  5. Health care delivery indicators – doctor–population and nurse–population ratios, population per health centre, population per hospital bed, population per health worker.
  6. Utilisation rates – full immunisation coverage, institutional deliveries, antenatal care coverage, contraceptive prevalence rate, bed-occupancy rate.
  7. Indicators of social and mental health – suicide, homicide, road traffic accidents, alcohol and drug use, violence and crime rates.
  8. Environmental indicators – proportion of population with access to safe drinking water and sanitation, air and noise pollution levels.
  9. Socio-economic indicators – per capita income, literacy (especially female literacy), unemployment, family size, housing (persons per room), dependency ratio.
  10. Health policy indicators – proportion of GDP and of government budget spent on health, political commitment, coverage of primary health care.
  11. Indicators of quality of life
    • Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI) – combines infant mortality, life expectancy at age one and literacy on a 0–100 scale.
    • Human Development Index (HDI) – combines life expectancy at birth, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and income (GNI per capita); India ranked 130 of 193 countries (HDI 0.685) in the Human Development Report 2025.
  12. Other indicators – social indicators of basic needs, "Health for All" and SDG indicators (e.g. universal health coverage service index).

(c) Uses and current values (4 marks) Uses of health indicators

  • To measure the health status of a community and identify its health problems and needs.
  • To compare health status between areas, groups and countries, and over time.
  • To plan, prioritise and allocate resources for health services.
  • To monitor and evaluate health programmes and progress towards targets (NHP 2017, SDGs).
  • To guide research and policy.

Current values of important indicators in India

  • Crude birth rate 18.4 and crude death rate 6.4 per 1,000 population, total fertility rate 1.9 (below replacement), IMR 25 per 1,000 live births (Sample Registration System, 2023).
  • Neonatal mortality rate about 19 and under-five mortality rate about 29 per 1,000 live births (SRS 2023).
  • MMR 88 per 1,00,000 live births (SRS 2021–23), with the latest bulletin for 2022–24 showing a marginal fall to 87.
  • Life expectancy at birth about 70 years.
  • NFHS-6 (2023–24) – stunting 29.3%, wasting 19.0%, underweight 31.8%; full immunisation 87.1%; institutional deliveries 90.6%.

Definitions and formulas of important indicators

  • Crude birth rate (CBR) = number of live births in a year ÷ mid-year population × 1,000.
  • Crude death rate (CDR) = number of deaths in a year ÷ mid-year population × 1,000.
  • Infant mortality rate (IMR) = deaths of infants below 1 year in a year ÷ live births in the same year × 1,000.
  • Neonatal mortality rate (NMR) = deaths of infants within the first 28 days of life ÷ live births × 1,000.
  • Under-five mortality rate (U5MR) = deaths of children below 5 years ÷ live births × 1,000.
  • Maternal mortality ratio (MMR) = maternal deaths (during pregnancy or within 42 days of its end, from causes related to or aggravated by pregnancy) ÷ live births × 1,00,000.
  • Total fertility rate (TFR) – the average number of children a woman would have if she passed through her reproductive years (15–49) bearing children at the current age-specific fertility rates; 2.1 is the replacement level.
  • Incidence rate = new cases during a period ÷ population at risk × 1,000; prevalence = all existing cases at a point or period ÷ total population × 100 or 1,000.

Limitations of health indicators

  • Data may be incomplete or inaccurate (under-registration of births and deaths, poor reporting).
  • National averages hide large differences between states, districts, rural–urban areas and social groups.
  • No single indicator reflects all dimensions of health; several must be used together.
  • Positive health and quality of life are difficult to measure.

Sources of data for health indicators in India

  • Census (every ten years) – population size, age and sex composition, literacy, housing.
  • Sample Registration System (SRS) – annual birth, death, fertility, infant and maternal mortality rates.
  • Civil Registration System – registration of births and deaths; Medical Certification of Cause of Death.
  • National Family Health Survey (NFHS) – fertility, family planning, maternal and child health, nutrition, immunisation.
  • Health Management Information System (HMIS) and programme portals (RCH, Ni-kshay, NCD portal) – service delivery data reported by health workers.
  • Disease surveillance (IDSP/IHIP), hospital records, national sample surveys and special studies.

Nursing importance

  • The community health nurse collects much of the data on which indicators are based (births, deaths, immunisation, ANC, nutrition) through registers and HMIS; accurate recording and use of these indicators help her identify priority problems in her area and plan care.

Conclusion Health indicators are measurable variables that reflect the health of a community; ideal indicators are valid, reliable, sensitive, specific, feasible and relevant. They include mortality, morbidity, disability, nutritional, health care delivery, utilisation, social, environmental, socio-economic, policy and quality-of-life indicators such as PQLI and HDI. They are used to assess, compare, plan, monitor and evaluate health – and India's current figures (IMR 25, MMR about 88, TFR 1.9) show both progress and the work that remains.

question: Explain the concept of community and its characteristics, and the community as a client.
answer_html:
Definition A community is a group of people living in a defined area, sharing common values, interests and needs, interacting with one another and having a sense of belonging, with institutions (schools, health centres, Panchayat) to meet their needs. WHO describes it as a social group determined by geographical boundaries and/or common values and interests.

Characteristics of a community

  1. People – a group of individuals and families.
  2. Place (territory) – a defined geographical area (village, ward, town), though some communities are not geographical.
  3. Common values, culture and interests – language, religion, customs and traditions.
  4. Interaction and interdependence – members communicate and depend on each other.
  5. Sense of belonging ("we-feeling") and shared identity.
  6. Social system and institutions – family, Panchayat or municipal ward, schools, health services, religious bodies, markets, transport.
  7. Common needs and problems, and the ability to act together to solve them.
  8. Leadership and organisation – formal (sarpanch, ward member) and informal leaders.

Types of community

  • Geographic (geopolitical) communities – rural (villages; agriculture; close relationships; fewer services), urban (towns, cities; slums; diverse population; more services but crowding and pollution), tribal (distinct culture, often in hilly and forest areas).
  • Communities of interest or function – people sharing a common concern or activity (factory workers, students, women's self-help groups, persons living with HIV).
  • Communities of solution – people who come together to solve a common problem (a watershed committee, a village water and sanitation committee).

The community as a client

  • In community health nursing, the whole community is the client – not only the individual or family.
  • The nurse assesses the health of the whole community (population characteristics, environment, health status, resources and services – a community diagnosis), identifies priority problems, plans and implements programmes with the community, and evaluates changes in the community's health.
  • The community is also a partner – its members take part in identifying needs, planning, decision-making and action (community participation), which ensures that programmes are acceptable and sustainable.

Implications for community health nursing

  • Understand the culture, beliefs, leaders and resources of the community before planning.
  • Work with VHSNCs, Mahila Arogya Samitis, self-help groups, Panchayats, schools and NGOs.
  • Focus on equity – reach vulnerable groups (women, children, elderly, migrants, tribal and slum dwellers).
  • Promote self-reliance rather than dependence on services.

Conclusion A community is a group of people in a defined area or with shared interests who interact, share values and needs and have a sense of belonging. Communities may be geographic (rural, urban, tribal), of interest or of solution. In community health nursing the community is both the client – whose health is assessed and improved – and the partner whose participation makes programmes successful.

question: Explain health promotion – its concept, the Ottawa Charter and the role of the community health nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Health promotion is "the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health" (WHO, Ottawa Charter, 1986). It goes beyond preventing disease – it aims at positive health and well-being by working on the determinants of health (education, income, environment, lifestyle and services).

The Ottawa Charter (First International Conference on Health Promotion, 1986) Five action areas

  1. Build healthy public policy – laws and policies that support health (tobacco control laws, food safety standards, helmet laws, taxes on tobacco and sugary drinks).
  2. Create supportive environments – safe, clean living and working conditions (sanitation, safe water, green spaces, safe roads).
  3. Strengthen community action – communities identify their priorities and act on them (VHSNCs, self-help groups, Panchayats).
  4. Develop personal skills – health education and life skills so that people can make healthy choices.
  5. Reorient health services – from curative care towards prevention and health promotion, with people-centred services.

Three basic strategies – advocate (for health-friendly conditions), enable (equal opportunities and resources to achieve full health potential) and mediate (between different sectors and interests).

Approaches to health promotion

  • Health education – changing knowledge, attitudes and behaviour.
  • Environmental modification – safe water, sanitation, housing, clean air.
  • Nutritional interventions – food fortification, supplementary nutrition, nutrition education.
  • Lifestyle and behavioural change – physical activity, healthy diet, avoidance of tobacco and alcohol, stress management.
  • Settings approach – health-promoting schools, workplaces, hospitals, cities and villages.

Health promotion initiatives in India (examples)

  • Fit India Movement, Eat Right India (less salt, sugar and fat; safe food), Swachh Bharat Mission, school health and wellness programme, tobacco-free educational institutions, yoga and wellness activities at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Educator – teach individuals, families and groups about healthy behaviours.
  • Advocate – for policies and environments that support health.
  • Mobiliser – involve the community, leaders and self-help groups in health action.
  • Role model – practise healthy behaviours herself.
  • Coordinator – work with schools, Anganwadis, Panchayats and other sectors.
  • Screening and early detection combined with promotive advice at every contact.

Conclusion Health promotion enables people to take control of and improve their health. The Ottawa Charter's five action areas – healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills and reoriented health services – with the strategies of advocacy, enabling and mediation, guide health promotion, and the community health nurse acts as educator, advocate, mobiliser, role model and coordinator.

question: Write Winslow's definition of public health.
answer_html:
C.-E. A. Winslow (1920) defined public health as "the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting physical health and efficiency through organised community efforts for:

  1. the sanitation of the environment,
  2. the control of community infections,
  3. the education of the individual in principles of personal hygiene,
  4. the organisation of medical and nursing services for the early diagnosis and preventive treatment of disease, and
  5. the development of social machinery which will ensure to every individual a standard of living adequate for the maintenance of health." The key idea is organised community effort for prevention and health promotion.

question: What is the Human Development Index (HDI)?
answer_html:
The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite index of human development published every year by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in the Human Development Report (introduced in 1990). Three dimensions

  1. A long and healthy life – life expectancy at birth.
  2. Knowledge – mean years of schooling of adults and expected years of schooling of children.
  3. A decent standard of living – gross national income (GNI) per capita (PPP US$). The value ranges from 0 to 1; countries are grouped as very high, high, medium and low human development. India's HDI was 0.685, ranked 130 of 193 countries (Human Development Report 2025), in the medium category.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Concepts of Community Health and Community Health Nursing
question: What is the Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI)?
answer_html:
The Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI), developed by Morris D. Morris (1979), measures the quality of life of a population by combining three indicators:

  1. Infant mortality rate.
  2. Life expectancy at age one.
  3. Basic literacy rate (percentage of population aged 15 and above who are literate). Each indicator is converted to a scale of 0 to 100 and the three are averaged with equal weight. The PQLI ranges from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). It reflects results of development (health and education) rather than income, and shows that a high income does not always mean a good quality of life.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Concepts of Community Health and Community Health Nursing
question: What is the spectrum of health?
answer_html:
The spectrum of health means that health and disease are not two separate states but points on a continuum, and a person's position on it changes from time to time (health is a dynamic process). The continuum runs from: Positive health → Better health → Freedom from sickness → Unrecognised sickness → Mild sickness → Severe sickness → Death.

  • Many people in the community are in the "unrecognised sickness" zone (the hidden part of the iceberg of disease).
  • Implication for nursing – the aim is to move people towards positive health through health promotion, early detection and timely treatment, and not only to treat those who are severely ill.

question: (a) Describe the organisation of the health care delivery system in India at the central, state and district levels. (5 marks) (b) Explain the rural health infrastructure – village level, sub-centre, primary health centre and community health centre – with population norms and functions. (7 marks) (c) Explain the urban health care system and the other agencies providing health care. (3 marks)

Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Central Council of Health and Family Welfare

answer_html:
Introduction Health is a State subject under the Constitution, but the Union government plays a major role through policy, funding and national programmes. Health care in India is delivered through the public sector (a three-tier primary–secondary–tertiary system), the private sector, AYUSH, voluntary agencies and health insurance schemes.

(a) Organisation at the central, state and district levels (5 marks) 1. Central level

  • Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) – headed by a Cabinet Minister, with the Department of Health and Family Welfare and the Department of Health Research (ICMR); the Ministry of AYUSH looks after traditional systems.
  • Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) – the technical adviser on medical and public health matters; supervises central institutions.
  • Central Council of Health and Family Welfare – a policy forum of Union and State Health Ministers.
  • Functions – national health policy, national health programmes (through the National Health Mission), medical and nursing education (NMC, Indian Nursing Council), drug regulation (CDSCO), international health, census and vital statistics coordination, central institutions (AIIMS, NCDC, NIMHANS).

2. State level

  • State Ministry of Health and the Directorate of Health Services (and Directorate of Medical Education); State Health Society under NHM.
  • Functions – implementing national and state programmes, managing hospitals and health centres, recruiting staff, training (including ANM and GNM schools), supervision and reporting.

3. District level

  • The district is the key unit of health administration; the District Health Officer / Chief Medical Officer heads health services with programme officers (RCH, immunisation, TB, NCD, vector-borne diseases), supported by the District Health Society.
  • The district hospital provides secondary care; block (taluka) health offices supervise PHCs and sub-centres.

(b) Rural health infrastructure – population norms and functions (7 marks) (As per the Indian Public Health Standards, 2022) 1. Village level

  • ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) – about one per 1,000 population; link between the community and the health system – mobilising for ANC, institutional delivery, immunisation, home-based newborn care, first-aid and drug kit (ORS, IFA, contraceptives), TB and NCD support.
  • Anganwadi worker (ICDS) – supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring, preschool education, referral.
  • Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) and the monthly Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Day (VHSND).

2. Sub Health Centre – Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM-SHC)

  • Population – 5,000 in plain areas, 3,000 in hilly, tribal and difficult areas.
  • Staff – Community Health Officer (CHO), MPW (female) / ANM, MPW (male), with ASHAs.
  • Functions – the most peripheral contact point providing comprehensive primary health care: antenatal and postnatal care, immunisation, family planning, child health, management of minor ailments, screening and follow-up of NCDs (hypertension, diabetes, oral, breast and cervical cancer), communicable disease control, mental health, elderly and palliative care, essential medicines and point-of-care tests, teleconsultation, health promotion (yoga, wellness), records and reports.

3. Primary Health Centre – Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM-PHC)

  • Population – 30,000 (plain), 20,000 (hilly/tribal); supervises about 6 sub-centres; usually 4–6 beds; many function 24×7 for deliveries.
  • Staff – medical officer(s), staff nurses, pharmacist, laboratory technician, health supervisors (LHV / male), clerk and support staff.
  • Functions – first contact with a doctor; outpatient and emergency care, deliveries and newborn care, family planning services, laboratory tests, implementation of national programmes, referral, health education, supervision and training of sub-centre staff and ASHAs, records and HMIS reporting.

4. Community Health Centre (CHC)

  • Population – 1,20,000 (plain), 80,000 (hilly/tribal); serves as a referral centre for about 4 PHCs; about 30 beds (more in some).
  • Staff – specialists (physician, surgeon, obstetrician–gynaecologist, paediatrician, anaesthetist), dental surgeon, nurses, pharmacists, laboratory and radiology staff.
  • Functions – first referral unit (FRU) with emergency obstetric care (caesarean section), blood storage, newborn stabilisation unit, X-ray and laboratory, emergency and specialist care, national programme services.

5. Sub-district (taluka) and district hospitals – secondary care with more specialities, sick newborn care units, blood banks, dialysis, and referral to medical college and tertiary hospitals.

(c) Urban health care and other agencies (3 marks) Urban health (National Urban Health Mission, 2013)

  • Urban Ayushman Arogya Mandirs for small populations in slums and vulnerable areas.
  • Urban PHC for about 50,000 population and Urban CHC for about 2.5 lakh (5 lakh in metros); municipal hospitals and dispensaries.
  • Urban ASHAs for slum populations and Mahila Arogya Samitis (women's health committees).

Other agencies

  • Private sector – hospitals, nursing homes, clinics and practitioners (providing a large share of outpatient care).
  • AYUSH – Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy services, often co-located with PHCs and CHCs.
  • Voluntary and non-governmental organisations – Indian Red Cross Society, Bharat Sevak Samaj, Hind Kusht Nivaran Sangh, trusts and mission hospitals.
  • Health insurance and social security – ESI (Employees' State Insurance), CGHS (Central Government Health Scheme), PM-JAY (Ayushman Bharat), state schemes (e.g. Mahatma Jyotiba Phule Jan Arogya Yojana in Maharashtra).
  • Other government departments – Railways, Defence and Labour health services.
  • International agencies – WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank and others (technical and financial support).

Role of the nurse in the health care delivery system

  • Provides services at every level – ASHA facilitator, ANM, CHO, staff nurse, LHV, public health nurse and nurse manager.
  • Ensures continuity of care and referral between levels; supervises and trains peripheral workers; maintains records and reports; links communities with services and schemes.

Referral system

  • Meaning – sending a patient from one level of care to a higher (or more appropriate) level for services that are not available at the first level, and sending him back (back-referral) with advice for follow-up.
  • Chain – village (ASHA) → AAM-SHC → AAM-PHC → CHC/FRU → sub-district/district hospital → medical college; emergency transport through 108/102 ambulances.
  • Importance – right care at the right level, reduced overcrowding of higher hospitals, continuity of care and cost-effectiveness.
  • Problems – self-referral to higher hospitals, poor communication between levels, lack of transport, non-availability of specialists, missing back-referral information.
  • Nurse's role – identify cases needing referral early (danger signs), give pre-referral care, write a clear referral slip, arrange transport, inform the receiving facility, and follow up the patient after return.

Nursing importance

  • Knowing the levels, norms and functions of health facilities helps the nurse refer patients correctly, use available services and identify gaps in her area.

Conclusion India's health care delivery system is organised at the central (MoHFW, DGHS), state (health directorates) and district levels. In rural areas it forms a three-tier network – ASHAs and VHSNCs at the village, AAM-Sub Health Centres for 5,000 (3,000) population, AAM-PHCs for 30,000 (20,000) and CHCs/FRUs for 1,20,000 (80,000), backed by district and tertiary hospitals – while NUHM provides urban AAMs, UPHCs and UCHCs. Private, AYUSH, voluntary, insurance and other agencies complete the system, with nurses working at every level.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: (a) Define health planning and explain the steps of the health planning cycle. (5 marks) (b) Explain health planning in India through the Five-Year Plans and NITI Aayog. (3 marks) (c) Describe the recommendations of the major health committees in India. (7 marks)
tags: High Level Expert Group on UHC 2011

diagram.caption: The health planning cycle
labels: analysis of health situation – establishment of objectives and goals – assessment of resources – fixing priorities – write-up of formulated plan – programming and implementation – monitoring – evaluation – back to situation analysis

answer_html:
(a) Definition and steps of the planning cycle (5 marks) Definition Planning is "a process of analysing and understanding a system, formulating its goals and objectives, assessing its capacities, formulating alternative courses of action and choosing the best one, implementing it, and monitoring and evaluating its results." Health planning is the orderly process of defining community health problems, identifying unmet needs and resources, establishing priority goals and setting out administrative action to achieve them. Its purpose is to make the best use of limited resources to improve the health of the people.

Steps of the health planning cycle

  1. Analysis of the health situation – collecting information on the population, health status (indicators), health problems, health services and their use, and the socio-economic and environmental conditions; this gives the "community diagnosis".
  2. Establishment of objectives and goals – what is to be achieved (e.g. reduce IMR from 25 to 20 in five years); objectives should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART).
  3. Assessment of resources – manpower, money, materials, buildings, equipment and time available, and those needed.
  4. Fixing priorities – problems are ranked by magnitude, severity, vulnerability to intervention, cost and community concern.
  5. Write-up of the formulated plan – a detailed written plan with activities, responsibilities, budget and timeframe.
  6. Programming and implementation – organising and carrying out the activities; delegation, coordination, supervision and training.
  7. Monitoring – continuous day-to-day follow-up of activities to ensure they are carried out as planned, and correction of deviations.
  8. Evaluation – measuring the effectiveness and impact of the plan (whether objectives were achieved), which provides information for the next planning cycle.

(b) Health planning in India – Five-Year Plans and NITI Aayog (3 marks)

  • After independence, the Planning Commission (1950) prepared Five-Year Plans; health was planned within them, guided by the recommendations of health committees.
    • First Plan (1951–56) – control of communicable diseases, water supply and sanitation, primary health centres, family planning.
    • Successive plans expanded PHCs and national programmes, training of multipurpose workers, the Minimum Needs Programme (5th Plan), primary health care and Health for All (6th Plan), and later the National Rural Health Mission (11th Plan, 2007–12) and universal health coverage (12th Plan, 2012–17).
  • In 2015 the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India), which works through long-term vision documents, strategy papers and indices (e.g. the SDG India Index and the State Health Index) in cooperation with the states. Health is now planned through the National Health Policy 2017, the National Health Mission and Ayushman Bharat.

(c) Recommendations of major health committees (7 marks)

  1. Bhore Committee (Health Survey and Development Committee, 1943–46; Sir Joseph Bhore)
    • Integration of preventive and curative services at all levels.
    • Development of primary health centres in two stages – a short-term plan of a PHC for about 40,000 population, and a long-term "three million plan" with primary health units of 75 beds for 10,000–20,000 people, secondary and district units.
    • Major changes in medical education – three months' training in preventive and social medicine to produce "social physicians"; emphasis on community participation.
  2. Mudaliar Committee (Health Survey and Planning Committee, 1959–61; Dr A. L. Mudaliar)
    • Consolidate the existing PHCs before expanding; strengthen sub-divisional and district hospitals.
    • Each PHC should cover not more than 40,000 population; improve the quality of PHC services; constitute an All India Health Service.
  3. Chadah Committee (1963) – for the maintenance phase of malaria eradication, one basic health worker per 10,000 population for house-to-house visits (malaria surveillance, vital statistics and family planning).
  4. Mukerji Committee (1965 and 1966) – recommended separate staff for family planning and delinking malaria work from family planning; strengthening of basic health services.
  5. Jungalwalla Committee (1967; Integration of Health Services) – unified cadre, common seniority, equal pay for equal work, special pay for special work, and no private practice by government doctors.
  6. Kartar Singh Committee (Committee on Multipurpose Workers, 1973)
    • Replace single-purpose workers with multipurpose health workers (male and female).
    • One sub-centre for 5,000 population with one male and one female health worker; a PHC for 50,000 population with 16 sub-centres; health assistants (male and female) to supervise them (one for 3–4 workers).
  7. Shrivastava Committee (Group on Medical Education and Support Manpower, 1975)
    • Create bands of para-professional and semi-professional health workers from the community itself (school teachers, postmasters, village volunteers).
    • Two cadres of health workers and health assistants between the community and the PHC; a referral services complex linking PHC, sub-divisional/taluk and district hospitals; a Medical and Health Education Commission.
    • This led to the Rural Health Scheme (1977) with community health volunteers (village health guides).
  8. Bajaj Committee (Expert Committee on Health Manpower Planning, Production and Management, 1986) – a National Health Manpower Policy, an educational commission for health sciences, health manpower cells at centre and states, and vocational courses in health.
  9. High Level Expert Group on Universal Health Coverage (2011; Dr K. Srinath Reddy) – increase public spending on health, free essential medicines and diagnostics, a strengthened primary care system and human resources, and a framework for UHC.

Types and approaches of planning in India today

  • Short-term (annual) and long-term (perspective) plans.
  • Decentralised, bottom-up planning – under NHM, village and block health plans are compiled into District Health Action Plans, then into the State Programme Implementation Plan (PIP), which is approved by the Union Ministry; this allows local needs and priorities to be included.
  • Intersectoral planning – coordination with water supply, sanitation, education, nutrition (ICDS), Panchayati Raj and rural development.
  • Evidence-based planning – using HMIS, NFHS, SRS and surveillance data, and gap analysis against IPHS.
  • Participatory planning – involving VHSNCs, Rogi Kalyan Samitis, Mahila Arogya Samitis and community monitoring.

Planning at the level of the community health nurse – the nurse applies the same cycle to her sub-centre area: she conducts a survey and prepares a community profile, identifies priority problems (e.g. low immunisation coverage in a hamlet), sets targets, plans outreach sessions and health education with ASHAs, and monitors progress through her registers every month.

Nursing importance

  • The present health system – PHCs, sub-centres with multipurpose workers, ASHAs and referral systems – grew out of these committees; the community health nurse uses the planning cycle to plan services for her own area, from situation analysis to evaluation.

Conclusion Health planning is the orderly process of defining health problems, setting objectives, assessing resources, fixing priorities, preparing and implementing a plan, and monitoring and evaluating it. In India health was planned through Five-Year Plans and is now guided by NITI Aayog and the National Health Policy. The Bhore, Mudaliar, Chadah, Mukerji, Jungalwalla, Kartar Singh, Shrivastava and Bajaj Committees and the HLEG on UHC shaped the integrated, primary-care-based health system that community health nurses work in today.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: Explain universal health coverage (UHC).
answer_html:
Definition Universal health coverage (UHC) means that all people have access to the full range of quality health services they need – promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative and palliative – when and where they need them, without suffering financial hardship (WHO). It is target 3.8 of the Sustainable Development Goals.

Three dimensions (the "UHC cube")

  1. Population coverage – who is covered? – extending services to everyone, especially the poor and vulnerable.
  2. Service coverage – which services are covered? – the range and quality of essential services (maternal and child health, communicable and non-communicable disease care, mental health, emergency care).
  3. Financial protection – what proportion of the cost is covered? – reducing out-of-pocket expenditure so that people are not pushed into poverty by health costs.

Key principles

  • Equity and non-discrimination; quality of services; people-centred primary health care as the foundation; financial risk protection through public funding and pooling; community participation and accountability.

UHC is not

  • Free coverage for every possible intervention, only health financing, or only individual treatment – it also includes population services such as health promotion, safe water and sanitation.

Measurement

  • UHC service coverage index (tracer indicators such as immunisation, ANC, family planning, TB and HIV treatment, hypertension and diabetes care, hospital access, health workforce).
  • Catastrophic health expenditure – households spending a large share of income on health.

UHC in India

  • The High Level Expert Group on UHC (2011) recommended increasing public health spending, free essential medicines and diagnostics and strengthening primary care.
  • The National Health Policy 2017 aims at UHC through assured comprehensive primary care, raising public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP and reducing catastrophic expenditure.
  • Measures – National Health Mission (free maternal and child services under JSSK, free drugs and diagnostics initiative), Ayushman Bharat – Ayushman Arogya Mandirs for comprehensive primary care and PM-JAY health insurance of ₹5 lakh per family per year for hospitalisation (now covering all persons aged 70 years and above), state insurance schemes, ESI and CGHS, Jan Aushadhi generic medicine stores, and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission.

Challenges – low public spending, high out-of-pocket expenditure, shortage of health workers, uneven quality, urban–rural gaps and a large private sector.

Role of the nurse

  • Delivering comprehensive primary health care (as ANM or CHO), reaching unreached groups, enrolling families in schemes (Ayushman card), health education, NCD screening, follow-up, maintaining quality and records, and advocating for equity.

Conclusion UHC means access for all to the quality health services they need without financial hardship, measured along the three dimensions of population, services and financial protection. India is moving towards UHC through NHM, Ayushman Bharat (AAMs and PM-JAY), free drugs and diagnostics and digital health, with nurses at the front line of primary care.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: Explain the National Health Policy, 2017.
tags: public health expenditure 2.5 percent of GDP
answer_html:
Introduction The National Health Policy 2017 (the third after 1983 and 2002) was approved by the Union Cabinet in March 2017 to respond to changing health priorities – the rising burden of NCDs, the growth of the health care industry and high costs of care.

Goal "The attainment of the highest possible level of health and well-being for all at all ages, through a preventive and promotive health care orientation in all developmental policies, and universal access to good quality health care services without anyone having to face financial hardship."

Key principles

  • Professionalism, integrity and ethics; equity; affordability; universality; patient-centred and quality care; accountability; inclusive partnerships; pluralism (including AYUSH); decentralisation; dynamism and adaptiveness.

Important targets

  • Life expectancy – increase from 67.5 to 70 years by 2025.
  • TFR – 2.1 at national and state levels by 2025.
  • Under-five mortality – 23 by 2025; MMR – 100 by 2020; IMR – 28 by 2019; neonatal mortality – 16 and stillbirths to single digit by 2025.
  • HIV – 90:90:90 by 2020; elimination of leprosy (2018), kala-azar and lymphatic filariasis (2017); TB cure rate above 85%.
  • NCDs – reduce premature mortality from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes and chronic respiratory diseases by 25% by 2025; reduce tobacco use (by 15% by 2020 and 30% by 2025).
  • Health financing – increase public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by 2025; states to spend more than 8% of their budget on health; reduce catastrophic household expenditure by 25% by 2025.
  • Health systems – ensure availability of paramedics and doctors as per IPHS norms in high-priority districts; full functional HMIS.

Key policy directions

  • Comprehensive primary health care through Health and Wellness Centres (now Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) – the foundation of the health system.
  • Free drugs, diagnostics and emergency care in public hospitals; strategic purchasing of secondary and tertiary care from public and private providers.
  • Focus on preventive and promotive health – the "Swasth Nagrik Abhiyan", seven priority areas such as Swachh Bharat, balanced diet and exercise, tobacco and alcohol control, Nirbhaya Nari (violence against women), reducing stress, workplace safety and reducing pollution.
  • Mainstreaming AYUSH; strengthening human resources (including mid-level providers and nurse practitioners); digital health; public–private partnerships; regulation of the private sector; research.

Role of the nurse

  • Implementing comprehensive primary care at AAMs as CHOs and ANMs; achieving maternal and child health targets; NCD screening; health promotion; data recording; and taking up expanded roles such as nurse practitioners envisaged by the policy.

Conclusion The National Health Policy 2017 aims at the highest possible level of health and well-being for all, with universal access to quality care without financial hardship. Its targets for life expectancy, fertility, child and maternal mortality, communicable disease elimination, NCDs, public spending (2.5% of GDP) and reduced catastrophic expenditure are pursued through comprehensive primary care at Health and Wellness Centres, free drugs and diagnostics, prevention and promotion, and stronger human resources, including nurses.

question: Explain the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) with special reference to health.
answer_html:
Introduction The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 global goals with 169 targets, adopted by all UN member states in September 2015 as the "2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development". They succeed the eight Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015) and aim to "leave no one behind" by ending poverty, protecting the planet and ensuring peace and prosperity for all by 2030.

The 17 SDGs

  1. No poverty. 2. Zero hunger. 3. Good health and well-being. 4. Quality education. 5. Gender equality. 6. Clean water and sanitation. 7. Affordable and clean energy. 8. Decent work and economic growth. 9. Industry, innovation and infrastructure. 10. Reduced inequalities. 11. Sustainable cities and communities. 12. Responsible consumption and production. 13. Climate action. 14. Life below water. 15. Life on land. 16. Peace, justice and strong institutions. 17. Partnerships for the goals.

SDG 3 – "Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages" – main targets (by 2030)

  • 3.1 Reduce the global maternal mortality ratio to less than 70 per 1,00,000 live births.
  • 3.2 End preventable deaths of newborns and under-fives – NMR 12 or less and U5MR 25 or less per 1,000 live births.
  • 3.3 End the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria and neglected tropical diseases; combat hepatitis, water-borne and other communicable diseases.
  • 3.4 Reduce premature mortality from NCDs by one-third and promote mental health and well-being.
  • 3.5 Strengthen prevention and treatment of substance abuse, including harmful use of alcohol.
  • 3.6 Halve global deaths and injuries from road traffic accidents.
  • 3.7 Universal access to sexual and reproductive health care, including family planning.
  • 3.8 Achieve universal health coverage, including financial risk protection and access to essential medicines and vaccines.
  • 3.9 Reduce deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and air, water and soil pollution.
  • Means of implementation – tobacco control (WHO FCTC), research and access to vaccines and medicines, health workforce development, and preparedness for health emergencies.

Other health-related goals – SDG 2 (nutrition – ending malnutrition), SDG 5 (ending violence against women, child marriage), SDG 6 (water and sanitation), SDG 11 (air quality, safe transport), SDG 13 (climate change).

SDGs in India

  • NITI Aayog coordinates implementation and publishes the SDG India Index; the national composite score rose to 71 in 2023–24 (from 66 in 2020–21).
  • Programmes such as NHM, Ayushman Bharat, POSHAN Abhiyaan, Swachh Bharat, Jal Jeevan Mission, TB Mukt Bharat and NP-NCD contribute to the health targets.

Role of the nurse

  • Working towards SDG 3 through maternal and newborn care, immunisation, nutrition, communicable and NCD control, mental health and family planning; promoting water, sanitation and hygiene; and recording data for monitoring progress.

Conclusion The SDGs are 17 interlinked goals to be achieved by 2030. SDG 3 targets include MMR below 70, NMR 12 and U5MR 25 or less, ending epidemics of AIDS, TB and malaria, reducing NCD mortality by one-third, halving road deaths and achieving universal health coverage; community health nurses are central to reaching these targets.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: Explain the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and the National Health Mission (NHM).
answer_html:
Introduction The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) was launched on 12 April 2005 to provide accessible, affordable, accountable, effective and reliable health care to the rural population, especially vulnerable groups, with special focus on 18 high-focus states. In 2013, NRHM and the newly launched National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) became sub-missions of the National Health Mission (NHM).

Goal and objectives

  • Reduce IMR and MMR; universal access to public health services (women's and child health, water, sanitation, immunisation, nutrition).
  • Prevention and control of communicable and non-communicable diseases, including locally endemic diseases.
  • Population stabilisation, gender and demographic balance.
  • Revitalise local health traditions and mainstream AYUSH; promote healthy lifestyles.
  • Access to integrated, comprehensive primary health care.

Core strategies and components

  1. ASHA – a trained female community health activist for every village (about 1 per 1,000 population).
  2. Decentralised planning and community participation – Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Committees, district health plans, community monitoring.
  3. Strengthening of sub-centres, PHCs and CHCs to Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS); untied funds and annual maintenance grants.
  4. Rogi Kalyan Samitis (patient welfare committees) for hospital management.
  5. Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) – cash incentive for institutional delivery; Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK, 2011) – free delivery including caesarean section, free drugs, diagnostics, diet, blood and transport for pregnant women and sick infants.
  6. Mobile medical units and the national ambulance service (108 for emergencies, 102 for pregnant women and children).
  7. Additional staff on contract – ANMs, staff nurses, doctors and specialists; training.
  8. Integration of vertical programmes (RCH, disease control) under one umbrella; AYUSH co-location.

National Health Mission (from 2013)

  • NRHM + NUHM; programme pillars – RMNCH+A (reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health), communicable disease control, NCD control, and health system strengthening.
  • Key initiatives – Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK), Home-Based Newborn Care, Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (ANC on the 9th of every month), free drugs and diagnostics service initiatives, Kayakalp (cleanliness awards), LaQshya (labour room quality), National Quality Assurance Standards, Mission Indradhanush, and comprehensive primary health care through Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.

Achievements

  • Large rise in institutional deliveries and immunisation; marked fall in IMR and MMR; strengthened infrastructure and workforce; community participation through ASHAs and VHSNCs.

Role of the nurse

  • ANMs, staff nurses and CHOs deliver NHM services; train and support ASHAs; organise VHSNDs and outreach; implement JSY/JSSK and other schemes; maintain RCH registers and HMIS data.

Conclusion NRHM (2005) transformed rural health care through ASHAs, decentralised planning, strengthening of facilities to IPHS, Rogi Kalyan Samitis, JSY and JSSK, ambulances and AYUSH mainstreaming. As part of NHM (with NUHM, 2013), it is now the main vehicle for RMNCH+A, disease control and health system strengthening in India.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: Explain Ayushman Bharat and its components.
answer_html:
Introduction Ayushman Bharat ("long-lived India"), launched in 2018, is the Government of India's flagship programme to move towards universal health coverage. It follows a continuum-of-care approach with two original components, later strengthened by digital and infrastructure missions.

1. Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly Health and Wellness Centres)

  • Existing sub-centres and PHCs (rural and urban) upgraded to provide comprehensive primary health care close to people's homes, free of cost; the first centre was opened in April 2018 (Bijapur, Chhattisgarh); more than 1.7 lakh are now functional.
  • Team at AAM-SHC – Community Health Officer (B.Sc. Nursing or trained mid-level provider), MPWs and ASHAs.
  • Expanded service packages – care in pregnancy and childbirth; neonatal and infant care; childhood and adolescent care; family planning and reproductive health; communicable diseases and national programmes; general outpatient care for common illnesses; screening and management of NCDs (hypertension, diabetes, common cancers); eye and ENT care; oral health; elderly and palliative care; emergency medical services; mental health.
  • Essential medicines and diagnostics, teleconsultation (e-Sanjeevani), wellness activities (yoga), and health promotion.

2. Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY)

  • Launched in September 2018 – the world's largest government-funded health assurance scheme.
  • Health cover of ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, cashless and paperless, at empanelled public and private hospitals across India (portable).
  • Covers poor and vulnerable families (identified from SECC data and state lists); from 2024 all senior citizens aged 70 years and above are eligible irrespective of income (Ayushman Vay Vandana card).
  • Includes pre- and post-hospitalisation expenses; no limit on family size or age; pre-existing diseases covered from day one; Ayushman cards for beneficiaries; implemented by the National Health Authority with state health agencies.

3. Supporting missions

  • Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (2021) – ABHA (health account) number, digital health records, registries of health facilities and professionals.
  • PM Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (2021) – strengthening critical care blocks, integrated public health laboratories and surveillance.

Role of the nurse

  • As CHO or ANM at AAMs – deliver the service packages, screen for NCDs, manage minor illnesses, provide teleconsultation support, maintain digital records, conduct wellness activities and home visits.
  • Help families obtain Ayushman/ABHA cards, explain entitlements, refer patients to empanelled hospitals and follow up after discharge.

Conclusion Ayushman Bharat combines comprehensive, free primary care through Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (led by CHOs) with financial protection for hospital care through PM-JAY (₹5 lakh per family per year, now including all aged 70+), supported by digital health and infrastructure missions – making nurses key players in India's journey towards universal health coverage.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: Write the steps of health planning.
answer_html:
Steps of the health planning cycle

  1. Analysis of the health situation – collecting data on population, health status, problems and services (community diagnosis).
  2. Establishment of objectives and goals – specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
  3. Assessment of resources – manpower, money, materials and time.
  4. Fixing priorities – according to magnitude, severity, feasibility and community concern.
  5. Write-up of the formulated plan – activities, responsibilities, budget and timeframe.
  6. Programming and implementation.
  7. Monitoring – continuous follow-up of activities.
  8. Evaluation – measuring achievement of objectives, which feeds into the next planning cycle.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: Write the important recommendations of the Bhore Committee.
tags: integration of preventive and curative services
answer_html:
The Bhore Committee (Health Survey and Development Committee, 1946), chaired by Sir Joseph Bhore, recommended:

  1. Integration of preventive and curative services at all administrative levels.
  2. Development of primary health centres – short-term: a PHC for about 40,000 population; long-term (three million plan): primary health units with 75-bed hospitals for 10,000–20,000 people, linked to secondary and district units.
  3. Major changes in medical education – three months' training in preventive and social medicine to prepare "social physicians".
  4. Community participation in health programmes and adequate health staff (including nurses and health visitors). It laid the foundation of the PHC-based health system in India.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: Who is an ASHA? List her roles.
answer_html:
ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) is a trained female community health activist introduced under NRHM (2005) – generally one for every 1,000 population – selected from the same village (preferably a married, widowed or divorced woman aged 25–45 years, literate, with good communication skills) and accountable to the Panchayat. Roles

  1. Link worker – between the community and the health system; escorts women and children to health facilities.
  2. Facilitator and mobiliser – for ANC, institutional delivery, immunisation, family planning, VHSNDs; creates health awareness.
  3. Home visits – home-based newborn and young child care; follow-up of TB and NCD patients.
  4. Provider of first-contact care – drug kit: ORS, zinc, IFA, paracetamol, contraceptives, pregnancy test kits; first aid.
  5. Activist – mobilises the community on health and sanitation; member of the VHSNC; records and reports.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: What is a Rogi Kalyan Samiti?
answer_html:
A Rogi Kalyan Samiti (RKS – patient welfare committee) is a registered society set up under NRHM at district hospitals, CHCs and PHCs to involve the community in the management of public health facilities.

  • Members – elected representatives (Panchayat/municipal), local NGOs, health officials and community members; chaired by the district collector or elected head at higher levels.
  • Functions – manage funds (untied grants, user charges, donations), improve services and patient amenities (cleanliness, drinking water, waiting areas, equipment), ensure free services to the poor, monitor quality and handle grievances.
  • At the level of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, similar committees are called Jan Arogya Samitis.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Health Care Planning and Organization of Health Care at Various Levels
question: What are the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS)?
answer_html:
The Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) are a set of uniform standards prescribed by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to improve the quality of public health facilities.

  • First issued in 2007 under NRHM, revised in 2012 and 2022.
  • They lay down norms for infrastructure, human resources, services, drugs, diagnostics, equipment, quality and governance for sub health centres (AAM-SHC), PHCs, CHCs, sub-district and district hospitals, both rural and urban.
  • IPHS 2022 incorporates comprehensive primary health care at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, National Quality Assurance Standards, IT-enabled services and population norms (e.g. SHC for 5,000 / 3,000; PHC for 30,000 / 20,000; CHC for 1,20,000 / 80,000).
  • They are used for planning, monitoring and assessing facilities.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: (a) Define safe and wholesome water and list the sources of water. (3 marks) (b) Explain the purification of water on a large scale and on a small (household) scale. (8 marks) (c) Explain the water-borne diseases and the role of the community health nurse in ensuring safe water supply. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Slow sand filter
labels: supernatant raw water (1–1.5 m) over a vital (schmutzdecke) layer on fine sand bed (about 1 m)
under-drainage system leading to the outlet

answer_html:
(a) Definition and sources (3 marks) Safe and wholesome water is water that is:

  • Free from pathogenic organisms;
  • Free from harmful chemical substances (arsenic, fluoride in excess, nitrates, heavy metals);
  • Pleasant to taste – free from colour, odour and turbidity; and
  • Usable for domestic purposes. Safe water is a basic human need and one of the most important determinants of health. The WHO recommends at least 50–100 litres per person per day for basic needs; Indian norms for rural piped supply under the Jal Jeevan Mission are 55 litres per person per day.

Sources of water

  1. Rain water – the purest natural source, but it collects impurities from the air and roofs; rain-water harvesting is encouraged.
  2. Surface water – rivers, streams, lakes, tanks, ponds and impounding reservoirs – easily polluted by sewage, industrial waste and animals; needs purification.
  3. Ground water – shallow wells (easily contaminated), deep wells, tube wells and bore wells, springs – usually safer but may contain excess fluoride, arsenic, iron or nitrates.

(b) Purification of water (8 marks) A. Large-scale purification (municipal water works)

  1. Storage – raw water is stored in reservoirs; natural purification occurs:
    • Physical – suspended impurities settle (about 90% in 24 hours).
    • Chemical – oxidation of organic matter by aerobic bacteria.
    • Biological – pathogenic organisms die (up to about 90% in 5–7 days); storage beyond 10–14 days allows algae to grow.
  2. Filtration
    • Slow sand (biological) filter
      • Raw water passes slowly through a bed of fine sand (about 1 m) over graded gravel.
      • A slimy "vital layer" (schmutzdecke) of algae, bacteria and protozoa forms on the sand surface within days and is the main purifying agent – it removes organic matter and 99.9% of bacteria.
      • Simple and cheap, but slow, needs large land area; cleaned by scraping the top layer.
    • Rapid sand (mechanical) filter
      • Coagulation – alum (aluminium sulphate) is added; rapid mixing, then flocculation (slow stirring) forms a sticky floc that traps impurities and bacteria.
      • Sedimentation in settling tanks.
      • Filtration through coarse sand at a high rate; filters are cleaned by backwashing.
      • Needs less space; suitable for turbid river water; widely used in Indian cities.
  3. Disinfection – chlorination
    • Chlorine kills pathogenic bacteria and viruses, oxidises iron, manganese and hydrogen sulphide, removes taste and odour and controls algae.
    • Principles – water should be clear (turbid water reduces effectiveness); the chlorine demand of the water must be met (break-point chlorination – the point at which all chlorine demand is satisfied and free residual chlorine begins to appear); a contact period of at least 1 hour; a free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/L at the end of the contact period, which protects against later contamination.
    • Methods – chlorine gas, chloramines, perchloron, sodium hypochlorite, bleaching powder (about 33% available chlorine).
    • Testing residual chlorine – orthotolidine (OT) test or orthotolidine–arsenite test (yellow colour compared with standards).
    • Super-chlorination (a high dose followed by dechlorination) is used in emergencies.
  4. Other methods in special situations – ozonation, ultraviolet radiation, defluoridation (Nalgonda technique), removal of arsenic and iron.

B. Small-scale (household) purification

  1. Boiling – bringing water to a rolling boil (for about 5–10 minutes) kills bacteria, viruses, spores and cysts; store in the same covered vessel; the most reliable household method.
  2. Chemical disinfection
    • Bleaching powder / stock chlorine solution – a few drops of stock solution per litre; wait 30 minutes.
    • Chlorine tablets (e.g. halazone or sodium dichloroisocyanurate tablets) – one tablet for the specified volume (usually 1 litre or more), with a 30-minute contact time; useful in camps and disasters.
    • Potassium permanganate is no longer recommended for drinking water.
  3. Filtration – ceramic candle filters (Pasteur–Chamberland, Berkefeld), activated carbon filters; cleaned regularly.
  4. Modern purifiers – UV purifiers and reverse osmosis (RO) units (RO also removes dissolved salts and fluoride but wastes water).
  5. Solar disinfection (SODIS) – clear plastic bottles of water exposed to sunlight for about 6 hours.
  6. Sedimentation with alum (for turbid water) followed by boiling or chlorination.
  7. Safe storage – narrow-mouthed, covered containers with a tap; use a long-handled ladle; do not dip hands or cups.

(c) Water-borne diseases and role of the nurse (4 marks) Water-related diseases

  • Caused by biological agents in water (water-borne) – cholera, typhoid and paratyphoid, bacillary and amoebic dysentery, viral hepatitis A and E, poliomyelitis, rotavirus diarrhoea, giardiasis, leptospirosis.
  • Water-washed (due to lack of water for hygiene) – scabies, trachoma, skin infections.
  • Water-based – schistosomiasis, guinea worm (eradicated in India).
  • Water-related vectors – malaria, dengue, filariasis (breeding in stored or stagnant water).
  • Chemical – fluorosis (dental and skeletal; excess fluoride above 1.5 mg/L), arsenicosis (skin lesions, cancers), methaemoglobinaemia (nitrates in infants), lead poisoning.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Survey of water sources in her area; identify contaminated sources and report.
  • Disinfection of wells with bleaching powder and monitoring of residual chlorine (OT test), especially during outbreaks, floods and the monsoon.
  • Collect water samples for bacteriological and chemical testing; use field test kits (H2S strip test) with ASHAs and the village water and sanitation committee.
  • Health education – boiling or chlorinating drinking water, safe storage and handling, hand washing, keeping the surroundings of wells clean (platform, drainage, parapet wall, no washing or bathing near the source).
  • Early detection and reporting of diarrhoea and jaundice clusters (IDSP/IHIP); distribution of ORS, zinc and chlorine tablets.
  • Coordination with the Jal Jeevan Mission ("Har Ghar Jal" – functional tap water connections to every rural household), Panchayats and the Public Health Engineering Department.

Hardness of water

  • Hardness is the soap-destroying power of water, due mainly to calcium and magnesium salts.
  • Temporary hardness – due to bicarbonates; removed by boiling or by adding lime (Clark's method).
  • Permanent hardness – due to sulphates and chlorides; removed by adding soda ash or by ion exchange (base exchange / permutit) softeners.
  • Hard water wastes soap and fuel, forms scales in boilers and pipes, and spoils the taste of food; moderately hard water (about 50–150 mg/L) is acceptable for drinking.

Nursing importance

  • Most diarrhoeal deaths and outbreaks of cholera, typhoid and hepatitis in villages can be traced to unsafe water; the nurse's work in well disinfection, testing, health education and outbreak reporting directly prevents them.

Conclusion Safe and wholesome water is free from pathogens and harmful chemicals, pleasant to taste and usable for domestic purposes; it comes from rain, surface and ground sources. Large-scale purification uses storage, slow or rapid sand filtration and chlorination to a free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/L after one hour, while household methods include boiling, chlorination, filtration, UV/RO, SODIS and safe storage. The community health nurse prevents water-borne and water-related diseases through surveys, well disinfection, testing, health education, surveillance and coordination with water programmes.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: (a) Explain the health hazards of improper excreta disposal and the concept of the sanitation barrier. (3 marks) (b) Describe the methods of excreta disposal in rural and urban areas, including sanitary latrines. (8 marks) (c) Explain the Swachh Bharat Mission and the role of the community health nurse. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: The F-diagram and the sanitation barrier
labels: faeces reach a new host through fluids (water)
fields (soil) and food; a sanitary latrine (primary barrier) blocks the faeces at source
fly control and food hygiene act as secondary barriers

answer_html:
(a) Health hazards and the sanitation barrier (3 marks) Health hazards of improper excreta disposal

  • Soil pollution and water pollution (wells, ponds, rivers) by human faeces, and breeding of flies.
  • Faecal–oral diseases – cholera, typhoid, bacillary and amoebic dysentery, viral hepatitis A and E, poliomyelitis, rotavirus and other diarrhoeas.
  • Worm infestations – roundworm, hookworm (through bare feet on contaminated soil), threadworm, tapeworm – leading to anaemia and malnutrition and stunting in children.
  • Social problems – loss of dignity, insecurity and violence for women and girls who must go out in the open, school drop-out of girls, and foul smell and nuisance.

Sanitation barrier

  • Faeces reach a new host through the "F-diagram" – fluids (water), fingers, flies, fields (soil) and food.
  • The sanitation barrier is the segregation of faeces from the environment by sanitary disposal (latrines), which breaks the chain of transmission at its source – the primary barrier.
  • Secondary barriers – safe water, hand washing with soap, fly control and food hygiene.

(b) Methods of excreta disposal (8 marks) Requirements of a sanitary latrine

  • Excreta should not contaminate the ground surface, surface water or ground water.
  • Excreta should not be accessible to flies or animals; there should be no handling of fresh excreta.
  • It should be free from odour and unsightly conditions, simple, inexpensive, acceptable and easy to maintain.
  • It should be located at least 15 m (50 feet) from a well and preferably downhill from the water source.

A. Methods in rural areas (unsewered)

  1. Bore-hole latrine – a hole of about 35–40 cm diameter bored 4–8 m deep with an auger, covered by a squatting plate; cheap but small capacity and not suitable where groundwater is high.
  2. Dug-well (pit) latrine – a pit about 75 cm in diameter and 3–3.5 m deep, lined with earthen rings, covered by a squatting plate; lasts several years.
  3. Water-seal latrine – the most suitable for rural India; a pan and trap holding water (water seal of about 2 cm) prevents access of flies and escape of smell; the excreta are flushed with a little water into a pit.
    • Designs: PRAI type (Planning Research and Action Institute, Lucknow) and RCA type (Research-cum-Action Project, Ministry of Health), with squatting plate, pan, trap, connecting pipe and a pit.
  4. Twin-pit pour-flush latrine – the model promoted under the Swachh Bharat Mission; two pits are used alternately; when one is full it is closed and the other is used; after 1–2 years the contents of the closed pit become safe, odourless manure ("sona khad") and can be removed by the family.
  5. Septic tank – a water-tight underground tank in which excreta undergo anaerobic digestion (liquefaction); the sludge settles, scum floats, and the effluent is discharged into a soakage pit; desludging is needed every 2–3 years; used in individual houses and institutions without sewerage.
  6. Aqua privy – a water-tight tank directly below the latrine with a drop pipe dipping into water.
  7. Others – chemical closets (trains, aircraft), trench latrines and shallow trench latrines for camps, fairs and disaster sites, bio-toilets.

B. Methods in urban areas (sewered)

  • Water carriage system (sewerage) – excreta and household waste water (sewage) are carried by underground sewers to a sewage treatment plant.
  • Sewage treatment
    • Primary treatment – screening (removal of large objects), grit chamber (sand and grit settle), primary sedimentation (about 50–70% of suspended solids settle as sludge).
    • Secondary (biological) treatment – trickling filter or activated sludge process, which oxidise organic matter with the help of aerobic bacteria; followed by secondary sedimentation.
    • Sludge digestion – anaerobic digestion producing methane (biogas) and manure.
    • Oxidation (stabilisation) ponds – shallow ponds where algae and bacteria purify sewage; useful for small towns.
    • Treated effluent may be disinfected before discharge into rivers or used for irrigation.
  • Faecal sludge and septage management (FSSM) – safe emptying, transport and treatment of septic-tank sludge in towns without full sewerage.
  • Manual scavenging is prohibited by law (2013 Act); mechanised cleaning must be used.
