(c) Swachh Bharat Mission and role of the nurse (4 marks) Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM)

  • Launched on 2 October 2014 to achieve a clean and open-defecation-free (ODF) India; two parts – SBM (Grameen) under the Ministry of Jal Shakti and SBM (Urban) under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs.
  • Phase I – construction of individual household latrines (with financial incentive to eligible families), community sanitary complexes and behaviour change; over 10 crore rural household toilets were built and rural India was declared ODF in 2019.
  • Phase II of SBM-G (2020–25) – ODF Plus: sustaining ODF behaviour and ensuring solid and liquid waste management and visual cleanliness in villages; SBM-U 2.0 aims at "garbage-free" cities.
  • Behaviour change through Swachhagrahis, campaigns such as Swachhata Hi Seva, Swachh Survekshan rankings for cities.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Survey sanitation coverage and latrine use in her area; identify households without toilets or not using them.
  • Behaviour change communication – the benefits of latrine use, hand washing with soap at critical times, safe disposal of children's faeces, menstrual hygiene.
  • Promote proper construction (distance from wells, water seal), maintenance and cleaning of latrines; link families with SBM incentives.
  • Promote school and Anganwadi sanitation; work with VHSNCs, Panchayats and self-help groups.
  • Monitor diarrhoea and worm infestation; support deworming and sanitation drives during outbreaks and disasters.

Excreta disposal in camps, fairs and disasters

  • Shallow trench latrines (about 30 cm wide, 90–150 cm deep) for short camps, with excreta covered with earth after each use.
  • Deep trench latrines for longer camps; mobile or prefabricated toilets and bio-toilets for large gatherings (melas, pilgrimages).
  • Roughly one latrine for every 20 persons in emergencies, separate and lockable for women, with lighting, hand-washing stations and regular cleaning, located away from water sources and kitchens.
  • Fly control, safe water and food hygiene are reinforced to prevent outbreaks.

Safe disposal of children's faeces – children's stools are as infectious as adults'; they should be put into the latrine immediately, potties washed with soap, and the child's hands and the caregiver's hands washed with soap.

Nursing importance

  • Safe excreta disposal is one of the most effective public health measures; the nurse's education and motivation of families are vital to convert toilets built into toilets used.

Conclusion Improper excreta disposal pollutes soil, water and food and spreads faecal–oral diseases and worms; the sanitation barrier – sanitary disposal of faeces – breaks this chain at its source. Rural methods include bore-hole, dug-well, water-seal (RCA/PRAI) and twin-pit pour-flush latrines and septic tanks, while urban areas use the water carriage system with sewage treatment and faecal sludge management. The Swachh Bharat Mission has made India ODF and now aims at ODF Plus, and the community health nurse promotes latrine use, hygiene and community action.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: (a) Define air pollution and list its sources and major pollutants. (4 marks) (b) Explain the health effects of air pollution, including indoor (household) air pollution. (5 marks) (c) Describe the prevention and control of air pollution and the role of the community health nurse. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Air Quality Index categories (India)
labels: with the main health messages for each band (sensitive groups – children
pregnant women and people with heart or lung disease – affected first)

answer_html:
(a) Definition, sources and pollutants (4 marks) Definition – air pollution is the presence in the outdoor or indoor air of substances (gases, particles, biological agents) in concentrations that are harmful to human health, other living beings or property, or that interfere with the comfortable enjoyment of life.

Sources

  • Natural – dust storms, volcanic eruptions, forest fires, pollen.
  • Man-made
    • Vehicles – exhaust from petrol and diesel engines (major source in cities).
    • Industries and thermal power plants – coal burning, brick kilns, cement and chemical factories.
    • Burning of crop residue (stubble), garbage and leaves; firecrackers.
    • Construction and road dust.
    • Domestic – burning of wood, dung cakes, crop waste, coal and kerosene for cooking and heating (indoor air pollution); tobacco smoke; mosquito coils and incense.

Major pollutants

  • Particulate matter – PM10 and especially fine particles PM2.5 (diameter 2.5 micrometres or less), which penetrate deep into the lungs and blood – the most harmful pollutant.
  • Sulphur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) – from fuel burning; cause respiratory irritation and acid rain.
  • Carbon monoxide (CO) – from incomplete combustion; combines with haemoglobin.
  • Ground-level ozone (O3) – formed from NO2 and hydrocarbons in sunlight (smog).
  • Lead, ammonia, benzene, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and biological agents (moulds, pollen).

(b) Health effects (5 marks)

  1. Respiratory system – irritation of eyes, nose and throat; cough; acute respiratory infections and pneumonia in children; asthma attacks; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD); reduced lung growth in children; lung cancer.
  2. Cardiovascular system – ischaemic heart disease, heart attacks, stroke, hypertension and arrhythmias; air pollution is now a leading risk factor for death from NCDs.
  3. Pregnancy and children – low birth weight, preterm birth, stillbirth; impaired cognitive development.
  4. Other effects – diabetes, kidney disease, cataract, dementia; CO poisoning (headache, confusion, death in closed rooms with charcoal heaters); lead – anaemia and brain damage in children.
  5. Vulnerable groups – children, the elderly, pregnant women, people with heart and lung diseases, outdoor workers and the poor.
  6. Indirect effects – climate change, acid rain, damage to crops and buildings, reduced visibility (accidents).

Indoor (household) air pollution

  • Caused mainly by cooking with solid fuels on traditional chulhas in poorly ventilated kitchens; women and young children spend hours near the fire.
  • Causes pneumonia in children, COPD and lung cancer in women, cataract, low birth weight and tuberculosis.
  • Prevention – clean fuels (LPG, electricity, biogas), improved cookstoves with chimneys, cooking outdoors or in ventilated kitchens, keeping children away from smoke; the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (2016) provides LPG connections to poor households.

(c) Prevention and control, and role of the nurse (6 marks) Measures

  1. Legislation and standards
    • Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; National Ambient Air Quality Standards; enforcement by the Central and State Pollution Control Boards.
    • WHO Air Quality Guidelines (2021) give stricter health-based limits (e.g. annual PM2.5 of 5 µg/m³).
  2. Monitoring and information
    • Air-quality monitoring stations; the Air Quality Index (AQI) – Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderately polluted (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very poor (301–400), Severe (401–500) – with health advisories.
  3. National Clean Air Programme (NCAP, 2019) – city action plans for more than 130 "non-attainment" cities to reduce particulate pollution substantially; the Graded Response Action Plan in Delhi–NCR for bad-air days.
  4. Vehicle measures – Bharat Stage VI fuel and emission norms (2020), pollution-under-control checks, public transport, electric vehicles, CNG, cycling and walking, phasing out old vehicles.
  5. Industrial measures – cleaner technologies, tall chimneys, filters, electrostatic precipitators and scrubbers, siting of industries away from residential areas, cleaner fuels in brick kilns.
  6. Agricultural and waste measures – alternatives to stubble burning (happy seeder, bio-decomposers), banning open burning of garbage, dust control at construction sites.
  7. Greening – planting trees and green belts.
  8. Household measures – clean cooking fuels, ventilation, no smoking indoors.
  9. Personal protection on bad-air days – reduce outdoor activity, keep windows closed, use well-fitting N95 masks when needed.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Health education on the dangers of chulha smoke, tobacco smoke and burning garbage; promote LPG use and ventilated kitchens; help families avail Ujjwala.
  • Advise vulnerable groups (asthma, COPD, heart patients, pregnant women, children) on AQI-based precautions; ensure their medicines are available.
  • Early detection and care of respiratory illnesses in children and adults; screening for COPD and asthma at AAMs.
  • Advocacy – support tree planting, anti-burning drives, school awareness, and community campaigns; report pollution sources.
  • Implement activities under the National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health (air-pollution-related illness surveillance).
  • Practise and model tobacco-free behaviour.

Factors influencing air pollution levels

  • Meteorological factors – in winter, temperature inversion (a layer of warm air above cold air near the ground) traps pollutants near the surface, producing smog; calm winds and fog worsen it, while wind and rain disperse and wash out pollutants.
  • Topography – valleys and enclosed basins trap pollutants.
  • Time of day and season – peaks during rush hours and in the post-monsoon crop-burning and winter season in north India.

Air pollution disasters (lessons)

  • The London smog (1952) caused thousands of deaths in a few days and led to clean air laws.
  • The Bhopal gas tragedy (December 1984) – leakage of methyl isocyanate from a pesticide factory – killed thousands and injured lakhs, showing the importance of industrial safety and emergency preparedness.

Monitoring of air quality

  • Continuous ambient air-quality monitoring stations under the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme measure PM10, PM2.5, SO2, NO2, CO, ozone and other pollutants; results are shown as the AQI on public displays and mobile applications ("Sameer").
  • Health surveillance of air-pollution-related illnesses (acute respiratory illness) at sentinel hospitals.

Prevention of carbon monoxide poisoning at home – never use charcoal or coal braziers (sigdi) or run generators in closed rooms; keep windows partly open when burning fuel indoors; ensure chimneys and flues are clear; recognise early symptoms (headache, dizziness, vomiting, drowsiness) and move the person to fresh air immediately.

Nursing importance

  • Air pollution affects every age group and is a leading environmental cause of death in India; the nurse can reduce household exposure – the most important source for rural women and children – through education and support for clean fuels.

Conclusion Air pollution is the presence of harmful gases and particles in the air from vehicles, industries, stubble burning, dust and household solid fuels; PM2.5 is the most dangerous pollutant. It causes respiratory infections, asthma, COPD, lung cancer, heart disease, stroke and adverse pregnancy outcomes, and indoor smoke from chulhas is especially harmful to women and children. It is controlled by laws, AQI monitoring, NCAP, cleaner vehicles, industries and fuels, greening and personal protection, with the nurse educating, protecting vulnerable groups and advocating for clean air.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: Explain the disinfection of a well.
answer_html:
Introduction Wells, especially shallow open wells, are easily contaminated and are a common source of outbreaks of diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid and hepatitis. Chlorination with bleaching powder is the most practical method of disinfecting wells; it is done routinely, during outbreaks and after floods.

Steps of well disinfection

  1. Find the volume of water in the well
    • Measure the diameter (d) of the well and the depth of water (h) in metres.
    • Volume (litres) = 3.14 × d² × h × 1,000 ÷ 4.
    • Example: a well 2 m in diameter with 5 m of water holds 3.14 × 4 × 5 × 1,000 ÷ 4 ≈ 15,700 litres.
  2. Find the amount of bleaching powder required
    • Horrock's apparatus – six white cups, one black cup, metal spoons, glass stirring rods and starch–iodide indicator.
    • One level spoonful (about 2 g) of bleaching powder is made into a paste in the black cup; well water is added and the solution is added in increasing amounts to the six white cups filled with well water; after 30 minutes, starch–iodide indicator is added.
    • The first cup showing a distinct blue colour indicates the dose: e.g. blue in the 3rd cup means 3 level spoons (6 g) of bleaching powder are needed to disinfect 455 litres (100 gallons) of that water.
    • As a rough guide, about 2.5 g of good-quality bleaching powder (33% available chlorine) per 1,000 litres is needed for well water of average quality.
  3. Prepare the solution – place the required bleaching powder in a bucket, make a thin paste with a little water, add more water to fill the bucket, stir well and allow the lime to settle for about 10 minutes.
  4. Add to the well – lower the bucket containing the clear supernatant into the well, below the water surface, and jerk it up and down several times to mix the chlorine thoroughly; discard the sediment.
  5. Contact period – allow at least 1 hour before water is drawn; preferably disinfect in the evening or at night when the well is not in use.
  6. Test for residual chlorine – using the orthotolidine (OT) test; a free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/L after one hour indicates satisfactory disinfection; if less, repeat the process.

Frequency

  • Routinely at regular intervals (weekly or as advised), and daily or more often during outbreaks, after floods and during the monsoon.

Continuous chlorination – pot chlorination (double-pot method)

  • An inner pot containing a mixture of bleaching powder and coarse sand is placed inside a larger outer pot with holes; the unit is lowered into the well and releases chlorine slowly for 2–3 weeks in a domestic well.

Other protective measures for wells

  • Parapet wall, cement platform with drainage, a cover, a fixed bucket with rope or a hand pump; no washing, bathing or animal access near the well; latrines at least 15 m away.

Role of the nurse

  • Survey and map wells; carry out or supervise disinfection with the MPW and ASHA; test residual chlorine; keep records; educate users and coordinate with the Panchayat; report outbreaks.

Conclusion A well is disinfected by calculating its water volume, finding the bleaching powder dose with Horrock's apparatus (about 2.5 g per 1,000 litres as a rough guide), adding the clear chlorine solution, allowing a contact period of one hour and confirming a free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/L by the OT test; pot chlorination provides continuous disinfection.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: Explain solid waste management in the community.
answer_html:
Introduction Solid waste (refuse) is the unwanted solid material produced by households, markets, institutions, industries and streets. Rapid urbanisation has made solid waste a major public health and environmental problem in India.

Types and sources

  • Domestic waste – kitchen waste (biodegradable), paper, plastics, glass, metals, cloth, ash.
  • Street sweepings, market and garden waste.
  • Commercial and institutional waste.
  • Construction and demolition waste.
  • Domestic hazardous waste – batteries, used sanitary napkins and diapers, expired medicines, paint, pesticide containers, bulbs.
  • Special categories – biomedical waste (handled under separate rules), e-waste, industrial waste.

Health hazards of improper disposal

  • Breeding of flies, mosquitoes and rats – diarrhoeal diseases, dengue, malaria, plague, leptospirosis.
  • Bad odour, smoke from open burning (air pollution), contamination of soil and water (leachate), blockage of drains (flooding), injury to rag pickers, and spoiling of the environment.

Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 – key points

  • Segregation at source by every household into wet (biodegradable), dry (recyclable) and domestic hazardous waste, stored in separate bins.
  • Door-to-door collection by local bodies; user fees; spot fines for littering and burning.
  • Processing of biodegradable waste by composting or biomethanation; recovery of recyclables; only residual inert waste to go to landfills.
  • Bulk generators (hotels, institutions) to process their own wet waste.

Steps of solid waste management

  1. Storage – covered, leak-proof bins; separate bins for wet and dry waste.
  2. Collection – door-to-door, regular (daily in cities).
  3. Transportation – in covered vehicles.
  4. Processing and disposal
    • Composting – decomposition of organic matter into manure (e.g. Bangalore method of anaerobic composting in trenches; aerobic windrow composting in towns).
    • Vermicomposting – using earthworms; suitable for households and villages.
    • Biomethanation (biogas plants) – produces gas for cooking and slurry manure.
    • Sanitary landfill – waste spread in layers, compacted and covered with earth daily; lined to prevent leachate; better than open dumping.
    • Incineration / waste-to-energy – burning at high temperature (for suitable dry waste); emissions must be controlled.
    • Recycling – paper, plastics, metals, glass.

The 3 Rs and plastic waste – Reduce, Reuse, Recycle; avoid single-use plastics (banned for many items since 2022); carry cloth bags; extended producer responsibility.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Educate families to segregate waste at source, avoid throwing waste in drains or burning it, and make compost pits or vermicompost at home and in villages.
  • Promote clean surroundings around homes, schools and Anganwadis; organise cleanliness drives with Panchayats, self-help groups and schools (SBM – ODF Plus).
  • Ensure safe disposal of waste at sub-centres and outreach sessions (biomedical waste rules).
  • Watch for fly, mosquito and rodent breeding and related diseases; protect sanitation workers' health.

Conclusion Solid waste from homes, markets and institutions causes disease, pollution and nuisance when poorly handled. The SWM Rules 2016 require segregation at source into wet, dry and hazardous waste, regular collection and processing by composting, vermicomposting, biomethanation, recycling, incineration and sanitary landfill. The nurse promotes segregation, composting, the 3 Rs and community cleanliness.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: Explain the standards of healthful housing and the health effects of poor housing.
answer_html:
Introduction Housing includes not only the physical structure but also the surroundings, services and facilities needed for the physical, mental and social well-being of the family. Poor housing is closely linked to infectious diseases, accidents and stress.

Criteria (standards) of healthful housing

  1. Site – elevated, well drained, away from nuisances (dust, smoke, noise, foul smells, industries), with safe access.
  2. Set-back – an open space all around the house for light and air; the built-up area should not cover the whole plot.
  3. Floor – impermeable, smooth, easy to clean, damp-proof, raised above the ground.
  4. Walls – strong, smooth, free from cracks (no hiding places for insects), low heat conduction, weather-resistant.
  5. Roof – rain-proof, insulated; a ceiling height of about 3 m (10 feet).
  6. Rooms – at least two living rooms, each of reasonable floor area (about 9–10 m² or more), allowing privacy and separation of sleeping arrangements.
  7. Windows and ventilation – window area at least one-fifth of the floor area, and doors and windows together at least two-fifths of the floor area; cross-ventilation.
  8. Lighting – adequate natural daylight in living rooms.
  9. Kitchen – separate, with a smoke outlet (chimney), clean water and drainage; clean cooking fuel.
  10. Water supply – safe, adequate water within or close to the house.
  11. Sanitation – a sanitary latrine in each house, bathing facilities, drainage for waste water, and arrangement for refuse disposal.
  12. Freedom from insects and rodents; safety from fire, collapse and falls.

Overcrowding

  • Persons per room – 1 room: 2 persons; 2 rooms: 3; 3 rooms: 5; 4 rooms: 7; 5 or more rooms: 10 (plus 2 for each additional room).
  • Floor space per person – about 110 sq ft or more for 2 persons, decreasing proportionately; children are counted as half.
  • Overcrowding is common in urban slums and poor rural homes.

Health effects of poor housing

  • Respiratory infections – common cold, pneumonia, tuberculosis, diphtheria, whooping cough (overcrowding and poor ventilation).
  • Skin and eye infections – scabies, impetigo, trachoma (overcrowding, lack of water).
  • Diarrhoeal diseases, worm infestations – lack of safe water and latrines.
  • Vector and rodent-borne diseases – malaria, dengue, plague, leptospirosis.
  • Accidents – falls, burns, electric shocks, house collapse.
  • Indoor air pollution from smoky kitchens – pneumonia, COPD.
  • Psychosocial effects – stress, lack of privacy, domestic conflict, poor school performance, juvenile delinquency.

Housing schemes – Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Gramin and Urban) aims at pucca houses with basic amenities for all, linked with SBM toilets, Ujjwala LPG and Jal Jeevan Mission water connections.

Role of the nurse – assess housing conditions during home visits; educate on ventilation, cleanliness, smoke-free kitchens, safe water storage and latrine use; link families to housing and welfare schemes; identify overcrowded homes for TB screening.

Conclusion Healthful housing requires a good site, set-back, sound floor, walls and roof, at least two rooms, adequate windows, light and ventilation, a smoke-free kitchen, safe water, a sanitary latrine and freedom from insects and rodents, without overcrowding. Poor housing leads to respiratory, skin, diarrhoeal and vector-borne diseases, accidents and psychosocial stress.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: Explain noise pollution – sources, health effects and control.
tags: Noise Pollution Regulation and Control Rules 2000
answer_html:
Definition Noise is unwanted sound. Noise pollution is the presence of sound in the environment at levels that are harmful or annoying to people. Sound intensity is measured in decibels (dB) – normal conversation is about 60 dB, heavy traffic about 80–90 dB, and pain begins at about 120–140 dB.

Sources

  • Road traffic (horns, engines), railways, aircraft.
  • Industries and workshops; construction machinery.
  • Loudspeakers, DJs and music systems at festivals, weddings and processions; firecrackers.
  • Domestic – generators, mixers, televisions.

Health effects A. Auditory effects

  • Temporary threshold shift (temporary hearing loss) and permanent noise-induced hearing loss after prolonged exposure (above about 85 dB for 8 hours a day); tinnitus; acoustic trauma from sudden very loud sounds (firecrackers). B. Non-auditory effects

  • Annoyance, irritability, interference with speech communication.

  • Sleep disturbance, fatigue.
  • Cardiovascular effects – raised blood pressure, increased heart rate; increased risk of hypertension and heart disease.
  • Stress, anxiety, headache; reduced concentration, work efficiency and learning in schoolchildren.
  • Accidents due to masking of warning signals.

Standards – Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 (ambient noise limits, day / night)

  • Industrial area – 75 / 70 dB(A).
  • Commercial area – 65 / 55 dB(A).
  • Residential area – 55 / 45 dB(A).
  • Silence zones (at least 100 m around hospitals, schools and courts) – 50 / 40 dB(A).
  • Loudspeakers and public address systems are not allowed between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. (except in closed premises or as permitted).

Control measures

  1. At the source – quieter machinery and vehicles, silencers, proper maintenance, restriction of horns, limits on firecrackers and loudspeakers.
  2. Along the path – sound-proofing and enclosures, noise barriers and green belts of trees, proper town planning (industries and highways away from residential areas, hospitals and schools).
  3. At the receiver – ear plugs and ear muffs for exposed workers, reducing duration of exposure, periodic audiometry.
  4. Legislation and enforcement – Noise Rules 2000, Motor Vehicles rules, Factories Act provisions.
  5. Education – public awareness of the dangers of noise, especially loud music through earphones among young people.

Role of the nurse – educate the community and students on noise hazards and safe listening; observe silence zones around health facilities; identify people with hearing loss for screening and referral (NPPCD); advocate for noise control during festivals.

Conclusion Noise pollution from traffic, industries, loudspeakers, firecrackers and construction causes hearing loss and tinnitus as well as annoyance, sleep disturbance, hypertension, stress and poor concentration. It is controlled at the source, along the path and at the receiver, through legal limits (Noise Rules 2000) and public education.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: Explain ecosystems and biodiversity, and their importance for human health.
answer_html:
A. Ecosystem

  • Definition – an ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with one another and with their non-living physical environment as a functional unit (the term was introduced by A. G. Tansley, 1935). Examples – forest, grassland, pond, river, ocean, desert, even a village pond or crop field.
  • Components
    • Abiotic – sunlight, air, water, soil, temperature, minerals.
    • Biotic – producers (green plants that make food by photosynthesis), consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores including humans) and decomposers (bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter and recycle nutrients).
  • Functions – energy flow through food chains and food webs (grass → deer → tiger), nutrient (biogeochemical) cycles (carbon, nitrogen, water cycles), and regulation of climate and populations.
  • Types – terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert, mountain) and aquatic (freshwater – ponds, lakes, rivers, wetlands; marine – oceans, estuaries, coral reefs).

B. Biodiversity

  • Definition – the variety of life on earth at all levels:
    • Genetic diversity – variation within a species (different varieties of rice).
    • Species diversity – variety of species in an area.
    • Ecosystem diversity – variety of habitats and ecosystems.
  • India is one of the world's mega-diverse countries and includes parts of four global biodiversity hotspots – the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).
  • Threats – habitat destruction (deforestation, urbanisation, mining), pollution, over-exploitation (hunting, overfishing), invasive species, climate change, and diseases.
  • Conservation
    • In situ (in natural habitats) – national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves, community reserves.
    • Ex situ (outside habitats) – zoos, botanical gardens, seed and gene banks.
    • Laws – Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Biological Diversity Act 2002; people's movements such as the Chipko movement.

C. Natural resources and their conservation – forests, water, land, minerals, energy and food resources should be used sustainably – afforestation, water harvesting, soil conservation, renewable energy (solar, wind), reducing waste.

D. Importance for human health

  • Ecosystems provide food, clean water, clean air, medicines (many drugs come from plants and microbes), fuel and livelihoods.
  • They regulate climate, floods and diseases; healthy ecosystems limit vectors and pests.
  • Loss of biodiversity and disturbance of ecosystems increase zoonotic diseases (Nipah, Kyasanur Forest Disease, avian influenza, COVID-19), malnutrition and natural disasters.
  • The One Health approach recognises that the health of people, animals and the environment is interconnected.

Role of the nurse – promote environmental awareness, tree planting, water conservation and waste reduction; educate on zoonoses; take part in One Health and climate-and-health activities.

Conclusion An ecosystem is a functional unit of living organisms and their environment, with producers, consumers and decomposers linked by energy flow and nutrient cycles. Biodiversity – genetic, species and ecosystem variety – is rich in India but threatened by habitat loss, pollution, over-exploitation, invasive species and climate change, and is conserved in situ and ex situ. Healthy ecosystems are essential for food, water, air, medicines and protection from disease.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: Explain the control of insects and rodents of public health importance.
answer_html:
Introduction Many insects and rodents transmit serious diseases. Their control is one of the most important environmental health measures in India.

Insects and rodents with diseases transmitted

  • Anopheles mosquito – malaria.
  • Culex mosquito – lymphatic filariasis, Japanese encephalitis, West Nile fever.
  • Aedes mosquito – dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever (breeds in clean stored water – coolers, tyres, containers).
  • Housefly – diarrhoea, dysentery, typhoid, cholera, trachoma (mechanical transmission).
  • Sandfly – kala-azar.
  • Rat flea – plague, murine typhus.
  • Lice – epidemic typhus, relapsing fever, trench fever.
  • Ticks and mites – Kyasanur Forest Disease, scrub typhus (mite), tick typhus.
  • Rats – plague (with fleas), leptospirosis (urine), rat-bite fever, food contamination and loss.

Principles – integrated vector management (IVM) – a combination of methods, chosen by local evidence, with community participation and intersectoral coordination.

Control measures 1. Environmental control (the most permanent)

  • Source reduction – eliminating breeding places: emptying, cleaning and covering water containers weekly ("dry day"), disposing of tyres and junk, filling pits, draining stagnant water, clearing weeds, proper sanitation and refuse disposal (for flies and rats).
  • Improvement of housing (screening of doors and windows), food storage and drainage.

2. Chemical control

  • Larvicides – temephos (Abate) in containers and water bodies; larvicidal oil on drains.
  • Adulticides – indoor residual spraying (IRS) of houses with insecticides such as synthetic pyrethroids; space spraying and fogging (malathion, pyrethrum) during outbreaks of dengue and chikungunya.
  • Insecticides for flies, lice (permethrin) and fleas.

3. Biological control

  • Larvivorous fish – Gambusia and guppy in ponds, tanks and wells; Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) as a biological larvicide.

4. Personal protection

  • Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), mosquito repellents, full-sleeved clothing, mesh on windows, avoiding outdoor exposure at peak biting times.

5. Rodent control

  • Environmental sanitation – proper storage of food grains, garbage disposal, removal of rat shelters.
  • Rat-proofing of buildings and godowns.
  • Trapping, rodenticides (zinc phosphide, anticoagulants such as bromadiolone), fumigation of burrows; flea control before killing rats during plague outbreaks (to prevent fleas moving to humans).

6. Legal and community measures – municipal bye-laws against breeding sites, community campaigns, school involvement.

Role of the nurse

  • Survey for breeding sites with ASHAs; teach families to keep water containers covered and observe a weekly dry day; promote LLIN use and personal protection; distribute larvivorous fish; report fever clusters; coordinate spraying and fogging with the vector-borne disease programme.

Conclusion Mosquitoes, flies, sandflies, fleas, lice, ticks, mites and rats transmit malaria, filariasis, dengue, kala-azar, plague, typhus and other diseases. They are controlled through integrated vector management – environmental source reduction, chemical larvicides and adulticides, biological agents such as larvivorous fish and Bti, personal protection with LLINs, rodent control and community participation.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: What are the standards of drinking water quality?
answer_html:
Drinking water quality in India is governed by the Bureau of Indian Standards – IS 10500 (2012), consistent with WHO guidelines:

  1. Physical – clear, colourless, odourless, agreeable taste; turbidity below about 1 NTU (up to 5 NTU permissible); pH 6.5–8.5.
  2. Chemical (acceptable limits) – total dissolved solids 500 mg/L (2,000 permissible in the absence of another source); fluoride 1.0 mg/L (1.5 permissible); nitrate 45 mg/L; arsenic 0.01 mg/L; chloride 250 mg/L; total hardness 200 mg/L.
  3. Residual free chlorine – at least 0.2 mg/L at the consumer's tap (0.5 mg/L after one hour of contact at the point of chlorination).
  4. Bacteriological – E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms must not be detectable in any 100 mL sample.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: What is climate change? State its effects on health.
answer_html:
Climate change refers to long-term changes in temperature and weather patterns, mainly due to human activities – burning of fossil fuels, deforestation and industry – which increase greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide) and cause global warming. Effects on health

  1. Heat waves – heat exhaustion, heat stroke, deaths among the elderly and outdoor workers.
  2. Spread of vector-borne diseases (malaria, dengue) to new areas and seasons.
  3. Water- and food-borne diseases after floods and droughts; malnutrition due to crop failure.
  4. Air pollution – respiratory and heart diseases.
  5. Extreme weather events – floods, cyclones, injuries, displacement and mental stress. India's National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health (2019) prepares the health system (heat action plans, surveillance); the Paris Agreement (2015) aims to limit warming to well below 2 °C.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: What is the sanitation barrier?
answer_html:
The sanitation barrier is the segregation of human faeces from the environment by sanitary disposal (sanitary latrines), so that faeces cannot reach a new host.

  • Faecal pathogens normally spread through the "F-diagram" – fluids (water), fingers, flies, fields (soil) and food.
  • A sanitary latrine acts as the primary barrier, breaking the chain of faecal–oral transmission at its source.
  • Secondary barriers – safe drinking water, hand washing with soap, fly control and food hygiene – block the routes after contamination. It prevents diarrhoeal diseases, typhoid, cholera, hepatitis A and E, polio and worm infestations.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: What is the greenhouse effect?
answer_html:
The greenhouse effect is the trapping of heat in the earth's atmosphere by certain gases, which allow sunlight to pass through but absorb and re-radiate the heat (infrared radiation) emitted by the earth's surface, keeping the earth warm – like the glass of a greenhouse.

  • Greenhouse gases – carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour, chlorofluorocarbons and ozone.
  • The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life, but human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture, industry) have increased these gases, producing an enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming, which drives climate change – rising temperatures, melting glaciers, rising sea levels and extreme weather.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Environmental Science, Environmental Health and Sanitation
question: What are ODF and ODF Plus?
answer_html:
• ODF (open defecation free) – a village or city where no visible faeces are found in the environment and every household, as well as public and community institutions, uses a safe technology option for the disposal of faeces (Swachh Bharat Mission). Rural India was declared ODF in 2019.
  • ODF Plus – a village that sustains its ODF status and also ensures solid and liquid waste management and is visually clean; villages are graded as aspiring, rising and model ODF Plus, under Phase II of SBM (Grameen). These concepts emphasise sustained behaviour change, not only construction of toilets.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Nutrition Assessment and Nutrition Education
question: (a) Explain the steps of planning and conducting a community nutrition survey. (7 marks) (b) Describe nutritional surveillance and the national sources of nutrition data in India. (4 marks) (c) Explain the role of the community health nurse in community nutrition assessment. (4 marks)
tags: assessment of nutritional status of a community

diagram.caption: Steps of a community nutrition survey
labels: define objectives – select area and sample – prepare tools and train team – obtain permission and community consent – collect data (anthropometry
prevalence) – make a community nutrition diagnosis – report and plan action – re-survey to evaluate

answer_html:
Introduction A community nutrition survey assesses the nutritional status of a population (not just of individuals) in order to identify the magnitude, distribution and causes of malnutrition, plan interventions and evaluate programmes. It differs from individual assessment because it uses representative samples, standard methods and population-level indicators.

(a) Planning and conducting a community nutrition survey (7 marks)

  1. Define the objectives
    • E.g. "to find the prevalence of stunting, wasting and underweight among under-five children and anaemia among women in the sub-centre area" or "to identify causes of malnutrition".
  2. Select the area and the population (sample)
    • Decide the target groups – under-five children (most vulnerable), adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women, the elderly.
    • Use a representative sample (random or cluster sampling) or a complete census in a small area; calculate sample size.
  3. Choose methods and prepare tools
    • Anthropometry – weight, length/height, MUAC, head circumference; standard electronic weighing scales, infantometers, stadiometers and MUAC tapes; results interpreted using WHO Child Growth Standards (z-scores) – weight-for-age (underweight), height-for-age (stunting), weight-for-height (wasting), BMI-for-age (overweight).
    • Clinical examination – signs such as oedema, pallor, Bitot's spots, goitre, angular stomatitis, hair and skin changes.
    • Biochemical tests – haemoglobin (anaemia), urinary iodine, serum vitamin A, ferritin, blood sugar and lipids where feasible.
    • Dietary survey – 24-hour recall, food frequency, household food consumption, infant and young child feeding practices.
    • Household and ecological data – income, food security, water and sanitation, morbidity (diarrhoea, infections), immunisation, culture and food taboos, access to ICDS and PDS.
    • Prepare a pre-tested schedule/questionnaire.
  4. Train and organise the team – standardised measurement techniques (to reduce errors), calibration of equipment, roles of ANMs, ASHAs, Anganwadi workers and supervisors; plan logistics and timetable.
  5. Obtain permission and community cooperation – inform Panchayat and leaders; explain the purpose; obtain consent; ensure privacy and confidentiality.
  6. Collect data – house-to-house or at Anganwadi centres; measure carefully (two readings where needed); refer children with severe malnutrition or illness immediately.
  7. Analyse the data
    • Calculate the prevalence of stunting, wasting, underweight, overweight and anaemia (below –2 SD = moderate, below –3 SD = severe); compare with district, state and NFHS figures.
    • Identify high-risk groups and areas and the causes (immediate – inadequate diet and disease; underlying – household food insecurity, poor care practices, unhealthy environment; basic – poverty, illiteracy, gender inequality).
  8. Community nutrition diagnosis, report and action plan
    • Share findings with the community and authorities; plan interventions – IYCF counselling, supplementary nutrition, management of severe acute malnutrition, IFA supplementation, deworming, kitchen gardens, sanitation, convergence with ICDS and Panchayat.
  9. Evaluate – repeat the survey after a period to measure change.
  10. Feedback to the community – findings are presented at the Gram Sabha, VHSNC or mothers' meeting in simple language and pictures, so that families understand the problem and take part in the solutions.

(b) Nutritional surveillance and national data sources (4 marks) Nutritional surveillance is the continuous collection, analysis and interpretation of data on the nutritional status of a population and its determinants, so that timely action can be taken (e.g. early warning of food shortage, rising malnutrition after drought).

  • Uses – identify trends and high-risk groups, plan and evaluate programmes, provide early warning, guide policy.
  • Sources of nutrition data in India
    • National Family Health Survey (NFHS) – stunting, wasting, underweight, anaemia, IYCF practices; NFHS-6 (2023–24) showed stunting 29.3%, wasting 19.0%, underweight 31.8% among under-fives.
    • Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey (CNNS, 2016–18) – micronutrient status and NCD risk factors in children and adolescents.
    • National Nutrition Monitoring Bureau (NNMB) surveys by the National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad (diet and nutrition of rural and tribal populations).
    • Poshan Tracker – real-time growth monitoring data from Anganwadi centres.
    • HMIS, NRC data, school health and RBSK screening data.

(c) Role of the community health nurse (4 marks)

  • Plan and participate in nutrition surveys; train ASHAs and Anganwadi workers in correct measurement.
  • Regular growth monitoring of children with the Anganwadi worker; plot and interpret growth charts in the MCP card; identify growth faltering, SAM and MAM early.
  • Screen pregnant women and adolescents for anaemia and low weight gain; check IFA compliance.
  • Refer complicated SAM to the Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre and follow up after discharge.
  • Nutrition counselling of mothers and families; promote breastfeeding, complementary feeding and diet diversity.
  • Coordinate with ICDS, PM POSHAN, PDS and Panchayats; maintain records and report nutrition indicators.

Indicators used in community nutrition assessment

  • Children under five – prevalence of underweight, stunting, wasting and overweight; SAM and MAM prevalence; low birth weight rate; anaemia prevalence.
  • Feeding practices – early initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding below 6 months, timely complementary feeding, minimum dietary diversity and minimum acceptable diet (6–23 months).
  • Women and adolescents – anaemia prevalence, BMI below 18.5 (chronic energy deficiency), overweight and obesity, weight gain in pregnancy.
  • Micronutrients – goitre rate and median urinary iodine, night blindness and Bitot's spots (Vitamin A deficiency), use of iodised salt at household level.
  • Programme coverage – IFA and deworming coverage, take-home ration and hot-cooked meal coverage, NRC admissions.

Quality control and common measurement errors

  • Errors arise from faulty or uncalibrated equipment, incorrect age (use the MCP card or birth certificate), measuring with clothes and shoes, wrong positioning (child's head not against the headboard, knees bent), and wrong reading or recording.
  • Prevent them by calibrating scales daily, using standard techniques (length lying down below 2 years, height standing above 2 years), two measurers for young children, repeat measurements, supervision and re-checking a sample of children.

Ethical considerations

  • Informed consent, privacy and dignity during examination, confidentiality of data, immediate referral of sick and severely malnourished children found during the survey, and sharing of results with the community.

Interpretation and use of results – an example

  • Suppose a survey of 400 under-five children in a sub-centre area finds stunting in 36%, wasting in 21% (SAM 6%) and anaemia in 60% of mothers. The nurse would compare these with district and NFHS figures, map the hamlets with the highest burden, and plan: line-listing and referral of SAM children, monthly growth monitoring, IYCF counselling, deworming and IFA, kitchen gardens, sanitation drives, and convergence with the Anganwadi supplementary nutrition programme – then repeat the survey after a year to see the change.

Nursing importance

  • The nurse is often the first to see malnutrition in the community; systematic surveys and continuous growth monitoring turn individual observations into a "community nutrition diagnosis" that guides local action.

Conclusion A community nutrition survey involves defining objectives, sampling, choosing anthropometric, clinical, biochemical, dietary and ecological methods, training the team, obtaining cooperation, collecting and analysing data, making a community nutrition diagnosis and planning action. Nutritional surveillance continuously monitors nutritional status through NFHS, CNNS, NNMB, Poshan Tracker and HMIS, and the community health nurse plays a central role in measurement, early identification, referral, counselling and coordination.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Nutrition Assessment and Nutrition Education
question: Explain the community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) in children.
answer_html:
Introduction Acute malnutrition (wasting) is a life-threatening condition in young children. Community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) treats most children with acute malnutrition in the community, and only those with medical complications in hospitals, so that more children are reached early and families are not burdened by long hospital stays. In India, a national protocol for the community management of malnutrition in children (2023, under Mission Poshan 2.0) operationalises this approach through Anganwadi centres and health workers.

Identification (children 6–59 months)

  • Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) – weight-for-height below –3 SD, or MUAC below 11.5 cm, or bilateral pitting oedema.
  • Moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) – weight-for-height between –3 and –2 SD, or MUAC 11.5–12.5 cm.
  • Identified through monthly growth monitoring at Anganwadi centres, home visits, VHSNDs, RBSK and active screening campaigns.

Components of CMAM

  1. Community mobilisation – awareness, early case finding, involvement of families and leaders.
  2. Screening and classification – MUAC, weight-for-height, oedema, appetite test, and check for medical complications (danger signs, severe infections, dehydration, hypothermia, severe anaemia).
  3. Inpatient care – children with SAM with medical complications, failed appetite test, or infants below 6 months are referred to a Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC) or hospital (WHO ten steps: treat hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, infections, micronutrient deficiencies, cautious feeding then catch-up growth).
  4. Outpatient / community care for SAM without complications and with good appetite
    • Energy-dense, nutrient-rich food (additional take-home ration or therapeutic food as per the national protocol), frequent small feeds, continued breastfeeding.
    • Routine medicines as per protocol – a course of oral amoxicillin, deworming, Vitamin A and iron–folic acid as indicated; treatment of infections.
    • Weekly or fortnightly follow-up – weight, MUAC, oedema, appetite, illness; referral if the child deteriorates.
  5. Management of MAM – supplementary nutrition through ICDS, counselling on feeding and hygiene, monthly monitoring.
  6. Discharge and follow-up – usually when weight-for-height is above –2 SD or MUAC is 12.5 cm or more, without oedema, for at least two consecutive visits; continued growth monitoring to prevent relapse.
  7. Prevention – breastfeeding, complementary feeding, maternal nutrition, immunisation, sanitation, diarrhoea management.

Role of the nurse

  • Train Anganwadi workers and ASHAs in MUAC measurement and danger signs; conduct medical check-ups of SAM children; give routine medicines; refer and follow up NRC cases; counsel mothers; maintain line lists; ensure convergence of health and ICDS services.

Conclusion CMAM identifies SAM (WHZ below –3 SD, MUAC below 11.5 cm or bilateral oedema) and MAM in the community, refers complicated cases to NRCs, and treats uncomplicated cases at home or Anganwadi centres with energy-dense food, routine medicines and regular follow-up until recovery, with prevention through good feeding and hygiene.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Nutrition Assessment and Nutrition Education
question: Explain the Eat Right India movement.
answer_html:
Introduction Eat Right India is a movement launched in 2018 by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to transform the country's food system so that all citizens have access to safe, healthy and sustainable food. It uses a combination of regulation, capacity building, collaboration and citizen empowerment.

Three pillars

  1. Eat Safe – ensuring hygiene and safety of food at every stage.
    • Hygiene rating of restaurants and food outlets; Clean Street Food Hubs; Eat Right Station (railway stations); BHOG (Blissful Hygienic Offering to God) for places of worship; clean fruit and vegetable markets.
    • Training of food handlers (FoSTaC – Food Safety Training and Certification); Food Safety on Wheels mobile testing labs; simple tests for adulteration at home.
  2. Eat Healthy – reducing unhealthy food components and promoting balanced diets.
    • Limiting industrial trans fats in oils and fats (to not more than 2%).
    • "Aaj Se Thoda Kam" – gradually reducing salt, sugar and fat in the diet.
    • Food fortification – fortified rice, wheat flour, oil, milk and double-fortified salt marked with the "+F" logo.
    • Eat Right School and Eat Right Campus – healthy food in schools, hostels, hospitals and workplaces; restricting junk food near schools.
    • Promotion of millets and local, seasonal foods.
  3. Eat Sustainable – environment-friendly food practices.
    • Reducing food waste (food-sharing initiatives), RUCO (Repurpose Used Cooking Oil) – collecting used oil for biodiesel instead of repeated frying, sustainable packaging, local and seasonal produce.

Other features

  • Eat Right Challenge for districts and cities; certification of "Eat Right Campuses".
  • Mass media campaigns and information for consumers on labels.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Educate families about balanced diet, less salt, sugar and oil, avoiding reuse of frying oil, reading food labels and choosing fortified (+F) foods.
  • Promote Eat Right School principles and healthy mid-day meals; discourage junk food and sugary drinks among children.
  • Teach simple home tests for adulteration and safe food handling; report unsafe food outlets.
  • Link Eat Right messages with NCD prevention at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.

Conclusion Eat Right India, launched by FSSAI in 2018, promotes safe, healthy and sustainable food through hygiene ratings, food-handler training, limits on trans fats, reduction of salt, sugar and fat, food fortification, school and campus initiatives, RUCO and reduction of food waste, with nurses reinforcing these messages in the community.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Nutrition Assessment and Nutrition Education
question: Explain community mobilisation for nutrition – Poshan Maah, Poshan Pakhwada, community-based events and nutri-gardens.
answer_html:
Introduction Improving nutrition requires behaviour change in families and communities, not only supply of food. Under POSHAN Abhiyaan and Mission Poshan 2.0, the government promotes a "Jan Andolan" (people's movement) for nutrition, using campaigns and community events.

1. Poshan Maah (National Nutrition Month)

  • Celebrated every September since 2018.
  • Activities on themes such as anaemia prevention, growth monitoring, complementary feeding, breastfeeding, hygiene and sanitation, millets and healthy diets; rallies, recipe demonstrations, quizzes, anaemia camps and home visits, involving Anganwadi workers, ASHAs, ANMs, schools, self-help groups and Panchayats.

2. Poshan Pakhwada (Nutrition Fortnight)

  • Observed in March every year (since 2019), with similar activities focused on specific themes (e.g. care of the first 1,000 days, millets, "Poshan bhi, Padhai bhi").

3. Community-based events (CBEs) at Anganwadi centres

  • Held regularly (twice a month) to celebrate key moments and convey nutrition messages:
    • Godh Bharai – a baby-shower ceremony for pregnant women with messages on diet, rest, IFA, ANC and institutional delivery.
    • Annaprashan Diwas – starting complementary feeding at 6 months with demonstration of thick, energy-dense foods.
    • Celebrations of suposhan (good nutrition), school readiness, hand washing and anaemia awareness.

4. Poshan Vatika (nutri-gardens / kitchen gardens)

  • Gardens at Anganwadi centres, schools and homes growing green leafy vegetables, fruits, pulses and medicinal plants, providing fresh, diverse food and teaching families about dietary diversity; often linked with MGNREGA and the agriculture department.

5. Other mobilisation strategies

  • Recipe demonstrations using local and millet-based foods; cooking competitions.
  • Home visits and counselling during the first 1,000 days; mothers' groups and fathers' involvement.
  • Use of media and folk media (songs, street plays), social media, and convergence with health, education, sanitation and agriculture departments.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Plan and participate in Poshan Maah and Pakhwada activities in her area; conduct anaemia testing and treatment camps (Anemia Mukt Bharat), growth monitoring and counselling.
  • Conduct Godh Bharai and Annaprashan sessions with Anganwadi workers; demonstrate recipes.
  • Promote nutri-gardens and diet diversity; involve VHSNCs, SHGs and Panchayats; record and report activities.

Conclusion Community mobilisation turns nutrition into a people's movement through Poshan Maah (September), Poshan Pakhwada (March), community-based events such as Godh Bharai and Annaprashan, Poshan Vatikas and recipe demonstrations, with nurses providing technical guidance, counselling and convergence.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Nutrition Assessment and Nutrition Education
question: What is the Poshan Tracker?
answer_html:
The Poshan Tracker is a mobile application and dashboard launched in 2021 by the Ministry of Women and Child Development for real-time monitoring of Anganwadi services under Mission Poshan 2.0.

  • Anganwadi workers record beneficiary registration (children, pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls), daily attendance, take-home ration and hot-cooked meal distribution, and monthly height and weight of children.
  • It automatically classifies children as stunted, wasted or underweight using WHO growth standards and flags SAM and MAM for action.
  • Data are available at block, district, state and national levels for planning and supervision.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Nutrition Assessment and Nutrition Education
question: What is Shree Anna (millets)? State its nutritional importance.
answer_html:
Shree Anna is the name given by the Government of India to millets (coarse cereals) to promote their production and consumption; the United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets on India's proposal. Examples – jowar (sorghum), bajra (pearl millet), ragi (finger millet) and small millets such as kodo, kutki, foxtail, barnyard and proso. Nutritional importance

  • Rich in dietary fibre, protein, iron (bajra), calcium (ragi), B vitamins and antioxidants.
  • Low glycaemic index – useful in diabetes and obesity; gluten-free.
  • Hardy, drought-tolerant and climate-resilient crops. They are being included in PDS, ICDS and PM POSHAN meals.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Nutrition Assessment and Nutrition Education
question: What is the Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey (CNNS)?
answer_html:
The Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey (CNNS, 2016–18) was conducted by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with UNICEF and the Population Council.

  • It was the first national survey to measure micronutrient status using biochemical markers (anaemia, iron, vitamin A, vitamin D, zinc, folate, vitamin B12, iodine) in children and adolescents aged 0–19 years, along with anthropometry and feeding practices.
  • It also measured early risk factors for NCDs in adolescents – prediabetes, high cholesterol and high blood pressure – showing the double burden of malnutrition (undernutrition with emerging overweight and NCD risk).
  • Its findings guide national nutrition programmes such as Anemia Mukt Bharat and fortification.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communication Management and Health Education
question: (a) Define health education and state its aims and objectives. (3 marks) (b) Explain the principles, approaches and models of health education. (6 marks) (c) Describe the methods of health education and the role of the community health nurse. (6 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition, aims and objectives (3 marks) Definition

  • Health education is "any combination of learning experiences designed to help individuals and communities improve their health, by increasing their knowledge or influencing their attitudes" (WHO).
  • It has also been described as "the translation of what is known about health into desirable individual and community behaviour patterns by means of an educational process" (Grout).

Aims (WHO)

  1. To encourage people to adopt and sustain health-promoting lifestyles and practices.
  2. To promote the proper use of the health services available to them.
  3. To arouse interest in health improvement and develop a sense of responsibility for their own health and that of the community.

Objectives – informing people (knowledge), motivating them (attitude change) and guiding them into action (practice).

Contents – human biology, nutrition, hygiene (personal and environmental), family health (maternal and child care, family planning), prevention of communicable and non-communicable diseases, mental health, prevention of accidents, and the use of health services.

(b) Principles, approaches and models (6 marks) Principles of health education

  1. Credibility – messages must be consistent with scientific knowledge and local culture and come from a trusted source.
  2. Interest – people learn what interests them and meets their felt needs.
  3. Participation – active involvement of the learners (discussion, planning) increases acceptance.
  4. Motivation – awakening the desire to learn and change (incentives, rewards, examples).
  5. Comprehension – use simple language, local terms and the level of the audience.
  6. Reinforcement – repetition of messages at intervals.
  7. Learning by doing – demonstration and return demonstration ("I hear and I forget; I see and I remember; I do and I understand").
  8. Known to unknown – start from what people already know.
  9. Setting an example – the health worker practises what she teaches.
  10. Good human relations – a friendly, respectful approach.
  11. Feedback – checking understanding and correcting misconceptions.
  12. Leaders – working through local leaders, teachers and influential persons.

Approaches

  • Regulatory approach – using laws and regulations (e.g. bans on smoking in public places, food safety laws) – effective but may not change attitudes.
  • Service approach – providing services at people's doorstep (e.g. immunisation outreach) – fails if people do not feel the need.
  • Health education approach – changing knowledge, attitudes and behaviour through education – slower but long-lasting.
  • Primary health care approach – active community participation in identifying needs and solving problems ("by the people, for the people").

Models

  • Medical model – treats health education as an extension of medical care; focuses on disease.
  • Motivation (KAP) model – knowledge leads to attitude change, which leads to change in practice; but a KAP gap often exists.
  • Social intervention model – changes in the social and physical environment and policies make healthy choices easier.
  • Health belief model (Rosenstock) – people act if they perceive susceptibility and severity of a disease, benefits of action outweighing barriers, with cues to action and self-efficacy.
  • Stages of change (transtheoretical) model – precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance; messages are matched to the stage.
  • Stages of adoption of new ideas – awareness, interest, evaluation, trial and adoption.

(c) Methods of health education and role of the nurse (6 marks) 1. Individual approach

  • Personal contact, interview and counselling during home visits, clinics and hospital care; personal letters and phone calls.
  • Advantages – two-way, personalised, confidential, allows discussion of individual problems; limitation – reaches few people.

2. Group approach

  • Lecture / health talk – for a group of about 20–30; short (15–20 minutes) with visual aids.
  • Demonstration – showing step by step how to do something (ORS preparation, hand washing, breast self-examination, cooking a weaning food) with return demonstration.
  • Group discussion – 6–12 members discuss a topic with a leader; promotes participation and decision-making.
  • Role play, case studies, puppet shows – for attitudes and behaviour.
  • Panel discussion, symposium, workshop, seminar and conference – for informed and professional groups.
  • Film shows and exhibitions.

3. Mass approach

  • Television and radio (including community radio), newspapers and magazines, posters, hoardings and wall paintings, health exhibitions and campaigns, folk media (street plays, folk songs), internet, social media and mobile phone messages (e.g. Kilkari audio messages to pregnant women and mothers).
  • Advantages – wide reach, quick, repetitive; limitations – mostly one-way, no feedback, may not change behaviour by itself; best combined with interpersonal communication.

Planning and evaluation of health education

  • Identify needs, define objectives, select content, methods and aids, implement, and evaluate (knowledge tests, observation of practices, coverage indicators such as ORS use or immunisation).

Role of the community health nurse

  • Assess learning needs of individuals, families and groups; plan and conduct health talks, demonstrations and group discussions in homes, Anganwadis, schools, workplaces and VHSNDs.
  • Use suitable aids (flash cards, flip charts, models, real objects) and local language; involve ASHAs, teachers, self-help groups and leaders.
  • Counsel individuals (pregnant women, TB and NCD patients, adolescents, couples).
  • Organise campaigns on special days (World Health Day, Breastfeeding Week, Poshan Maah, World TB Day) and use media wisely.
  • Set an example of healthy behaviour; evaluate the impact of education and give follow-up.

Barriers to effective health education in the community

  • Audience-related – illiteracy, poverty and pressing daily needs, strong traditional beliefs and taboos, fear, fatalism, language differences.
  • Health worker-related – lack of preparation and skills, use of technical language, poor rapport, inconsistency between what is taught and what is practised.
  • System-related – lack of services to support the advice (e.g. no ORS, no toilets), lack of IEC material, time constraints.
  • Overcoming them – needs-based, participatory sessions in local language; demonstration; working with trusted local leaders; linking education with services; repeated contacts.

Evaluation of health education

  • Process evaluation – were sessions held as planned, how many attended, quality of delivery.
  • Impact evaluation – change in knowledge and attitudes (questions, pre- and post-tests).
  • Outcome evaluation – change in practices and health status (ORS use, exclusive breastfeeding rate, latrine use, immunisation coverage, reduction in diarrhoea).

Special days used for health education – World Health Day (7 April), World TB Day (24 March), World No Tobacco Day (31 May), World Breastfeeding Week (1–7 August), World AIDS Day (1 December), Global Handwashing Day (15 October) – each provides a focus for campaigns, rallies and school activities.

Nursing importance

  • Almost every contact the nurse has with people is an opportunity for health education; effective education changes behaviours that prevent diseases far more cheaply than treatment.

Conclusion Health education is a combination of learning experiences that helps people improve their health by changing knowledge, attitudes and practices. It is guided by principles such as credibility, interest, participation, motivation, comprehension, reinforcement and learning by doing; delivered through regulatory, service, educational and primary health care approaches; explained by models such as KAP, the health belief model and stages of change; and conveyed by individual, group and mass methods – with the community health nurse as planner, teacher, counsellor, motivator and role model.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communication Management and Health Education
question: Explain IEC and BCC in community health, with the IEC materials used.
answer_html:
IEC (Information, Education and Communication)

  • An approach that attempts to change or reinforce health-related behaviour in a target audience, concerning a specific problem and within a defined period, through communication methods and principles.
  • Focuses on providing information and creating awareness using materials and media.

BCC (Behaviour Change Communication)

  • An interactive process with communities to develop tailored messages and approaches using a variety of communication channels, in order to develop positive behaviours, promote and sustain behaviour change and create a supportive environment.
  • Goes beyond awareness to actual, sustained change in practice.

Differences

  • IEC is mainly information-centred and often one-way; BCC is behaviour-centred, participatory and two-way.
  • IEC aims at knowledge and awareness; BCC aims at specific, measurable behaviours (e.g. exclusive breastfeeding, latrine use) and addresses barriers to change.
  • BCC uses audience research, interpersonal communication, community mobilisation and media together.

Steps in planning a BCC strategy

  1. Identify the problem and the target behaviour.
  2. Analyse the target audience (primary – mothers; secondary – husbands, mothers-in-law; tertiary – leaders) and the barriers and motivators.
  3. Set measurable communication objectives.
  4. Develop messages – simple, culturally appropriate, positive, actionable.
  5. Select channels – interpersonal, group, mass and folk media, digital media.
  6. Pre-test materials with a sample of the audience; revise.
  7. Implement, monitor and evaluate behaviour change.

IEC materials and aids

  • Print – posters, pamphlets and leaflets, booklets, wall writings, banners, hoardings.
  • Interpersonal aids – flip charts and flash cards (pictures with key messages for small groups), flannelgraphs, models and specimens, real objects (ORS packet, condoms, IFA tablets).
  • Audio-visual – videos, films, slides, audio messages, songs.
  • Folk and traditional media – puppets, street plays, folk songs.
  • Digital – social media posts, WhatsApp messages, mobile apps, IVR messages.

Characteristics of good IEC material

  • Simple, clear and in local language; pictures relevant to the local culture; one main message; accurate and consistent with programme guidelines; attractive; pre-tested; gives a clear action ("Give ORS after every loose stool").

Role of the nurse

  • Use IEC materials skilfully during home visits, group sessions and clinics; adapt messages to the audience; pre-test locally; display posters at sub-centres and Anganwadis; combine materials with counselling and demonstration; evaluate whether behaviours change.

Conclusion IEC provides information and awareness through communication materials, while BCC is an interactive, participatory process aimed at specific and sustained behaviour change. Good IEC materials – print, flip charts, flash cards, models, audio-visual, folk and digital media – must be simple, local, accurate and pre-tested, and the nurse combines them with interpersonal communication.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communication Management and Health Education
question: Explain the role of mass media in health education.
tags: combining mass media with interpersonal communication
answer_html:
Introduction Mass media are channels that carry messages to large numbers of people at the same time. They are powerful tools for creating awareness, setting the public agenda and reinforcing health messages, especially during campaigns and emergencies.

Types of mass media

  1. Television – health programmes, advertisements, serials with health themes, news; reaches both literate and illiterate audiences.
  2. Radio – All India Radio and community radio; cheap and accessible in rural areas, in local languages.
  3. Print media – newspapers, magazines, health columns, posters, pamphlets, hoardings and wall paintings.
  4. Cinema – short films and advertisements before movies.
  5. Internet and social media – websites, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp; growing rapidly among young people.
  6. Mobile phones (mHealth) – SMS and voice messages, e.g. Kilkari (weekly audio messages to pregnant women and mothers about pregnancy, childbirth and child care), apps, helplines.
  7. Outdoor media – banners at bus stands, railway stations, buses and health facilities.

Advantages

  • Wide reach in a short time; low cost per person reached.
  • Can create awareness and interest and keep issues in the public mind (e.g. polio, COVID-19 vaccination, TB).
  • Messages can be repeated and made attractive.
  • Useful in emergencies and outbreaks for quick information.

Limitations

  • Mostly one-way – no immediate feedback; cannot answer individual questions.
  • Messages are general, not tailored to individuals.
  • May not reach the poorest, illiterate or remote groups; requires electricity, devices and connectivity.
  • Awareness does not always lead to behaviour change.
  • Social media may spread misinformation and rumours (e.g. about vaccines).

Making mass media effective

  • Use simple, culturally appropriate messages; repetition across channels; trusted celebrities and local leaders.
  • Combine mass media with interpersonal communication – health workers follow up the messages through home visits and group sessions.
  • Monitor and counter misinformation with correct information.

Role of the nurse

  • Reinforce mass-media messages during home visits and clinics; discuss what people have seen or heard; clarify doubts and myths.
  • Use local media – community radio talks, newspaper articles, social media groups of the village, WhatsApp messages from verified sources.
  • Help women register for services such as Kilkari; guide young people to reliable online information.

Conclusion Mass media – television, radio, print, cinema, internet, social media and mobile phones – can reach large audiences quickly and create awareness, but are largely one-way and may spread misinformation; they are most effective when combined with interpersonal communication by nurses and other health workers.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communication Management and Health Education
question: Explain the use of folk (traditional) media in health education.
answer_html:
Introduction Folk media are the traditional forms of communication and entertainment of a community – songs, dances, drama, puppetry and storytelling – rooted in local culture and language. They are effective for health education in rural India, where people trust and enjoy these forms.

Common forms of folk media in India

  • Puppetry – string puppets (kathputli of Rajasthan), shadow and glove puppets; very popular with children.
  • Street plays (nukkad natak) – short dramas performed in streets and markets on themes such as dowry, alcoholism, girl child, sanitation, TB, HIV.
  • Folk songs and devotional music – bhajans, kirtans, qawwali, songs at weddings and festivals carrying health messages.
  • Storytelling forms – Harikatha, Burrakatha (Andhra Pradesh), Kathakalakshepam.
  • Folk theatre and dance – Yakshagana (Karnataka), Tamasha and Lavani (Maharashtra), Powada (ballads of Maharashtra), Bhavai (Gujarat), Nautanki (Uttar Pradesh), Jatra (Bengal and Odisha).
  • Rangoli and wall paintings at festivals; mela stalls.

Advantages

  • Culturally acceptable and familiar; uses local language and idioms.
  • Entertaining – attracts large audiences, including illiterate people, women and children.
  • Participatory – the audience can interact; local artists can be involved.
  • Low cost and flexible; messages are easily remembered through songs and stories.
  • Can address sensitive topics (gender, family planning, HIV) indirectly through characters.

Limitations

  • Needs skilled, trained performers; messages may get distorted or diluted by entertainment.
  • Limited reach compared with mass media; performances need planning and permissions.
  • Must be pre-tested to ensure the message is correct and not offensive.

Planning a folk media programme

  1. Identify the health problem and target audience.
  2. Select the suitable folk form and local artists; train them on correct messages.
  3. Prepare the script with simple, clear, positive messages and a clear call to action.
  4. Pre-test with a small audience; finalise.
  5. Arrange the venue and timing (market days, fairs, festivals, evenings).
  6. Perform, followed by discussion and distribution of IEC material; link with services (e.g. a health camp).
  7. Evaluate audience response and later behaviour change.

Use in national programmes – the Song and Drama Division (Ministry of Information and Broadcasting) and state health departments use folk troupes for campaigns on family welfare, TB, HIV/AIDS, leprosy, sanitation and immunisation.

Role of the nurse – identify local folk artists and forms; help prepare accurate scripts; organise performances with ASHAs, SHGs and schools; follow up with counselling and services.

Conclusion Folk media such as puppetry, street plays, folk songs, storytelling and regional theatre (Tamasha, Powada, Burrakatha, Nautanki) are culturally acceptable, entertaining and participatory channels that carry health messages effectively to rural and illiterate audiences, provided the messages are accurate, pre-tested and followed up by health services.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communication Management and Health Education
question: Explain how to plan and conduct a health talk in the community.
answer_html:
Introduction A health talk is a short, informal educational session given to a small group (about 15–30 people) on a specific health topic. It is the most common method of group health education used by community health nurses at Anganwadis, sub-centres, schools and VHSNDs.

A. Planning (before the talk)

  1. Know the audience – age, sex, education, language, culture, needs and existing knowledge (e.g. mothers of young children).
  2. Select the topic according to felt needs and current problems (diarrhoea in the monsoon, anaemia, breastfeeding).
  3. Set objectives – what the audience should know or be able to do at the end (e.g. "mothers will be able to prepare ORS correctly").
  4. Prepare the content – a few key points, simple and relevant, with local examples; avoid too much information.
  5. Choose methods and aids – flash cards, flip chart, poster, model, real objects for demonstration (ORS packet, clean vessel, measuring glass).
  6. Arrange time and place – convenient for the audience (avoid working hours), a quiet, shaded, comfortable place with seating in a semicircle; inform the participants beforehand through ASHA/AWW.
  7. Duration – about 15–20 minutes with time for questions.

B. Conducting the talk

  1. Introduction – greet the audience, introduce yourself, build rapport, state the topic and why it matters to them (e.g. a local case).
  2. Body – explain the key points step by step in local language, using simple words, examples and visual aids; demonstrate where possible; maintain eye contact; speak clearly and audibly.
  3. Interaction – ask questions, encourage the audience to share experiences and doubts; correct misconceptions gently; praise good practices.
  4. Return demonstration – ask one or two participants to repeat the skill.
  5. Summary – repeat the main messages and give a clear take-home message ("Give ORS after every loose stool and continue breastfeeding"); distribute leaflets if useful.
  6. Closing – thank the audience; inform them where to get services.

C. Evaluation and follow-up

  • Ask oral questions; observe return demonstrations; later, during home visits, check whether the practice has been adopted.
  • Record the topic, date, participants and feedback; plan the next session.

Do's and don'ts
