  • Do – be punctual, well prepared, friendly and confident; respect beliefs; keep it short; use aids that everyone can see; involve the audience.
  • Don't – use technical terms, read from notes, criticise local customs harshly, give too many messages, or argue with participants.

Conclusion A good health talk is planned around the audience's needs with clear objectives, simple content and suitable aids, delivered through an engaging introduction, clear explanation with demonstration, interaction, return demonstration and summary, and evaluated by questions and later observation of practice.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communication Management and Health Education
question: What is social and behaviour change communication (SBCC)?
answer_html:
Social and behaviour change communication (SBCC) is the strategic use of communication to promote positive health behaviours at individual, family, community and societal levels, by changing not only individual behaviour but also social norms and the environment that influence it. Three main approaches

  1. Advocacy – to obtain political and policy support and resources.
  2. Social mobilisation – to engage communities, leaders, institutions and partners.
  3. Behaviour change communication – interpersonal, group and media communication with individuals and families. SBCC is research-based, audience-centred and participatory and uses multiple channels (interpersonal, mass, folk and digital media) – e.g. campaigns for breastfeeding, sanitation, immunisation and TB.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communication Management and Health Education
question: What is the health belief model?
answer_html:
The health belief model (Rosenstock and colleagues, 1950s) explains why people do or do not take health actions. A person is likely to act (e.g. get screened, take a vaccine) when:

  1. Perceived susceptibility – he believes he is at risk of the disease.
  2. Perceived severity – he believes the disease is serious.
  3. Perceived benefits – he believes the action will reduce the risk or severity.
  4. Perceived barriers – he sees few obstacles (cost, pain, time, fear).
  5. Cues to action – a trigger such as a symptom, advice or a health campaign.
  6. Self-efficacy – confidence in his ability to take the action. Health education uses the model to increase perceived risk and benefits and reduce barriers.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communication Management and Health Education
question: What is the GATHER approach in counselling?
answer_html:
GATHER is a widely used framework for counselling, especially in family planning:

  • G – Greet the client warmly and respectfully; ensure privacy.
  • A – Ask about her needs, concerns, health and previous experience.
  • T – Tell her about the available options (methods), their benefits and side effects.
  • H – Help her choose the option best suited to her needs (informed choice).
  • E – Explain how to use the chosen method, possible side effects and what to do.
  • R – Return – plan a return or follow-up visit; welcome her to come back at any time. It ensures two-way, client-centred, informed decision-making.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communication Management and Health Education
question: What is the KAP gap?
answer_html:
The KAP gap is the difference between people's knowledge and attitude on one hand and their actual practice on the other. People may know a health fact and agree with it, yet not practise it.

  • Example – most mothers know that ORS prevents dehydration, but many do not give it during diarrhoea; people know tobacco is harmful but continue to use it.
  • Causes – lack of motivation, cultural beliefs, family pressure, cost, lack of access, habits and lack of skills.
  • Bridging the gap – motivation, demonstration and practice, removing barriers (making services available), involving family and leaders, reinforcement and follow-up – the real aim of health education is to change practice, not only knowledge.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Community Health Nursing Approaches, Concepts, Roles and Responsibilities of Community Health Nursing Personnel
question: (a) Define home visit and state its purposes. (3 marks) (b) Explain the principles of home visiting and the steps of conducting a home visit. (8 marks) (c) Describe the qualities of effective communication during a home visit. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Steps of a home visit
labels: plan route and time) – during visit (greet and introduce

answer_html:
(a) Definition and purposes (3 marks) Definition A home visit is a planned, purposeful, family-nurse contact in the home, which allows the community health nurse to assess the home and family situation and to provide the necessary nursing care, health education and related activities with the participation of the family (Ruth Freeman).

Purposes

  1. To assess the health needs of the family and its members in their real environment (housing, water, sanitation, food, relationships, resources).
  2. To provide nursing care – antenatal and postnatal care, newborn care, care of the sick, elderly and disabled.
  3. To give health education and demonstration using the family's own materials (ORS preparation, complementary food, hand washing).
  4. To follow up patients – TB, leprosy, hypertension, diabetes, mental illness, discharged patients, defaulters.
  5. Early detection of illness and risk factors (high-risk pregnancy, malnutrition, danger signs in newborns).
  6. To establish rapport and trust, and to motivate the family for services (immunisation, family planning, institutional delivery).
  7. To help the family use its own resources and community services, and to make referrals.
  8. To collect data for family records and surveys.

(b) Principles and steps of home visiting (8 marks) Principles

  1. Purposeful and planned – each visit has clear objectives based on the family's needs.
  2. Based on priorities – vulnerable members (newborns, postnatal mothers, pregnant women, sick children, the elderly) are given priority.
  3. Flexible – plans are adapted to the situation found in the home.
  4. Family participation and self-reliance – the family is involved in identifying problems and planning care; the nurse helps them to help themselves.
  5. Respect for the family's culture, beliefs, values, privacy and decisions.
  6. Teaching and demonstration with locally available, low-cost materials.
  7. Good interpersonal relationship and communication.
  8. Safety of the nurse and family, and infection control – use of the bag technique and hand washing.
  9. Confidentiality of information.
  10. Continuity – each visit is followed up; evaluation of progress at every visit.
  11. Accurate recording and reporting.
  12. Coordination with other health workers and agencies (ASHA, Anganwadi worker, PHC, social welfare).
  13. Economy of time and effort – visits are short and well organised; families visited in a planned route.

Steps of a home visit A. Pre-visit (planning)

  • Review the family folder and previous records; list problems and objectives.
  • Decide priorities – newborns and postnatal mothers first, then antenatal mothers, children, the sick and elderly; infectious cases (e.g. TB, skin infections) are visited last to prevent spread.
  • Prepare the community health nursing bag, IEC materials, records and medicines.
  • Plan the route and time convenient to the family; inform the family through the ASHA if possible.

B. During the visit

  1. Greet the family courteously, introduce yourself (or be introduced by the ASHA) and explain the purpose of the visit.
  2. Establish rapport – sit with the family, show interest, use local language.
  3. Assess – observe the house and surroundings, interview family members, examine the mother, child or patient (vital signs, weight, Hb, BP), check MCP card and medicines.
  4. Identify problems together with the family and decide priorities.
  5. Provide care using the bag technique – dressing, injections where needed, newborn care, examination of the pregnant woman.
  6. Health education and demonstration relevant to the problem; check understanding by return demonstration.
  7. Plan with the family – what they will do, what the nurse will do; involve the decision-makers (husband, mother-in-law).
  8. Refer when needed, with a referral slip and transport information.
  9. Fix the date of the next visit, summarise the advice and take leave courteously.

C. Post-visit

  • Record findings, care given, advice and plans in the family folder and registers.
  • Evaluate whether objectives were achieved; plan follow-up.
  • Report cases needing action (outbreaks, high-risk cases) to the PHC.
  • Clean and replenish the bag; dispose of waste safely.

(c) Qualities of effective communication during a home visit (4 marks)

  1. Clear and simple language – the local dialect, short sentences, no medical jargon.
  2. Active listening – attention to what the family says and feels; not interrupting.
  3. Empathy and respect – understanding their situation and feelings; addressing elders respectfully.
  4. Non-judgemental attitude – not blaming or criticising their practices; correcting gently.
  5. Appropriate non-verbal communication – a smile, relaxed posture, culturally appropriate eye contact and touch, sitting at the same level.
  6. Two-way communication – encouraging questions and feedback; checking understanding (teach-back: "Can you tell me how you will prepare ORS?").
  7. Honesty and consistency – giving correct information and keeping promises.
  8. Patience – allowing time, repeating when needed.
  9. Cultural sensitivity – awareness of customs, gender norms and taboos; communicating with the right family members.
  10. Confidentiality – private matters discussed privately.
  11. Positive reinforcement – praising good practices to encourage continuation.
  12. Communication that is clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous (the "7 Cs").

Advantages and limitations of home visits

  • Advantages – care and teaching in the real home situation; involvement of the whole family; better understanding of social and environmental factors; reaches those who cannot come to the clinic (newborns, the sick, elderly, women with restrictions); builds trust.
  • Limitations – time-consuming and costly in travel; fewer people reached per day; possible interruptions and lack of privacy; safety concerns in some areas.

Frequency of home visits (examples)

  • Home-based newborn care – ASHA visits on days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42 after institutional delivery (extra visits for low birth weight babies).
  • Home-based care of the young child – quarterly visits from 3 to 15 months.
  • Antenatal mothers – at least monthly, more often for high-risk cases; TB, leprosy and NCD patients – as per programme schedules; defaulters – immediately.

Safety of the nurse during home visits

  • Inform the supervisor or colleagues of the route; visit in daylight; go with the ASHA in unfamiliar or difficult areas; keep a mobile phone; be alert to aggressive animals, unsafe structures and hostile situations; leave if there is a threat.

Documentation of a home visit – date and time, purpose, persons met, findings (observation, examination, measurements), problems identified, care and advice given, the family's response, referral made, and the plan and date of the next visit.

Nursing importance

  • Home visits are the heart of community health nursing; through them the nurse sees the real conditions in which families live and can give care and advice that fits their situation.

Conclusion A home visit is a planned family–nurse contact in the home to assess needs and provide care, education and follow-up. It is guided by principles such as purposeful planning, priorities, flexibility, family participation, respect, demonstration with local materials, safety, confidentiality, continuity, recording and coordination, and proceeds through pre-visit planning, the visit itself (using the bag technique) and post-visit recording and evaluation. Effective communication – simple, empathetic, respectful, two-way, culturally sensitive and confidential – makes the visit successful.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Community Health Nursing Approaches, Concepts, Roles and Responsibilities of Community Health Nursing Personnel
question: (a) Explain the community health nursing process. (3 marks) (b) Describe the methods of community assessment and the formulation of a community diagnosis. (7 marks) (c) Explain the planning, implementation and evaluation of community health nursing services. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: The community health nursing process
labels: PRA) – community diagnosis and prioritisation – planning (goals
resources) – implementation (with community participation and intersectoral coordination) – evaluation (structure

answer_html:
(a) The community health nursing process (3 marks)

  • The nursing process applied to the community as the client – a systematic, scientific and continuous problem-solving method used to identify and meet the health needs of a community.
  • Steps – assessment, community diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation, carried out with the community (community participation) and in coordination with other sectors.
  • Characteristics – population-focused, emphasises prevention and health promotion, uses epidemiological data, involves partnership with families, groups and leaders, and is cyclical (evaluation leads to reassessment).

(b) Community assessment and community diagnosis (7 marks) A. Components to be assessed

  1. Demographic – population size, age–sex distribution, families, birth and death rates, migration, vulnerable groups (pregnant women, under-fives, elderly, disabled).
  2. Socio-economic and cultural – occupations, income, literacy, caste and religious groups, customs, beliefs, food habits, health practices, leadership and power structure.
  3. Environmental – housing, water sources, sanitation and latrines, drainage, waste disposal, breeding sites, roads, pollution, hazards.
  4. Health status – vital statistics (IMR, MMR), morbidity (common illnesses, TB, malaria, NCDs, malnutrition, anaemia), disability, immunisation and ANC coverage.
  5. Health resources and services – sub-centre/AAM, PHC, private practitioners, AYUSH, Anganwadis, schools, NGOs, transport, communication, and their use by the community.
  6. Community organisation – Panchayat, VHSNC, self-help groups, youth clubs, religious bodies.

B. Methods of data collection

  • Community survey – house-to-house survey with a structured schedule (family folder data); the most complete method.
  • Windshield survey – systematic observation while moving through the community (housing, people, services, environment) to get a quick general picture.
  • Key informant interviews – with leaders, teachers, ASHAs, Anganwadi workers, local practitioners.
  • Focus group discussions – with women's groups, adolescents, farmers on specific issues.
  • Participatory rural appraisal (PRA) – social and resource mapping, transect walk, seasonal calendar (e.g. malaria peaks), Venn diagrams of institutions, ranking exercises – done by the community with the nurse.
  • Community meetings (Gram Sabha, VHSNC).
  • Secondary data – census, HMIS, NFHS, sub-centre registers (eligible couple, ANC, immunisation, births and deaths), school records, disease surveillance data.

C. Analysis and community diagnosis

  • Compile and analyse data; calculate rates and percentages; compare with district, state and national figures; identify health problems, risk factors, needs and strengths.
  • Community diagnosis – a summary statement of the community's health status and problems, e.g. "High prevalence of anaemia (65%) among adolescent girls of village X related to inadequate dietary iron, worm infestation and poor IFA compliance, as evidenced by low haemoglobin and food habits survey."
  • Prioritisation of problems using criteria such as magnitude (how many are affected), severity (deaths, disability), vulnerability to intervention (feasibility), community concern, cost and available resources, and urgency.

(c) Planning, implementation and evaluation (5 marks) Planning

  • Set goals and SMART objectives (e.g. "increase full immunisation coverage in the hamlet from 70% to 95% in one year").
  • Choose strategies and activities – health education, outreach sessions, screening camps, home visits, IFA distribution, sanitation drives.
  • Prepare an action plan – who will do what, when, where, with what resources and budget.
  • Involve the community and other sectors in planning.

Implementation

  • Carry out activities through the health team (CHO, ANM, MPW, ASHA, Anganwadi worker) with community participation (VHSNC, SHGs, youth groups, school children).
  • Intersectoral coordination – ICDS, education, water and sanitation, agriculture, Panchayati Raj.
  • Supervise, motivate, maintain records and solve problems as they arise.

Evaluation

  • Structure evaluation – adequacy of staff, supplies, facilities.
  • Process evaluation – whether activities were carried out as planned (number of sessions, coverage).
  • Outcome evaluation – changes in knowledge, practices and health indicators (coverage, prevalence, mortality).
  • Use evaluation results to reassess and replan – the process is a continuous cycle.

Example – community diagnosis and plan

  • Assessment finding – in a village of 1,500 people, the immunisation register and house survey show that only 68% of children aged 12–23 months are fully immunised; most defaulters belong to a migrant labour hamlet; mothers fear fever after vaccines; the session site is far from the hamlet.
  • Community diagnosis – "Low full immunisation coverage (68%) among children of 12–23 months in village X, related to fear of side effects, distance from the session site and seasonal migration, as evidenced by the immunisation register and survey."
  • Objective – raise full immunisation coverage to at least 90% within one year.
  • Plan and implementation – a due list prepared with the ASHA; an additional session site in the hamlet on a convenient day; counselling of mothers about minor side effects and their management; involvement of the sarpanch and women's SHG; tracking of migrant families through U-WIN; reminders on the day before sessions.
  • Evaluation – monthly review of coverage, dropout rates (e.g. Pentavalent 1 to 3) and AEFI reports; reassessment after one year.

Principles of community participation

  • Involve the community from the beginning – in identifying problems, setting priorities, planning and evaluation.
  • Respect local knowledge, culture and leadership; work through existing groups (VHSNC, SHGs, youth clubs, Gram Sabha).
  • Share information openly; build local capacity so that the community becomes self-reliant.
  • Ensure participation of the poor, women and marginalised groups, not only of influential persons.

Contents of a community survey schedule (examples) – household identification and caste/religion, family members with age, sex, education and occupation, income, housing and environmental sanitation, water source, latrine, cooking fuel, vital events in the past year, illnesses and disabilities, immunisation and family planning status, food habits, health care use, and health insurance.

Approaches used in community health nursing

  • Nursing process approach – systematic assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation.
  • Epidemiological approach – using data on the distribution and determinants of disease to identify high-risk groups and target interventions.
  • Problem-solving approach – defining problems clearly, finding causes and trying solutions step by step.
  • Family-centred and life-cycle approach – the family as the unit of care across all stages of life.
  • Evidence-based and rights-based approaches – using current guidelines, research and respect for the rights and dignity of people.
  • Empowerment approach – building the community's capacity to manage its own health.

Role of the community health nurse in the process – she leads the survey with ASHAs and MPWs, analyses data from her registers, presents the findings to the VHSNC and Gram Sabha, helps the community choose priorities, prepares the sub-centre action plan, mobilises resources and partners, and monitors indicators every month.

Nursing importance

  • Applying the nursing process to the whole community enables the nurse to move from caring for individuals to improving the health of populations, targeting resources to the most important problems.

Conclusion The community health nursing process applies assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation to the community as client. Assessment uses surveys, windshield surveys, interviews, focus groups, PRA techniques and secondary data on demographic, socio-economic, environmental, health status and resource components, leading to a prioritised community diagnosis. Plans with SMART objectives are implemented with community participation and intersectoral coordination and evaluated for structure, process and outcome.

question: Explain the qualities of a community health nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction The community health nurse works largely independently in the field, with people of different cultures and in difficult conditions. Her effectiveness depends on a combination of personal, professional and social qualities.

A. Personal qualities

  1. Good physical health and stamina – for field work, travel and long hours.
  2. Pleasant personality – friendly, cheerful, approachable, neat and suitably dressed.
  3. Emotional maturity and stability – remains calm in emergencies and difficult situations.
  4. Patience, tolerance and perseverance – behaviour change in the community is slow.
  5. Honesty, integrity and sincerity – trusted by the community.
  6. Empathy, kindness and respect for people, irrespective of caste, religion, gender or economic status.
  7. Adaptability and resourcefulness – improvises with locally available materials; adjusts to rural, urban and tribal settings.
  8. Tact, sense of humour and good judgement.
  9. Punctuality, self-discipline and reliability.
  10. Courage and initiative – to work in remote areas and take decisions.

B. Professional qualities

  1. Sound knowledge of community health nursing, epidemiology, national health programmes and current guidelines.
  2. Competence in nursing skills – antenatal, intranatal and postnatal care, newborn care, immunisation, first aid, NCD screening, laboratory tests, bag technique.
  3. Communication and teaching skills – health education, counselling, use of IEC material, local language.
  4. Leadership and management skills – planning, organising, supervising ASHAs and MPWs, team building, decision-making, problem-solving.
  5. Accurate recording and reporting; use of digital applications.
  6. Ethical and legal awareness – confidentiality, consent, rights of clients, medico-legal duties.
  7. Research-mindedness – evidence-based practice, data use.
  8. Commitment to continuing education and professional development.
  9. Ability to work in a team and to coordinate with other departments.

C. Social qualities

  1. Cultural sensitivity – understanding and respecting local customs and beliefs.
  2. Good human relations with families, leaders and colleagues.
  3. Community involvement – ability to mobilise and organise people; respect for community decisions.
  4. Commitment to equity and social justice – special attention to the poor and vulnerable.
  5. Role model – practises healthy behaviours herself.

Conclusion A good community health nurse combines personal qualities (health, maturity, patience, honesty, empathy, adaptability, resourcefulness), professional qualities (knowledge, skills, communication, leadership, recording, ethics, research-mindedness, teamwork) and social qualities (cultural sensitivity, human relations, community involvement, commitment to equity and role modelling).

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Community Health Nursing Approaches, Concepts, Roles and Responsibilities of Community Health Nursing Personnel
question: Explain the roles and functions of the nurse in community health.
tags: role of nurse in community health
answer_html:
Introduction The community health nurse works with individuals, families, groups and the whole community to promote health, prevent disease, provide care and support rehabilitation. She plays many roles at different levels of the health system (ANM, CHO, PHN, supervisor).

Roles

  1. Care provider – direct nursing care at homes, sub-centres, clinics and camps: antenatal, intranatal and postnatal care, newborn and child care, treatment of minor ailments, first aid, care of the sick and elderly.
  2. Health educator – teaches healthy practices to individuals, families, schools and community groups.
  3. Counsellor – helps people make informed decisions (family planning, HIV testing, adherence to TB and NCD treatment, adolescent problems).
  4. Advocate – speaks for the needs and rights of vulnerable people; helps them access schemes and services.
  5. Case manager and coordinator – coordinates care across levels (referral and follow-up), and with ICDS, schools, Panchayat and NGOs.
  6. Collaborator and team member – works with doctors, MPWs, ASHAs, Anganwadi workers and other departments.
  7. Leader and manager – plans and organises services, manages supplies, drugs, cold chain and records; leads the AAM team (as CHO).
  8. Supervisor and trainer – supervises and trains ASHAs, Anganwadi workers, dais and student nurses.
  9. Community organiser and mobiliser – organises VHSNDs, campaigns and health committees; promotes community participation.
  10. Change agent – introduces new practices (KMC, ORS, latrine use) and helps the community accept change.
  11. Researcher – collects data, participates in surveys and research, uses evidence.
  12. Epidemiologist / surveillance worker – detects and reports outbreaks; participates in investigation and control.
  13. Consultant – gives expert advice to individuals, groups and organisations.

Functions in specific areas

  • Maternal and child health – registration, ANC, institutional delivery promotion, postnatal and newborn care, growth monitoring, IMNCI.
  • Family planning and reproductive health – counselling, distribution of contraceptives, IUCD insertion.
  • Immunisation – sessions, cold chain, due lists, AEFI management.
  • Communicable disease control – TB, malaria, leprosy, HIV, dengue – detection, treatment support, contact tracing.
  • Non-communicable diseases – population-based screening, follow-up, lifestyle counselling.
  • School health, adolescent health, occupational health, mental health, geriatric care, palliative care.
  • Environmental health – water, sanitation, vector control.
  • Disaster management – emergency care, prevention of outbreaks.
  • Records and reports – registers, MCP cards, HMIS and digital portals.

Conclusion In community health, the nurse is care provider, educator, counsellor, advocate, case manager, collaborator, leader and manager, supervisor and trainer, community organiser, change agent, researcher and surveillance worker – carrying out these roles across maternal and child health, family planning, immunisation, communicable and non-communicable disease control, school, occupational, environmental and mental health, disasters and record keeping.

question: Explain the bag technique in community health nursing.
answer_html:
Definition The bag technique is a tool used by the community health nurse during home visits to carry out nursing procedures with aseptic precautions, using a specially equipped community health nursing bag – minimising the spread of infection from one family to another while providing care.

Contents of the bag (typical)

  • Outer pocket / top – apron, hand towel, soap in a soap box, newspapers or paper bags, nail brush.
  • Inside
    • Thermometer(s) in a case, BP apparatus and stethoscope, measuring tape, weighing scale (spring balance for newborns).
    • Kidney tray, gallipot, scissors, artery and dissecting forceps, cotton, gauze, bandages, gloves.
    • Antiseptic lotion, spirit swabs, povidone-iodine, savlon.
    • Disposable syringes and needles, a puncture-proof sharps container.
    • Testing materials – urine testing strips (sugar and albumin), haemoglobin testing kit, rapid diagnostic test kits (malaria, pregnancy), glucometer.
    • Common medicines as per protocol – ORS, zinc, IFA, paracetamol, albendazole, antacid, contraceptives.
    • MCP cards, referral slips, forms, family folder, pen.
  • The bag should be clean, durable, washable and kept packed and ready.

Principles

  1. The bag is a clean area – it should not be placed on the floor, bed or on unclean surfaces.
  2. Hand washing before and after care is the key to preventing cross-infection.
  3. Only clean hands enter the bag; articles taken out are not returned until cleaned.
  4. The bag is placed on a clean, flat surface on a newspaper, out of reach of children and animals.
  5. Minimum articles are taken out for each procedure.
  6. Used articles are cleaned before being returned; waste is disposed of safely.
  7. The bag is cleaned and replenished after every visit.
  8. In homes with infectious disease, extra precautions are taken (bag not opened unnecessarily; such homes visited last).

Steps

  1. Choose a convenient, clean place, spread a newspaper and place the bag on it.
  2. Take out the apron and hand towel; wear the apron.
  3. Take out the soap; wash hands with soap and water (ask the family for water and a basin), dry with own towel.
  4. Open the bag and take out only the articles needed; place them on a clean paper; close the bag.
  5. Carry out the procedure (examination, dressing, injection, test) with aseptic technique; involve the family in watching (teaching).
  6. Clean the used articles (wash with soap and water, wipe with spirit) and dry them before returning them to the bag; discard disposables in a paper bag; put sharps in the sharps container.
  7. Wash hands again; remove the apron by folding the soiled side inwards and keep it in the outer pocket.
  8. Dispose of the waste paper bag safely (burn or bury, or carry back for disposal as per BMW rules).
  9. Record the procedure; replenish supplies later.

Conclusion The bag technique enables the community health nurse to give safe, aseptic care in homes by using a clean, well-equipped bag, placing it on a newspaper, washing hands, taking out only needed articles, cleaning items before returning them, disposing of waste safely and replenishing the bag after each visit.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Community Health Nursing Approaches, Concepts, Roles and Responsibilities of Community Health Nursing Personnel
question: Explain the roles and responsibilities of the Community Health Officer (CHO) at an Ayushman Arogya Mandir.
answer_html:
Introduction The Community Health Officer (CHO) is a mid-level health provider who leads the primary health care team at an Ayushman Arogya Mandir – Sub Health Centre (AAM-SHC) under Ayushman Bharat. CHOs are mainly B.Sc. nurses (or other eligible professionals) trained in community health through a certificate course or bridge programme. They bring comprehensive primary health care close to the community.

Roles and responsibilities 1. Clinical and service delivery

  • Provide the expanded service packages – maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health; family planning; management of common illnesses and minor injuries as per standard treatment protocols.
  • Population-based screening of persons aged 30 years and above for hypertension, diabetes and oral, breast and cervical cancers; follow-up and dispensing of medicines prescribed by medical officers; screening for TB, leprosy, mental health problems, eye and ENT problems.
  • Elderly and palliative care; emergency first aid and stabilisation.
  • Teleconsultation with the PHC medical officer or specialists through e-Sanjeevani.
  • Point-of-care diagnostics available at the centre.

2. Public health functions

  • Disease surveillance and outbreak reporting (IHIP), vector control activities, implementation of national programmes.
  • Health promotion – wellness sessions (yoga, meditation), health days, campaigns, school and Anganwadi activities.
  • Community mobilisation through the Jan Arogya Samiti, VHSNC and SHGs.

3. Team leadership and supervision

  • Leads the team of MPWs (female and male) and ASHAs; allocates work, supervises home visits, builds capacity and reviews performance.
  • Coordinates with Anganwadi workers, schools and Panchayat.

4. Management

  • Indent, storage and stock management of drugs, diagnostics and consumables; maintenance of equipment.
  • Management of untied funds and records of expenditure.
  • Digital records and reporting – AAM portal, NCD portal, RCH portal, Ni-kshay, U-WIN and others; ABHA creation.
  • Quality assurance (National Quality Assurance Standards for AAM-SHCs), infection control, biomedical waste management.

5. Referral and continuity of care

  • Referral to the PHC/CHC with transport; follow-up after discharge; linking with PM-JAY.

Performance – CHOs receive performance-linked incentives based on indicators of service delivery.

Conclusion The CHO is the clinical, public health and managerial leader of the AAM-SHC – providing comprehensive primary care including NCD screening and teleconsultation, conducting surveillance and health promotion, leading MPWs and ASHAs, managing drugs, funds and digital records, and ensuring referral and continuity of care – a major expanded role for B.Sc. nurses in India.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Community Health Nursing Approaches, Concepts, Roles and Responsibilities of Community Health Nursing Personnel
question: Explain the records and reports maintained in community health nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Records and reports are the written or digital documentation of services provided and information collected by community health workers. They are essential for continuity of care, planning, monitoring, evaluation and legal purposes.

Purposes

  • Continuity of care and follow-up of individuals and families; identification of due beneficiaries (due lists).
  • Planning and evaluation of services; calculation of coverage and health indicators.
  • Supervision and accountability; legal evidence (births, deaths, medico-legal cases).
  • Research, teaching and reporting to higher levels (HMIS).

Types of records

  1. Family records – the family folder (family health card) for every household: members, ages, health status, immunisation, family planning, illnesses, environment, visits.
  2. Registers at the sub-centre / AAM
    • Eligible couple register (for family planning).
    • Antenatal (MCH) register, delivery register, postnatal register.
    • Birth and death registers.
    • Immunisation register and due lists; child health and growth monitoring records.
    • Family planning register (methods, follow-up).
    • NCD register – population enumeration, CBAC (Community-Based Assessment Checklist) risk scores, screening results and treatment follow-up.
    • Communicable disease registers – TB (Ni-kshay), leprosy, fever/malaria (blood smear and RDT), outbreak records.
    • Stock and equipment registers, cold-chain temperature logs, untied fund records.
  3. Cards held by clients – Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card, immunisation cards, NCD personal health cards, TB treatment cards.

Reports

  • Monthly HMIS report of services (ANC, deliveries, immunisation, family planning, disease cases).
  • Weekly IDSP S-form (syndromic surveillance) through IHIP; immediate reporting of outbreaks.
  • Programme reports (NTEP, NCVBDC, NLEP, NP-NCD); special survey reports; annual reports.

Digital records – the RCH portal (name-based tracking of mothers and children), ANMOL tablet application for ANMs, AAM portal, NCD portal, Ni-kshay, U-WIN (immunisation), ABHA-linked digital health records.

Principles of good record keeping

  • Accurate, complete, concise, legible and written in standard terms.
  • Timely – recorded at the time of care; reports sent by due dates.
  • Dated and signed; corrections made properly (single line, initials).
  • Confidential and stored safely; used only for authorised purposes.
  • Uniform formats and regular verification by supervisors.

Conclusion Community health nursing records include family folders, registers (eligible couple, ANC, delivery, births and deaths, immunisation, family planning, NCD, communicable diseases, stock), client-held cards and digital portals, while reports include monthly HMIS, weekly IDSP and programme reports. Accurate, timely, confidential records ensure continuity of care, planning, evaluation and accountability.

question: What are standing orders?
answer_html:
Standing orders are written instructions, approved and signed by the competent medical authority, that authorise nurses and health workers to give specified treatment or care in defined situations without waiting for a doctor's individual order – especially in the community and in emergencies. Features

  • Clear, specific, written, dated and signed; reviewed periodically.
  • Specify the condition, drug or procedure, dose, route and when to refer. Examples – ORS and zinc for diarrhoea; paracetamol for fever; first dose of antibiotic before referral (IMNCI); management of PPH with oxytocin and misoprostol by ANMs; treatment of anaphylaxis with adrenaline during immunisation. They allow prompt care while protecting the nurse legally.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Community Health Nursing Approaches, Concepts, Roles and Responsibilities of Community Health Nursing Personnel
question: What is a windshield survey?
answer_html:
A windshield survey is a method of community assessment by systematic observation while moving through the community – on foot, by vehicle or bicycle – "as if looking through the windshield of a car". What is observed

  • Housing and its condition, overcrowding, slums.
  • Water sources, drains, garbage, latrines, breeding sites.
  • People – age groups, activities, street children, the elderly.
  • Services – schools, Anganwadis, health centres, shops, transport, places of worship, markets.
  • Signs of decay or development, hazards and pollution. Use – gives a quick overall picture of the community and helps plan a detailed survey; it is subjective and must be supplemented by other methods.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Community Health Nursing Approaches, Concepts, Roles and Responsibilities of Community Health Nursing Personnel
question: What is an eligible couple register?
answer_html:
An eligible couple is a currently married couple in which the wife is in the reproductive age group (15–49 years). The eligible couple register is maintained by the ANM at the sub-centre (with the help of ASHAs) and contains, for each eligible couple: names and ages of husband and wife, address, number and ages of living children, family planning method used (or none), date of adoption, pregnancy status and follow-up. Uses

  • Identifies couples needing family planning services and counselling.
  • Helps in planning and evaluating the family planning programme (couple protection rate).
  • Helps in early registration of pregnancies. It is updated regularly (usually every April) through house-to-house surveys.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Assisting Individuals and Families to Promote and Maintain their Health
question: (a) Explain why the family is the unit of care in community health nursing, and the family health tasks. (4 marks) (b) Describe family health assessment and the tools used. (6 marks) (c) Explain the family nursing process with examples of family nursing diagnoses. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Family assessment tools – genogram and ecomap
labels: genogram: a three-generation family tree using squares for males
with ages and illnesses noted; ecomap: the family in a central circle linked to outer circles (school
with arrows showing flow of support

answer_html:
(a) Family as the unit of care and family health tasks (4 marks) Definition – a family is a group of persons related by marriage, blood or adoption, usually living together, interacting with one another in their social roles and sharing a common culture. Types include nuclear, joint (extended), single-parent and others.

Why the family is the unit of care

  • The family is the basic unit of society and the primary unit of health care – most care of the sick, children and elderly is given at home.
  • Illness of one member affects all – emotionally, financially and in daily functioning.
  • Health beliefs, habits and behaviours (diet, hygiene, tobacco use, care-seeking) are learned and shared within the family.
  • Many health problems are shared – infections (TB, scabies), poor sanitation, malnutrition, genetic disorders.
  • The family decides whether and where care is sought; working with the family improves adherence and outcomes.
  • The family is a resource for prevention, care and rehabilitation.

Characteristics of a healthy family – good communication, mutual support and respect, shared values, flexible roles, ability to cope with stress and crisis, links with the community, and care for the health of each member.

Family health tasks (Freeman) – a family must be able to:

  1. Recognise the presence of a health problem or disturbance in growth and development.
  2. Make decisions about seeking appropriate care.
  3. Provide care to members who are sick, disabled, dependent or at risk.
  4. Maintain a home environment conducive to health and personal development.
  5. Use community resources (health services, schemes, support groups) appropriately. The nurse assesses how well the family performs these tasks and helps it to do so.

(b) Family health assessment and tools (6 marks) Areas assessed

  1. Family structure – members, ages, sex, education, occupation, roles, decision-maker, type of family.
  2. Family functions – economic (income, expenditure), affection and support, socialisation of children, reproduction, health care.
  3. Stage of the family life cycle (Duvall) – beginning family, childbearing, preschool, school-age, teenage, launching, middle-aged and ageing families – each with its own developmental tasks and health needs.
  4. Health status of each member – illnesses, disabilities, immunisation, nutrition, pregnancy, family planning, risk behaviours.
  5. Home environment – housing, ventilation, water, latrine, waste disposal, kitchen and fuel, animals, safety hazards.
  6. Family dynamics and coping – communication, relationships, conflicts, alcohol use, violence, stress and coping strategies.
  7. Resources and use of services – social support, schemes availed (ration card, PM-JAY, pensions), access to health services.

Tools

  • Family folder (family health record) – a file kept for each family with identification data, members, health status, environment, problems and visits.
  • Genogram – a three-generation family tree using standard symbols, showing relationships, ages, deaths and hereditary or chronic illnesses (diabetes, hypertension, mental illness).
  • Ecomap (Ann Hartman) – a diagram showing the family's relationships with outside systems (school, workplace, health centre, relatives, friends, religious groups, SHG) – strong, weak or stressful – and the flow of support.
  • Family APGAR (Smilkstein) – a 5-item questionnaire on Adaptation, Partnership, Growth, Affection and Resolve, scoring family functioning.
  • Family coping index (Freeman) – rates the family's ability to cope with health problems in areas such as physical independence, therapeutic competence, knowledge, attitude, emotional competence, family living patterns, physical environment and use of resources.
  • Observation, interview, physical examination, records and the MCP card.

(c) Family nursing process and examples of diagnoses (5 marks) Steps

  1. Assessment – as above, with the family's participation.
  2. Family nursing diagnosis – identifying health threats, health deficits, foreseeable crises and the family's ability to perform health tasks.
  3. Planning – setting goals with the family (contracting – an agreement about who will do what), giving priority to the family's felt needs and urgent problems.
  4. Implementation – direct care (home nursing, newborn care, dressing), health education and demonstration, counselling (family planning, adherence, conflicts), referral and linking with schemes, mobilising family and community resources, follow-up visits.
  5. Evaluation – changes in health status and practices; family's ability to manage independently; revision of the plan.

Examples of family nursing diagnoses

  • Health threat – "Risk of diarrhoeal disease in the family related to unsafe drinking water and open defecation."
  • Health deficit – "Moderate acute malnutrition of the 2-year-old child related to inadequate complementary feeding."
  • Foreseeable crisis / stress point – "Risk of complications related to pregnancy of a 17-year-old daughter-in-law" or "Anticipated stress related to the father's retirement."
  • Inability to perform health tasks – "Inability to provide care to the bedridden grandmother related to lack of knowledge of positioning and pressure-area care."
  • Ineffective family coping related to the father's alcohol dependence.

Role of the nurse in family health care

  • Builds a trusting relationship with all members; respects the family's culture and decisions; encourages self-reliance; coordinates with ASHAs, Anganwadi workers and other services; keeps the family folder up to date; uses every visit for promotion and prevention across the life cycle.

Health needs at stages of the family life cycle (Duvall)

  1. Beginning family (married couple without children) – premarital and marital counselling, preconception care (folic acid, Hb, rubella and thalassaemia screening where indicated), family planning for spacing the first pregnancy, adjustment to new roles.
  2. Childbearing family (oldest child up to 30 months) – antenatal, intranatal and postnatal care, newborn care, breastfeeding, immunisation, birth spacing, support to the mother for rest and nutrition.
  3. Family with preschool children – growth monitoring, complementary and family feeding, immunisation boosters, prevention of accidents and poisoning, early childhood stimulation, Anganwadi enrolment.
  4. Family with school-age children – school health, personal hygiene, dental and eye care, deworming, healthy eating, safety on the road.
  5. Family with teenagers – adolescent health (puberty, menstrual hygiene, nutrition, anaemia), prevention of substance use, early marriage and violence, communication between parents and teenagers.
  6. Launching family (children leaving home) – support for education, career and marriage decisions; adjustment of parents.
  7. Middle-aged family (empty nest to retirement) – screening for hypertension, diabetes and cancers, menopause care, lifestyle changes, financial planning.
  8. Ageing family – geriatric care, management of chronic illness and disability, fall prevention, social security and pensions, coping with loss of a spouse, palliative care.

Home-based care by the family

  • The nurse teaches family members to give simple care at home – bed bath, positioning and pressure-area care, feeding, medication supervision, wound care, recording temperature – using household articles and improvised equipment (a pressure-relieving ring from cloth, a bedpan from a basin).
  • She explains danger signs that need prompt referral, arranges supplies through the AAM, and supports the caregiver to prevent burnout.

Contents of the family folder – identification (house number, head of family, address), list of members with age, sex, education and occupation, socio-economic status, housing and sanitation, vital events, immunisation and family planning record, health problems of each member, nursing diagnoses, plans, and a record of each home visit.

Nursing importance

  • Working with the family as a unit allows the nurse to solve problems at their root – in the home, habits and relationships – and to involve the people who will actually provide day-to-day care.

Conclusion The family is the basic unit of society and of health care, and the community health nurse helps it perform Freeman's family health tasks. Family health assessment covers structure, functions, life-cycle stage, health status, environment, dynamics and resources, using the family folder, genogram, ecomap, family APGAR and the family coping index. The family nursing process then proceeds from diagnoses (health threats, deficits, foreseeable crises, inability to perform tasks) to planning with the family, implementation and evaluation.

question: (a) Explain the health problems and needs of adolescents. (5 marks) (b) Describe the Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) – its objectives, thematic areas and strategies. (7 marks) (c) Explain the role of the community health nurse in adolescent health. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Six thematic areas of RKSK
labels: nutrition; sexual and reproductive health; non-communicable diseases; substance misuse; injuries and violence (including gender-based violence); mental health – delivered through adolescent friendly health clinics

answer_html:
(a) Health problems and needs of adolescents (5 marks) Adolescence is the period of transition from childhood to adulthood, defined by WHO as 10–19 years of age. Adolescents form about one-fifth of India's population. Rapid physical, sexual, emotional and social changes occur, and behaviours formed now affect health throughout life.

Health problems

  1. Nutritional problems – anaemia (especially in girls), undernutrition and thinness, stunting, and increasingly overweight and obesity from junk food and inactivity.
  2. Sexual and reproductive health problems – early marriage and teenage pregnancy (risk of obstructed labour, low birth weight, maternal death), unsafe abortion, reproductive tract and sexually transmitted infections including HIV, menstrual problems and poor menstrual hygiene, lack of correct information about puberty.
  3. Mental health problems – stress (examinations, career), depression, anxiety, suicide (a leading cause of death among young people), self-harm, eating problems, internet and gaming addiction.
  4. Substance use – tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, inhalants and other drugs.
  5. Injuries and violence – road traffic accidents (two-wheelers), drowning, sexual abuse, gender-based violence, bullying, cyber-bullying.
  6. Non-communicable disease risk factors – unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, tobacco, hypertension and diabetes beginning in youth.
  7. Other problems – acne, skin infections, dental caries, refractive errors, worm infestations, school drop-out, child labour.

Needs – correct information and life skills, nutrition, safe environments, friendly health services with confidentiality, counselling, parental and peer support, opportunities for education and recreation, and protection from violence and early marriage.

(b) Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) (7 marks) Introduction – launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on 7 January 2014 under NHM; covers adolescents aged 10–19 years – boys and girls, married and unmarried, in and out of school, in rural and urban areas. It shifts from a clinic-based to a community-based, holistic approach.

Objectives (six thematic areas)

  1. Improve nutrition – reduce anaemia and malnutrition; also overweight and obesity.
  2. Improve sexual and reproductive health – reduce teenage pregnancies, improve knowledge and access to services.
  3. Promote mental health – emotional well-being, coping skills.
  4. Prevent injuries and violence, including gender-based violence.
  5. Prevent substance misuse.
  6. Address conditions for non-communicable diseases – healthy lifestyles.

Strategies and components

  1. Adolescent Friendly Health Clinics (AFHCs) – at PHCs, CHCs and district hospitals, with trained counsellors offering confidential counselling and services (nutrition, menstrual problems, contraception, RTI/STI, mental health, substance use).
  2. Peer education – "Saathiya" – trained adolescent peer educators (boys and girls) in villages who conduct sessions with their peers, provide information and refer to AFHCs; supported by the Saathiya Resource Kit and the Saathiya Salah mobile application.
  3. Adolescent Health and Wellness Days – quarterly village-level events with activities, quizzes, health check-ups and counselling.
  4. Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS) – weekly IFA tablets for adolescents (in schools and through Anganwadis for out-of-school girls) with biannual deworming (albendazole).
  5. Menstrual Hygiene Scheme – awareness and provision of low-cost sanitary napkins to adolescent girls in rural areas, with safe disposal.
  6. School-based activities – now through the Ayushman Bharat School Health and Wellness Programme (health and wellness ambassadors among teachers).
  7. Community-based interventions – involvement of parents, Panchayats, teachers and youth groups; convergence with education, women and child development and youth affairs departments.
  8. Counselling and IEC on life skills, gender equality, prevention of early marriage and violence; linkage with Tele-MANAS for mental health.

(c) Role of the community health nurse (3 marks)

  • Provide adolescent-friendly services – confidential, respectful, non-judgemental counselling and care; screen for anaemia, nutritional status, menstrual problems and mental health concerns.
  • Distribute WIFS and deworming tablets and monitor compliance; promote menstrual hygiene.
  • Train and support Saathiyas; organise Adolescent Health and Wellness Days and school sessions on life skills, puberty, nutrition and substance-use prevention.
  • Prevent early marriage and teenage pregnancy – counselling of families, awareness of the legal age of marriage, linkage with child protection services.
  • Identify and refer adolescents facing abuse, violence, depression or suicidal thoughts; maintain records and coordinate with schools and Anganwadis.

Characteristics of adolescent-friendly health services (WHO)

  • Accessible – convenient timings, low or no cost, close to where adolescents live or study.
  • Acceptable – confidential, private, non-judgemental and respectful; staff are trained to talk with young people.
  • Equitable – available to all adolescents, married or unmarried, boys and girls, in or out of school.
  • Appropriate – the services adolescents actually need are provided at one point.
  • Effective – the right care is given in the right way and produces positive results.

Psychosocial assessment of an adolescent – HEADSSS

  • Home (family relationships, conflicts), Education and employment (school performance, drop-out, work), Activities (friends, hobbies, screen time), Drugs (tobacco, alcohol and other substances), Sexuality (relationships, knowledge, risk), Suicide and depression (mood, self-harm thoughts), Safety (violence, abuse, bullying, road safety).
  • The interview is done in private after assuring confidentiality, explaining its limits (e.g. danger to life or abuse that must be reported).

Anaemia Mukt Bharat and adolescents – under Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018), adolescents of 10–19 years receive a weekly blue IFA tablet (60 mg elemental iron and 500 mcg folic acid) and albendazole 400 mg twice a year, along with testing and treatment of anaemia, behaviour change communication on iron-rich foods and fortified foods.

Key messages for adolescents

  • Eat a balanced diet with green leafy vegetables, pulses, millets, fruits and milk; avoid junk food.
  • Daily physical activity and adequate sleep; limit screen time.
  • Personal and menstrual hygiene; seek help for menstrual problems.
  • Say no to tobacco, alcohol and drugs; wear a helmet and follow road rules.
  • Talk to a trusted adult, Saathiya, counsellor or Tele-MANAS (14416) when stressed or unsafe.
  • Know the legal age of marriage and the right to be protected from abuse.

Physical and psychological changes of adolescence – growth spurt and development of secondary sexual characteristics (menarche in girls, voice change and nocturnal emissions in boys); search for identity, mood swings, greater influence of peers, abstract thinking and desire for independence. Lack of correct information about these changes causes anxiety and risky behaviour, so education about puberty is a core service.

Linkages for adolescent health – the nurse links adolescents with the Ayushman Bharat School Health and Wellness Programme, RBSK (screening up to 18 years), the Scheme for Adolescent Girls through Anganwadis (under Mission Poshan 2.0), Child Marriage Prohibition Officers, Childline 1098 and the nearest Adolescent Friendly Health Clinic for counselling.

Nursing importance

  • Investing in adolescents' health brings a "triple dividend" – healthier adolescents today, healthier adults tomorrow and healthier children in the next generation.

Conclusion Adolescents (10–19 years) face nutritional, sexual and reproductive, mental health, substance-use, injury and violence problems and early NCD risks. RKSK (2014) addresses six thematic areas through Adolescent Friendly Health Clinics, Saathiya peer educators, Adolescent Health and Wellness Days, WIFS, the Menstrual Hygiene Scheme, school health and community action, and the community health nurse provides friendly services, supplementation, counselling, peer-educator support and referral.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Assisting Individuals and Families to Promote and Maintain their Health
question: Explain the role of the community health nurse in preventing violence against women and children.
answer_html:
Introduction Violence against women and children – domestic violence, sexual abuse, dowry harassment, child marriage, child labour, trafficking and neglect – is widespread and causes physical injury, mental illness, unwanted pregnancy, STIs and death. The community health nurse is often the first contact for victims and can play a major preventive and protective role.

Types of abuse – physical, sexual, emotional/psychological, economic (denial of money, property), and neglect (especially of children and the elderly).

Signs suggesting abuse

  • Repeated or unexplained injuries, bruises of different ages, burns, fractures; injuries inconsistent with the history; delay in seeking care.
  • Fear, anxiety, depression, withdrawal, suicidal attempts; a controlling partner who answers for the woman.
  • In children – sudden behaviour change, fear of a particular person, bed-wetting, school problems, sexualised behaviour, genital injuries or STIs, malnutrition and neglect.

Legal framework (to be known and explained)

  • Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005; Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (offences of cruelty by husband or relatives, dowry death, rape and sexual harassment).
  • Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 – mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse by anyone who knows of it, including health workers.
  • Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 (legal age 18 for girls, 21 for boys); Juvenile Justice Act, 2015; Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act; PCPNDT Act against sex-selection.

Role of the community health nurse

  1. Prevention and awareness
    • Educate the community on gender equality, the value of the girl child, harmful effects of child marriage, dowry and alcohol; legal rights and helplines.
    • Work with SHGs, Panchayats, schools, adolescent groups (Saathiya) and men's groups; promote positive parenting.
  2. Early identification
    • Be alert to signs of abuse during home visits, ANC, immunisation and school health; ask sensitively in private (routine enquiry, especially in pregnancy).
  3. Immediate care
    • First aid and treatment of injuries; refer for medico-legal examination and care (emergency contraception, STI prophylaxis, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, psychological first aid) as per national guidelines, with consent and dignity.
  4. Documentation and reporting
    • Record findings accurately and objectively (injuries, statements); inform the medical officer; report child sexual abuse to the police or Special Juvenile Police Unit (POCSO); inform the Child Welfare Committee in cases of child neglect or child marriage.
  5. Referral and linkage
    • One Stop Centres (Sakhi), Women Helpline 181, emergency number 112, Childline 1098, Protection Officers under the DV Act, legal aid services, shelter homes, counselling services, Tele-MANAS.
  6. Counselling and support – listen without blame; maintain confidentiality; assess safety and help make a safety plan; support the survivor's decisions; follow-up visits.
  7. Advocacy – for safe spaces, girls' education and enforcement of laws.

Conclusion The community health nurse prevents and responds to violence against women and children by raising awareness, identifying signs early, giving immediate care, documenting and reporting (mandatory under POCSO), referring to One Stop Centres, helplines, police and Child Welfare Committees, counselling and supporting survivors, and advocating for gender equality.

question: Explain women's empowerment and the role of the community health nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Women's empowerment is the process by which women gain power and control over their own lives – the ability to make strategic life choices, access resources and opportunities, and participate fully and equally in decisions at home, in the community and in society.

Dimensions

  1. Economic – income, employment, ownership of property, access to credit and bank accounts.
  2. Social – freedom from discrimination and violence, mobility, dignity, participation in community life.
  3. Educational – literacy, schooling, skills and information.
  4. Political – participation in Panchayats, legislatures and decision-making bodies.
  5. Health – control over her own health and reproductive decisions, access to services, nutrition.
  6. Psychological – self-confidence and self-esteem.

Why empowerment matters for health

  • Empowered, educated women marry later, have fewer and healthier children, use ANC and institutional delivery, immunise and feed their children better and seek care early; female literacy is strongly linked to lower IMR and MMR.
  • Empowerment reduces vulnerability to violence, early marriage, trafficking and HIV.

Government initiatives (examples)

  • Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015) – improving the child sex ratio and girls' education.
  • Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana – savings scheme for the girl child.
  • Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana – maternity cash benefit for nutrition and rest (also for the second child if a girl).
  • Mission Shakti – One Stop Centres, Women Helpline 181, Shakti Sadan (shelter), Sakhi Niwas (working women's hostels), Palna (crèches).
  • Self-help groups under DAY-NRLM, the Lakhpati Didi initiative, Stand-Up India and MUDRA loans for women entrepreneurs.
  • Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana – LPG connections in women's names.
  • Reservation of seats for women in Panchayati Raj institutions (one-third, and 50% in many states) and the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (2023) for one-third reservation in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies.
  • Laws on domestic violence, dowry, sexual harassment at the workplace (POSH Act, 2013) and maternity benefits.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Health education on women's health, nutrition, birth spacing, rights and entitlements; encourage girls' education and delay of marriage.
  • Promote decision-making by women about their own health and family planning through counselling (involving husbands).
  • Link women with schemes – PMMVY, JSY, Ayushman card, SHGs, bank accounts.
  • Support SHGs and Mahila Arogya Samitis; encourage women's participation in VHSNCs and Gram Sabhas.
  • Identify and support women facing violence; refer to One Stop Centres.
  • Act as a role model of an empowered working woman.

Conclusion Women's empowerment – economic, social, educational, political, health and psychological – is a key determinant of family and community health. Schemes such as BBBP, PMMVY, Mission Shakti, SHGs under DAY-NRLM, Ujjwala and political reservation support it, and the community health nurse promotes it through education, counselling, linkage to schemes, support for women's groups and protection from violence.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Assisting Individuals and Families to Promote and Maintain their Health
question: Explain the role of self-help groups (SHGs) in community health.
answer_html:
Definition A self-help group (SHG) is a small, voluntary, informal group of about 10–20 people, usually women, from a similar socio-economic background, who come together to save regularly, give small loans to members and solve common problems through mutual help.

Characteristics

  • Homogeneous membership; regular meetings (weekly or monthly); regular savings; internal lending at low interest; rotating leadership; record keeping; democratic decision-making.
  • Linked with banks under the SHG–Bank Linkage Programme (NABARD, 1992) and supported by the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM, "Aajeevika") in rural areas and the urban livelihoods mission in towns; SHGs form village organisations and cluster-level federations.

Benefits for members

  • Financial inclusion, freedom from moneylenders, income-generating activities, skills, confidence, leadership and social status; empowerment of women.

Role of SHGs in community health

  1. Health awareness – discussion of health topics in meetings (nutrition, ANC, institutional delivery, immunisation, family planning, hygiene, TB, NCDs).
  2. Sanitation – motivating members to build and use toilets; cleanliness drives; waste management.
  3. Nutrition – kitchen gardens (Poshan Vatika), millet promotion, take-home ration production and community kitchens in some states.
  4. Menstrual hygiene – awareness and production and sale of low-cost sanitary napkins.
  5. Health financing – loans for emergencies, hospital costs and transport during delivery; enrolment in insurance.
  6. Community monitoring and advocacy – monitoring services at the sub-centre and Anganwadi; demanding services and entitlements; action against alcohol and domestic violence.
  7. Support to programmes – acting as Ni-kshay Mitras (TB), mobilising for immunisation and screening camps; members may become ASHAs or Mahila Arogya Samiti members (urban).

Role of the community health nurse

  • Attend SHG meetings to give health education; identify SHG leaders as health volunteers.
  • Involve SHGs in campaigns (Poshan Maah, sanitation, TB, NCD screening, VHSNDs).
  • Encourage income-generating activities related to health (sanitary napkin units, nutri-gardens).
  • Coordinate with NRLM staff and the Panchayat.

Conclusion SHGs are small, voluntary groups – mostly of women – that save and lend together and are supported by NABARD and DAY-NRLM. They empower women and contribute to community health through awareness, sanitation, nutrition, menstrual hygiene, health financing, community monitoring and support to health programmes, with the nurse as educator and partner.
