question: Explain community-based rehabilitation (CBR) of persons with disabilities and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Disability results from the interaction between a person's impairment and barriers in the environment that prevent full participation in society. Most persons with disabilities live in rural areas with little access to institutional rehabilitation. Community-based rehabilitation (CBR), promoted by WHO since the late 1970s, brings rehabilitation into the community.

Definition CBR is a strategy within community development for the rehabilitation, equalisation of opportunities and social inclusion of all persons with disabilities, implemented through the combined efforts of persons with disabilities themselves, their families, communities and appropriate health, education, vocational and social services.

Objectives

  • Ensure that persons with disabilities can maximise their physical and mental abilities, access regular services and opportunities, and become active contributors to the community.
  • Change community attitudes and remove barriers.

Components – the CBR matrix (WHO)

  1. Health – promotion, prevention, medical care, rehabilitation, assistive devices.
  2. Education – early childhood, inclusive schooling, non-formal education, lifelong learning.
  3. Livelihood – skills development, self-employment, wage employment, social protection.
  4. Social – personal assistance, relationships, culture, recreation, sports, access to justice.
  5. Empowerment – advocacy, self-help groups of persons with disabilities, community mobilisation, political participation.

Legal and programme support in India

  • Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 – recognises 21 types of disabilities (including blindness, low vision, locomotor disability, hearing impairment, intellectual disability, autism, mental illness, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, acid attack survivors); benchmark disability (40% or more) entitles to reservation in government jobs (4%) and higher education (5%), free education up to 18 years and other benefits.
  • Disability certificate and UDID card (Unique Disability ID); disability pensions; ADIP scheme for aids and appliances; District Disability Rehabilitation Centres; District Early Intervention Centres under RBSK for children with developmental delays.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Prevention – immunisation, good antenatal and intranatal care, newborn care, nutrition (iodine, Vitamin A), injury prevention, NCD control.
  • Early identification and intervention – screening of newborns and children for developmental delays (RBSK), hearing and vision screening, identification of disabled persons during surveys.
  • Home-based care – teaching positioning, exercises, ADL training, prevention of pressure sores and contractures, bladder and bowel care, use of aids; training caregivers.
  • Referral and linkage – to rehabilitation services, special schools, vocational training, certification and schemes.
  • Counselling and psychosocial support for persons and families; reducing stigma; promoting inclusion in schools and community activities.
  • Supporting SHGs of persons with disabilities and advocating for accessible facilities.

Conclusion CBR is a community development strategy for the rehabilitation, equal opportunities and inclusion of persons with disabilities through health, education, livelihood, social and empowerment components. Supported by the RPwD Act 2016, UDID, ADIP and early intervention services, the community health nurse contributes through prevention, early identification, home-based rehabilitation, caregiver training, referral, counselling and advocacy.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Assisting Individuals and Families to Promote and Maintain their Health
question: What is the family APGAR?
answer_html:
The family APGAR (Gabriel Smilkstein, 1978) is a brief questionnaire to assess family functioning from a family member's point of view. It has five components:

  • A – Adaptation – satisfaction with help received from the family in times of trouble.
  • P – Partnership – sharing of decision-making and communication.
  • G – Growth – family support for new activities and personal growth.
  • A – Affection – expression of love and response to emotions.
  • R – Resolve – commitment to spend time together. Each item is scored 0 (hardly ever), 1 (some of the time) or 2 (almost always); a total of 7–10 suggests a highly functional family, 4–6 moderate dysfunction and 0–3 severe dysfunction.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Assisting Individuals and Families to Promote and Maintain their Health
question: What is a One Stop Centre (Sakhi)?
answer_html:
One Stop Centres (OSCs), also called "Sakhi" centres, were launched on 1 April 2015 by the Ministry of Women and Child Development (now under Mission Shakti, funded through the Nirbhaya Fund).

  • They provide integrated support under one roof to women affected by violence (domestic, sexual, dowry-related, acid attacks, trafficking) in private or public spaces.
  • Services – emergency response and rescue, medical assistance, police assistance (FIR registration), legal aid and counselling, psychosocial counselling, and temporary shelter, often with video-conferencing facilities for statements.
  • They are located in or near hospitals and are linked with the Women Helpline 181 and emergency number 112.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Assisting Individuals and Families to Promote and Maintain their Health
question: Write the main features of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
tags: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
answer_html:
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (in force from 2006) provides civil remedies to women facing violence in the home.

  • Domestic violence includes physical, sexual, verbal and emotional, and economic abuse (including dowry harassment).
  • It protects any woman in a domestic relationship – wife, live-in partner, mother, sister, daughter, widow.
  • Protection Officers and registered service providers help the woman file a Domestic Incident Report and approach the Magistrate; a complaint can be made by the woman or anyone on her behalf.
  • Reliefs – protection orders, residence orders (right to live in the shared household), monetary relief, custody orders for children and compensation.
  • Breach of a protection order is a punishable offence.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Assisting Individuals and Families to Promote and Maintain their Health
question: Who are Saathiyas under RKSK?
answer_html:
Saathiyas ("companions") are trained adolescent peer educators under the Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK).

  • Usually four per village (or per 1,000 population) – two boys and two girls, selected from among adolescents with the help of the ASHA and community.
  • Roles – conduct regular group sessions with peers on nutrition, puberty and reproductive health, mental health, substance misuse, injuries and violence, and NCD prevention; provide accurate information; build life skills; refer adolescents to Adolescent Friendly Health Clinics and ASHAs; help organise Adolescent Health and Wellness Days.
  • Supported by the Saathiya Resource Kit and the Saathiya Salah mobile application.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: (a) Define epidemiology and explain its aims and the epidemiological approach. (3 marks) (b) Explain the dynamics of disease transmission. (3 marks) (c) Describe the epidemiological methods. (6 marks) (d) Explain the uses of epidemiology in community health nursing. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Classification of epidemiological methods
labels: cohort); experimental studies – randomised controlled trials

answer_html:
(a) Definition, aims and approach (3 marks) Definition Epidemiology is "the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the control of health problems" (John M. Last, Dictionary of Epidemiology).

  • The word comes from Greek: epi (upon), demos (people) and logos (study) – the study of what happens to people.
  • Its three components are disease frequency (measurement – rates and ratios), distribution (by time, place and person) and determinants (causes and risk factors).

Aims (International Epidemiological Association)

  1. To describe the distribution and magnitude of health and disease problems in human populations.
  2. To identify aetiological factors (risk factors) in the causation of disease.
  3. To provide the data essential for the planning, implementation and evaluation of services for the prevention, control and treatment of disease, and for setting priorities among those services. The ultimate aim is to eliminate or reduce health problems and to promote the health and well-being of society.

Epidemiological approach – it rests on two processes:

  • Asking questions – What is the event (the problem)? What is its magnitude? Where did it happen? When did it happen? Who is affected? Why did it occur? And for action – What can be done to reduce the problem? How can it be prevented? What resources are needed? What results can be expected?
  • Making comparisons – comparing two or more groups (e.g. smokers and non-smokers, vaccinated and unvaccinated) to find differences that suggest causes, while making sure that the groups are comparable (by randomisation or matching).

(b) Dynamics of disease transmission (3 marks) Communicable diseases spread through a chain of three links: the source or reservoir, the mode of transmission and the susceptible host.

  1. Source and reservoir
    • Reservoir – the person, animal, arthropod, plant, soil or substance in which an infectious agent normally lives and multiplies. Source – the person, animal, object or substance from which the agent passes to a host.
    • Human reservoir – cases (clinical, subclinical, latent) and carriers (incubatory, convalescent and healthy carriers; temporary or chronic – e.g. typhoid, hepatitis B, diphtheria carriers). Carriers are dangerous because they are unrecognised and move freely.
    • Animal reservoir – zoonoses such as rabies, plague, leptospirosis, Japanese encephalitis and Kyasanur forest disease.
    • Non-living reservoir – soil and inanimate matter (tetanus, anthrax spores, fungi).
  2. Modes of transmission
    • Direct – direct contact (skin-to-skin, sexual contact – STIs, leprosy, scabies), droplet infection (influenza, diphtheria, whooping cough, COVID-19), contact with soil (hookworm, tetanus), inoculation into skin or mucosa (rabies by bite), transplacental (vertical) transmission (syphilis, HIV, rubella, hepatitis B).
    • Indirect – vehicle-borne (water, food, milk, blood – cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E, HIV and hepatitis B through blood); vector-borne – mechanical (houseflies) or biological (mosquitoes – malaria, dengue, filaria, JE; sandfly – kala-azar); airborne (droplet nuclei and dust – TB, measles, chickenpox); fomite-borne (towels, utensils, toys – trachoma, skin infections); unclean hands and fingers (faeco-oral diseases).
  3. Susceptible host
    • The agent must find a portal of entry (respiratory, alimentary, genito-urinary tract, skin) and escape the host's defences. Susceptibility depends on age, nutrition, immunity (natural or acquired, including vaccination), genetic factors and general health. Herd immunity in the community protects susceptible people by reducing transmission.

(c) Epidemiological methods (6 marks) 1. Observational studies A. Descriptive epidemiology – the first phase; it describes the occurrence of disease by time, place and person.

  • Time – short-term fluctuations (epidemics, e.g. food poisoning), periodic fluctuations – seasonal (malaria and dengue in monsoon, measles in late winter and spring) and cyclic (influenza in two- to three-year cycles), and long-term or secular trends (rise of diabetes and heart disease, fall of polio).
  • Place – international, national (state-wise), rural–urban differences and local distribution shown by spot maps (cases of cholera around a contaminated well).
  • Person – age (measles in children, cancers in the elderly), sex, marital status, occupation, social class, behaviour (smoking, alcohol, diet, physical activity), stress and migration.

  • Steps – defining the population; defining the disease; describing the disease by time, place and person; measuring the disease (rates); comparing with known indices; and formulating an aetiological hypothesis. B. Analytical epidemiology – tests the hypothesis; the unit of study is the individual.

  • Ecological (correlational) study – compares populations or groups (e.g. average salt intake and stroke rates in different countries).

  • Cross-sectional (prevalence) study – a "snapshot" of a population at one point of time (e.g. NFHS; prevalence of hypertension by age and sex).
  • Case-control study (retrospective) – starts with cases (people with the disease) and controls (without it), and looks backwards for past exposure. Controls are matched for age and sex. Measure – odds ratio. Quick and cheap, good for rare diseases, but prone to recall bias. Classic example – smoking and lung cancer (Doll and Hill, 1950).

  • Cohort study (prospective, incidence or follow-up study) – starts with exposed and non-exposed healthy people and follows them forward to see who develops the disease. Measures – incidence, relative risk and attributable risk. Gives direct evidence of risk but is costly, long and suffers from loss to follow-up. Classic example – the Framingham Heart Study on cardiovascular risk factors. 2. Experimental epidemiology

  • Randomised controlled trial (RCT) – the "gold standard"; steps: drawing up a protocol → selecting reference and experimental populations → randomisation into study and control groups → intervention (drug, vaccine, procedure) → follow-up → assessment of outcome. Blinding (single, double or triple) prevents bias.

  • Field trials – on healthy people at risk, usually in the community (e.g. vaccine trials).
  • Community trials – the whole community is the unit of intervention (e.g. water fluoridation, community health education for heart disease prevention).
  • Non-randomised trials – used when randomisation is not possible or ethical (e.g. before-and-after studies, natural experiments).
  • All human experiments require ethical approval and informed consent (ICMR National Ethical Guidelines).

(d) Uses of epidemiology in community health nursing (3 marks) Uses (J. N. Morris)

  1. To study historically the rise and fall of diseases in the population.
  2. Community diagnosis – the presence, nature and distribution of health and disease in the community.
  3. Planning and evaluation of health services.
  4. Evaluation of individual risks and chances.
  5. Identification of syndromes (grouping of signs and symptoms).
  6. Completing the natural history of disease.
  7. Searching for causes of health and disease.

Applications in community health nursing

  • Community assessment and diagnosis – using rates (IMR, MMR, prevalence of anaemia) to identify priority problems and high-risk groups (pregnant women, under-fives, the elderly, slum dwellers).
  • Planning and targeting services – deciding where to place session sites, which households to visit first, what health education to give.
  • Surveillance and outbreak control – detecting an unusual rise in fever or diarrhoea cases, reporting through IHIP, investigating and controlling outbreaks.
  • Screening and early detection – NCD screening of people aged 30 and above, antenatal screening, school health screening.
  • Evaluation of programmes – immunisation coverage, reduction in disease incidence.
  • Health education based on evidence of risk factors (tobacco, salt, sanitation).
  • Research – participation in surveys and studies; evidence-based practice.
  • Record keeping – accurate registers form the basis of epidemiological data.

Nursing importance

  • Epidemiology gives the community health nurse the "diagnostic tools" for the community – she uses its data and methods to decide who is at risk, what the problem is and whether her interventions are working.

Conclusion Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states in populations and its application to the control of health problems. Its aims are to describe disease magnitude, identify causes and provide data for planning and evaluation, using the approach of asking questions and making comparisons. Diseases spread through a chain of source or reservoir, mode of transmission and susceptible host. Epidemiological methods are observational (descriptive by time, place and person; analytical – ecological, cross-sectional, case-control and cohort) and experimental (RCTs, field and community trials). In community health nursing, epidemiology is used for community diagnosis, targeting services, surveillance, outbreak control, screening, evaluation, health education and research.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: (a) Define an epidemic and explain the types of epidemics with the epidemic curve. (5 marks) (b) Describe the steps in the investigation of an epidemic. (7 marks) (c) Explain the role of the community health nurse in epidemic control. (3 marks)
tags: data analysis by time place person

diagram.caption: Shapes of epidemic curves
labels: point-source epidemic – a sharp rise and fall within one incubation period; continuous common-source epidemic – a rise followed by a plateau until the source is removed; propagated epidemic – a gradual rise with successive waves one incubation period apart

answer_html:
(a) Epidemic and types of epidemics (5 marks) Definitions

  • An epidemic is "the occurrence in a community or region of cases of an illness, specific health-related behaviour or other health-related events clearly in excess of normal expectancy."
  • What counts as "excess" depends on the disease and place: a single case of a disease long absent from an area (e.g. polio, or cholera in a place where it does not normally occur) or a new disease is treated as an epidemic and requires immediate investigation.
  • An outbreak is an epidemic limited to a localised increase (a village, hostel or wedding party).

Types of epidemics 1. Common-source epidemics – many people are exposed to the same source.

  • (a) Single exposure or "point-source" epidemic – exposure is brief and simultaneous (e.g. food poisoning after a wedding meal, chemical leak such as the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984).
    • Features of the curve – a sharp rise and rapid fall; all cases occur within one incubation period; clustering of cases in a narrow time interval; no secondary waves.

  • (b) Continuous or repeated exposure epidemic – exposure to the source continues over time (e.g. a contaminated well or water pipeline causing cholera, typhoid or hepatitis; a leaking sewage line).

    • Features of the curve – the cases rise and then form a plateau or irregular prolonged peak that continues until the source is identified and removed; it may go beyond one incubation period. 2. Propagated (progressive) epidemics – result from person-to-person transmission (e.g. hepatitis A, measles, chickenpox, influenza, secondary spread of cholera, COVID-19).

    • Features of the curve – a gradual rise, cases occurring in successive generations about one incubation period apart, and a slow tailing off over a long period; it continues until the number of susceptibles falls or control measures work. It is more likely where there is overcrowding, poor sanitation and low immunity. 3. Slow (modern) epidemics – a gradual rise over years in non-communicable diseases (coronary heart disease, diabetes, lung cancer, road traffic injuries) linked to changes in lifestyle and environment.

The epidemic curve – a graph (histogram) of the number of cases (y-axis) against the time of onset (x-axis). It tells us:

  • The type of epidemic (point source, continuous or propagated).
  • The probable time of exposure (by counting back one average incubation period from the peak).
  • The probable disease (from the incubation period) and whether the epidemic is over or continuing.

(b) Steps in the investigation of an epidemic (7 marks) Objectives – to define the magnitude of the epidemic (time, place, person), to identify the source and mode of spread, to identify the causal factors, and to recommend control measures to stop it and prevent recurrence.

Steps

  1. Verification of the diagnosis
    • Examine the first cases clinically, review records and collect samples (stool, blood, water, food) for laboratory confirmation. Investigation and treatment begin without waiting for laboratory results.
  2. Confirmation of the existence of an epidemic
    • Compare the present number of cases with the usual number for the same place and season (from previous years' records). Rule out artefacts (better reporting, new diagnostic test, change in case definition).
  3. Defining the population at risk
    • Obtain a map of the area; count the population (house-to-house enumeration or census data) by age and sex to calculate rates.
  4. Rapid search for all cases and their characteristics
    • Prepare a simple case definition (e.g. "any person in village X with three or more loose watery stools in 24 hours since 1 August").
    • House-to-house search (active case finding) by the health team with ASHAs; record each case in a line list – name, age, sex, address, date and time of onset, symptoms, water source, food eaten, contact with other cases, outcome.
  5. Data analysis
    • Time – plot the epidemic curve.
    • Place – a spot map showing cases by household, water source or hostel room.
    • Person – age, sex, occupation, exposure; calculate attack rates (overall and by group), secondary attack rates and the case fatality rate.
  6. Formulation of hypotheses
    • About the probable source, mode of spread and agent (e.g. "the outbreak is due to contamination of the public well near the drain").
  7. Testing of hypotheses
    • Compare attack rates among the exposed and non-exposed (those who drank from the well vs. those who used another source; ate a particular food vs. did not); laboratory testing of water or food; a simple case-control study.
  8. Evaluation of ecological factors
    • Study the environment that made the epidemic possible – broken pipelines, open defecation, drainage, floods, breeding sites, overcrowding, festivals or migration.
  9. Further investigation of the population at risk
    • Identify susceptible groups and carriers; serological surveys; follow-up of contacts.
  10. Writing the report
    • Background, methods, findings (curves, maps, tables), the source and mode of spread identified, control measures taken and recommendations for preventing recurrence; shared with the district and state authorities and the community.

Control measures (begin at once, alongside the investigation)

  • Treatment of cases (ORS, IV fluids, antibiotics), setting up temporary treatment centres (ORS corners).
  • Control of the source – disinfection of wells and water (chlorination, Horrock's test), repair of pipelines, banning sale of contaminated food, vector control (source reduction, fogging, larvicides).
  • Interrupting transmission – hand washing, safe disposal of excreta, food hygiene, isolation of cases where needed.
  • Protecting susceptibles – immunisation (e.g. measles outbreak response), chemoprophylaxis (e.g. for contacts in meningococcal disease), health education.
  • Strengthened surveillance until two incubation periods pass without new cases.

Example – In a village, 40 cases of acute watery diarrhoea with two deaths are reported in five days. The ANM verifies the cases and reports through IHIP; the Rapid Response Team confirms Vibrio cholerae in stool samples. A line list shows that most cases use a public well near an open drain; the attack rate among well users is much higher than among those using a hand pump. The well is closed and super-chlorinated, ORS depots are set up, households are given chlorine tablets, and health education on boiling water and hand washing is given. New cases stop after a week.

(c) Role of the community health nurse in epidemic control (3 marks)

  • Early detection and reporting – notices clusters of cases during home visits and reports immediately (IHIP; P-form and S-form data); maintains records.
  • Case finding and line listing – participates in house-to-house surveys with ASHAs; collects and transports samples correctly.
  • Care of patients – ORS, first aid, referral of severe cases; organises temporary treatment points and transport.
  • Control activities – disinfection of water sources, distribution of chlorine tablets, vector control, isolation measures, mass immunisation or chemoprophylaxis as directed.
  • Health education – hand washing, safe water, food hygiene, use of toilets, mosquito protection; counters rumours and panic.
  • Coordination and follow-up – works with the Rapid Response Team, Panchayat, schools and water supply department; continues surveillance and follow-up until the outbreak ends.

Nursing importance

  • The nurse at the periphery is usually the first to notice an outbreak; prompt reporting and simple control measures can prevent many cases and deaths.

Conclusion An epidemic is the occurrence of cases clearly in excess of normal expectancy. Epidemics may be common-source (point-source or continuous), propagated or slow (modern), each with a typical epidemic curve that helps estimate the time of exposure and type of spread. Investigation proceeds through verification of diagnosis, confirmation of the epidemic, defining the population at risk, rapid case search with a line list, analysis by time, place and person, formulation and testing of hypotheses, evaluation of ecological factors, further study of the population at risk and a written report, with control measures started at once. The community health nurse detects, reports, treats, controls, educates and coordinates.

question: Explain the natural history of disease and the iceberg phenomenon of disease.

diagram.caption: Natural history of disease and the iceberg of disease
labels: carrier state or death) with levels of prevention below; an iceberg with clinical cases above the waterline and undiagnosed

answer_html:
Natural history of disease The natural history of disease is the way in which a disease evolves over time from its earliest stage to its end – recovery, disability or death – in the absence of treatment. Leavell and Clark (1958) described two phases. 1. Prepathogenesis phase – the period before the onset of disease in man. The agent, host and environment interact; the person is not yet ill but is exposed to risk factors ("man in the midst of disease"). Example – an unvaccinated child living in an overcrowded house where measles is present. 2. Pathogenesis phase – begins with the entry of the agent into the host (or the start of a disease process).

  • Incubation period / early pathogenesis – the agent multiplies or changes occur in tissues; the person has no symptoms (subclinical stage).
  • Early discernible lesions – first signs and symptoms appear.
  • Advanced disease – clinical illness with complications.
  • Outcome – recovery, disability (defect), carrier state, chronic disease or death.
  • For non-communicable diseases the natural history is long and the onset is gradual – risk factors act over years before the disease appears (e.g. smoking → atherosclerosis → myocardial infarction).

Relation to levels of prevention

  • Primordial prevention – preventing the emergence of risk factors (healthy lifestyles in children).
  • Primary prevention (prepathogenesis) – health promotion and specific protection (immunisation, iodised salt).
  • Secondary prevention (early pathogenesis) – early diagnosis and prompt treatment (screening, case finding).
  • Tertiary prevention (late pathogenesis) – disability limitation and rehabilitation.

Iceberg phenomenon of disease

  • Disease in a community may be compared with an iceberg. The floating tip above the water represents the clinical (apparent) cases – those seen by doctors and recorded in hospitals.
  • The submerged portion – much larger – represents the hidden mass of disease: latent, inapparent, subclinical, undiagnosed and carrier states, and people who have not sought care.
  • The waterline is the demarcation between apparent and inapparent disease.
  • Examples – hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, malnutrition, mental illness, tuberculosis and HIV (many undiagnosed); polio and hepatitis A (most infections inapparent). Diseases like rabies and measles show little iceberg because nearly all infections are clinical.

Importance

  • Hospital data show only the tip and underestimate the true burden.
  • Screening and case finding in the community bring the submerged part to light (e.g. NCD screening of all persons aged 30 and above).
  • Undetected cases and carriers continue to spread infection or develop complications, so community health nurses must search for them actively.

Conclusion The natural history of disease runs from the prepathogenesis phase (agent–host–environment interaction) through the pathogenesis phase (subclinical, clinical, advanced disease) to recovery, disability, carrier state or death, and guides the levels of prevention. The iceberg phenomenon reminds us that clinical cases are only the visible tip, and that screening and case finding are needed to detect the large hidden mass of disease in the community.

unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: Explain the concepts of disease causation – the epidemiological triad, multifactorial causation and the web of causation.

diagram.caption: Web of causation of myocardial infarction
labels: changes in lifestyle (diet rich in fat and salt
which interact to cause coronary atherosclerosis and coronary thrombosis

answer_html:
1. Germ theory of disease

  • In the late nineteenth century, the work of Pasteur and Koch showed that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases – a one-to-one relationship (agent → disease).
  • Limitation – it does not explain why only some exposed persons become ill, or the causation of non-communicable diseases.

2. Epidemiological triad (agent, host and environment)

  • Disease results from the interaction of agent, host and environment.
  • Agent factors – biological (bacteria, viruses, parasites), nutrient (excess or deficiency – obesity, PEM, vitamin deficiencies), physical (heat, cold, radiation, noise), chemical (endogenous – urea, ketones; exogenous – pesticides, lead, tobacco), mechanical (injuries) and social agents (poverty, alcoholism).
  • Host factors – demographic (age, sex, ethnicity), biological (genetics, immunity, nutritional status), socio-economic (education, occupation, income, housing) and lifestyle (diet, exercise, tobacco and alcohol use, sexual behaviour).
  • Environmental factors – physical (climate, water, air, housing), biological (vectors, animal reservoirs, plants) and psychosocial (customs, culture, health services, stress).
  • An imbalance in favour of the agent (more virulent organism, lowered host resistance, unfavourable environment) leads to disease.

3. Multifactorial causation

  • Proposed by Pettenkofer; most diseases, especially NCDs (coronary heart disease, cancer, diabetes), result from many factors acting together; no single factor is sufficient.
  • Even infections need contributory factors – e.g. tuberculosis needs M. tuberculosis plus malnutrition, overcrowding, HIV, diabetes or smoking.

4. Web of causation (MacMahon and Pugh, 1970)

  • Considers all the predisposing factors of every type and their complex interrelationships – causes are like a spider's web, with chains of causes interconnected.
  • Example – myocardial infarction: lifestyle changes → diet rich in fat and salt, smoking, inactivity, stress → obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes → coronary atherosclerosis → coronary thrombosis → MI.
  • Importance – disease can be prevented by breaking the web at one or more points (stopping smoking, controlling BP) even when all causes are not known.

5. Wheel model

  • The host (with a genetic core) is at the hub, surrounded by the biological, social and physical environment; the size of each segment varies with the disease.

Risk factors – attributes or exposures significantly associated with disease; modifiable (smoking, diet, inactivity, alcohol, BP) and non-modifiable (age, sex, heredity).

Criteria for causal association (Bradford Hill) – strength of association, consistency, specificity, temporal relationship (cause precedes effect), biological gradient (dose–response), biological plausibility, coherence, experimental evidence and analogy.

Conclusion Ideas of causation have moved from the one-to-one germ theory to the epidemiological triad of agent, host and environment, multifactorial causation, the web of causation and the wheel model. These models explain why only some exposed people fall ill and show that disease can be prevented by acting on modifiable risk factors and breaking the web of causation.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: Explain incidence and prevalence – definitions, calculation, relationship and uses.
tags: relationship P equals I times D
answer_html:
Introduction Morbidity (illness) in a community is measured mainly by incidence and prevalence. Both are needed to describe the burden of disease and to plan services.

1. Incidence

  • Definition – the number of new cases occurring in a defined population during a specified period of time.
  • Incidence rate = (Number of new cases of a specified disease during a given period ÷ Population at risk during that period) × 1,000.
  • Example – if 60 new cases of TB occur in a year in a population of 30,000, the incidence = 60/30,000 × 1,000 = 2 per 1,000 per year (200 per lakh).
  • Special incidence rates – attack rate (used in epidemics) and secondary attack rate.
  • Uses
    • Measures the risk of developing a disease.
    • Studies aetiology (comparing incidence in exposed and non-exposed groups).
    • Evaluates the effectiveness of preventive measures (e.g. fall in measles incidence after vaccination).
    • Detects epidemics (a rise in incidence).

2. Prevalence

  • Definition – the total number of all cases (old and new) existing in a population at a given point or period of time.
  • Point prevalence = (Number of all current cases at a given point of time ÷ Estimated population at the same point) × 100.
  • Period prevalence = (Number of existing cases during a period – old plus new ÷ Average or mid-period population) × 100.
  • Example – if a survey of 2,000 adults finds 500 with hypertension, the point prevalence = 500/2,000 × 100 = 25%.
  • Uses
    • Measures the burden of disease, especially chronic diseases (hypertension, diabetes, leprosy, anaemia).
    • Helps in planning health services – staff, drugs, beds.
    • Used in community diagnosis and in deciding priorities.

3. Relationship between incidence and prevalence

  • Prevalence = Incidence × Mean duration (P = I × D), when conditions are stable.
  • A disease with high incidence but short duration (common cold, acute diarrhoea) has a low prevalence; a chronic disease with low incidence but long duration (diabetes, leprosy before MDT) has a high prevalence.
  • Prevalence increases with longer duration of illness, treatment that prolongs life without cure (e.g. ART for HIV), rising incidence, in-migration of cases, out-migration of healthy people and better detection.
  • Prevalence decreases with shorter duration, high case fatality, falling incidence, improved cure rates (e.g. MDT for leprosy), in-migration of healthy people and out-migration of cases.

Differences in brief

  • Incidence counts only new cases and measures risk (rate of occurrence); it is better for acute diseases and research on causation.
  • Prevalence counts all existing cases and measures burden; it is better for chronic diseases and planning.

Conclusion Incidence measures the rate at which new cases occur and is used to assess risk, causation and the effect of prevention, while prevalence measures all existing cases and is used to assess burden and plan services. They are linked by the relationship P = I × D.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: Explain screening for disease – definition, types, criteria and evaluation of a screening test.
answer_html:
Definition Screening is "the search for unrecognised disease or defect by means of rapidly applied tests, examinations or other procedures in apparently healthy individuals" (Commission on Chronic Illness, USA, 1951). It sorts out those who probably have the disease from those who probably do not; positive cases must be confirmed by diagnostic tests. It works on the hidden part of the "iceberg".

Uses

  • Case detection (prescriptive screening) – early diagnosis and treatment for the person's own benefit (e.g. cervical cancer, hypertension).
  • Control of disease (prospective screening) – detecting cases to protect others (e.g. TB, syphilis and HIV in pregnancy, screening of blood donors).
  • Research – finding the natural history and prevalence of chronic diseases.
  • Educational opportunity – creating awareness during screening camps.

Types

  1. Mass screening – of whole population groups (e.g. population-based NCD screening of everyone aged 30 years and above).
  2. High-risk or selective screening – of groups at higher risk (e.g. GDM screening in pregnancy, sickle cell screening in tribal areas, HIV testing of key populations).
  3. Multiphasic screening – several tests at one time (e.g. BP, blood sugar, Hb, vision, BMI in a health check-up).
  4. Opportunistic screening (case finding) – when people visit for other reasons (e.g. checking BP of every adult attending the OPD).

Criteria for a screening programme (Wilson and Jungner, WHO, 1968)

  • The condition is an important health problem.
  • It has a recognisable latent or early symptomatic stage and its natural history is understood.
  • An accepted treatment and facilities for diagnosis and treatment are available.
  • A suitable test exists – simple, safe, acceptable, rapid, inexpensive, valid and reliable.
  • There is an agreed policy on whom to treat; the cost of case-finding is balanced against overall medical expenditure; case-finding is a continuing process.

Evaluation of a screening test

  • Validity – ability to distinguish those who have the disease from those who do not:
    • Sensitivity = true positives ÷ (true positives + false negatives) × 100 – ability to identify correctly those who have the disease.
    • Specificity = true negatives ÷ (true negatives + false positives) × 100 – ability to identify correctly those who do not have the disease.
    • Positive predictive value = true positives ÷ all test positives × 100; negative predictive value = true negatives ÷ all test negatives × 100.
  • Reliability (repeatability) – consistent results on repeated testing by the same or different observers.
  • Yield – the amount of previously unrecognised disease brought to treatment.
  • False negatives give false reassurance; false positives cause anxiety and unnecessary investigations.

Indian examples – population-based screening for hypertension, diabetes and oral, breast (clinical breast examination) and cervical cancers (VIA – visual inspection with acetic acid) at AAMs; RBSK screening of children for the 4 Ds (defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays including disabilities); antenatal screening for anaemia, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and GDM; newborn hearing screening; vision screening in schools.

Role of the nurse – mobilising people, performing simple tests correctly (BP, glucometer, Hb, VIA where trained), counselling before and after, referral and follow-up of positives (screening is useless without follow-up) and maintaining records.

Conclusion Screening is the search for unrecognised disease in apparently healthy people by rapid tests; it may be mass, selective, multiphasic or opportunistic, should meet the Wilson and Jungner criteria, and its test is judged by sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, reliability and yield. Positive cases must always be confirmed and treated.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: Explain epidemiological surveillance – definition, objectives, types and steps.
answer_html:
Definition

  • Surveillance is the continuous scrutiny of the factors that determine the occurrence and distribution of disease and other conditions of ill health.
  • WHO describes public health surveillance as the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis and interpretation of health data, and the timely dissemination of the results to those who need to know, so that action can be taken.
  • Monitoring is the routine measurement of a variable to detect change (e.g. monitoring water quality, growth monitoring of a child); surveillance is "information for action" – it is linked to a response.

Objectives

  1. To provide information about new and changing trends in the health status of a population (morbidity, mortality, risk factors).
  2. To detect outbreaks early and start prompt control measures.
  3. To provide feedback to the people who report data and to those who plan services.
  4. To evaluate the impact of control programmes and interventions.
  5. To identify high-risk groups and areas, and to guide planning and allocation of resources.
  6. To provide data for research and to meet national and international reporting requirements (International Health Regulations).

Types

  1. Passive surveillance – health facilities report cases as they come (routine reporting); cheap but incomplete.
  2. Active surveillance – health workers actively search for cases (e.g. house-to-house fever surveillance by MPWs for malaria; acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance for polio; contact tracing in TB).
  3. Sentinel surveillance – data collected from selected sites or groups that represent the population (e.g. HIV sentinel surveillance among antenatal women and high-risk groups; sentinel hospitals for dengue and JE).
  4. Syndromic surveillance – based on symptoms or syndromes before laboratory confirmation (e.g. fever with rash, acute diarrhoea) – allows early warning.
  5. Laboratory-based surveillance – confirmed cases reported by laboratories.
  6. Event-based surveillance – unstructured information from media and community reports (rumour registers).
  7. Community-based surveillance – reporting of unusual events by ASHAs, Anganwadi workers and community volunteers.
  8. Integrated surveillance – combining several diseases in one system (India's IDSP, now IHIP).

Steps (components) of a surveillance system

  1. Case definition – standard definitions (suspected, probable, confirmed).
  2. Data collection – from defined sources and in standard formats.
  3. Compilation and analysis – by time, place and person; comparison with thresholds.
  4. Interpretation – detecting unusual trends or clusters.
  5. Dissemination and feedback – reports, bulletins and alerts to health officials and reporting units.
  6. Action – investigation and control of outbreaks; programme changes.
  7. Evaluation of the surveillance system – timeliness, completeness, sensitivity and usefulness.

Role of the nurse – accurate and timely reporting of cases from the sub-centre/AAM, active case search during outbreaks, collection of samples, maintenance of registers and supporting ASHAs in community-based surveillance.

Conclusion Surveillance is the ongoing systematic collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination of health data for action. It may be passive, active, sentinel, syndromic, laboratory-based, event-based, community-based or integrated, and works through case definitions, data collection, analysis, interpretation, feedback, action and evaluation.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: Differentiate between disease control, elimination and eradication, with examples from India.
tags: elimination as a public health problem
answer_html:
1. Disease control

  • Definition – operations or programmes aimed at reducing the incidence, duration (and thus the risk of transmission), effects (complications and disability) and financial burden of a disease, to a level at which it is no longer a major public health problem.
  • The agent continues to exist in the community; continuous efforts are needed.
  • Examples – tuberculosis, diarrhoeal diseases, dengue, NCDs such as hypertension and diabetes.

2. Elimination

  • Lies between control and eradication.
  • Elimination of transmission – reduction of incidence of infection to zero in a defined geographical area (a country or region); continued measures are needed to prevent re-introduction (e.g. measles, polio in a region).
  • Elimination as a public health problem – reduction of the disease below a defined threshold set by WHO (e.g. leprosy prevalence below 1 per 10,000 population; kala-azar below 1 case per 10,000 at block level).
  • Indian examples
    • Polio – last wild polio case on 13 January 2011; India (with the South-East Asia Region) certified polio-free on 27 March 2014.
    • Maternal and neonatal tetanus – elimination validated in 2015.
    • Yaws – declared free in 2006 (WHO recognition 2016).
    • Leprosy – eliminated as a public health problem at the national level in 2005; the aim now is zero transmission.
    • Trachoma – WHO validated its elimination as a public health problem on 8 October 2024.
    • Ongoing targets – lymphatic filariasis (2027), malaria (zero indigenous cases by 2027 and elimination by 2030), kala-azar (close to elimination), TB elimination efforts, measles-rubella elimination.

3. Eradication

  • Definition – the termination of all transmission of infection by extermination of the infectious agent worldwide. It is absolute – "all or none"; control measures are no longer needed after eradication.
  • Examples – smallpox (last case in India in 1975; India declared free in 1977; global eradication declared by WHO in 1980) – the only human disease eradicated so far; rinderpest in animals (2011). Polio is targeted for eradication (wild poliovirus types 2 and 3 have been eradicated; type 1 persists in a few countries). Guinea worm disease (dracunculiasis) – India certified free in 2000; it is close to global eradication.

Requirements for eradication – no animal reservoir, an effective tool (vaccine or treatment), easy diagnosis, short infectious period, no long carrier state, lifelong immunity after infection or vaccination, and strong political will and international cooperation.

Key differences in brief

  • Control reduces disease to an acceptable level; the agent remains.
  • Elimination brings disease or transmission to zero (or below a threshold) in a defined area; the agent may exist elsewhere.
  • Eradication removes the agent from the whole world permanently.

Conclusion Control reduces the frequency and impact of a disease, elimination reduces it to zero transmission or below a threshold in a defined area (polio, MNT, yaws, trachoma in India), and eradication is worldwide extermination of the agent, achieved so far only for smallpox among human diseases. Nurses contribute to all three through immunisation, surveillance, case finding and health education.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: Define epidemiology.
answer_html:
Epidemiology is "the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the control of health problems" (John M. Last).

  • Distribution – frequency and pattern of disease by time, place and person.
  • Determinants – causes and risk factors (agent, host, environment, behaviour).
  • Specified populations – the focus is on groups, not individuals.
  • Application to control – the purpose is prevention and control of disease and promotion of health. The word comes from Greek epi (upon), demos (people) and logos (study). Its aims are to describe the magnitude of disease, identify causes and provide data for planning and evaluating health services.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: What is the incubation period? Give its importance.
answer_html:
The incubation period is the time interval between invasion of the body by an infectious agent and the appearance of the first sign or symptom of the disease. Examples – staphylococcal food poisoning 1–6 hours; cholera a few hours to 5 days; typhoid about 10–14 days; measles about 10 days to fever; chickenpox 14–16 days; hepatitis A 15–50 days; hepatitis B 30–180 days; rabies usually 1–3 months (very variable). Importance

  • Tracing the source of infection and the time of exposure (point-source outbreaks).
  • Fixing the period of quarantine and surveillance of contacts (maximum incubation period).
  • Passive or active immunisation during the incubation period can prevent or modify disease (e.g. rabies post-exposure vaccination).
  • Prognosis – a short incubation period often means severe disease (tetanus, rabies). In non-communicable diseases the equivalent term is the latent period.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: Define attack rate and secondary attack rate.
answer_html:
Attack rate – an incidence rate used during an epidemic, usually expressed as a percentage:

  • Attack rate = (Number of new cases of a specified disease during a specified time interval ÷ Total population at risk during the same interval) × 100.

  • Example – if 40 out of 200 guests who ate at a wedding develop food poisoning, the attack rate = 20%. Secondary attack rate (SAR) – the number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of the incubation period following exposure to the primary case, divided by the total number of exposed susceptible contacts:

  • SAR = (Number of contacts who develop the disease within one incubation period ÷ Total number of susceptible contacts) × 100.

  • The primary case is excluded from both numerator and denominator. Use – SAR measures the infectiousness (communicability) of a disease and the effectiveness of control measures (e.g. isolation, vaccination of contacts).

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: Differentiate between endemic, epidemic, pandemic and sporadic occurrence of disease.
answer_html:
• Sporadic – cases occur irregularly, here and there, from time to time, generally infrequently, with no apparent connection between them (e.g. tetanus, sporadic cases of food poisoning).
  • Endemic – the constant presence of a disease or infectious agent within a given geographic area or population group, without importation from outside; the usual or expected frequency (e.g. malaria in some tribal areas, dental caries, common cold).
  • Epidemic – occurrence of cases clearly in excess of normal expectancy in a community or region (e.g. a cholera outbreak in a village after floods, dengue in monsoon).
  • Pandemic – an epidemic spreading over a very wide area – several countries or continents – affecting a large number of people (e.g. COVID-19 in 2020, H1N1 influenza in 2009).
  • Exotic – diseases imported into a country where they do not otherwise occur (e.g. yellow fever if introduced into India). Thus, the difference lies in the frequency of cases and the extent of the area affected.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: What is the case fatality rate?
answer_html:
The case fatality rate (CFR) is the proportion of cases of a particular disease that die from that disease, usually within a specified time period:

  • CFR = (Total number of deaths due to a particular disease ÷ Total number of cases of the same disease) × 100.

  • Example – if 4 of 200 cholera patients die, the CFR = 2%. Uses and interpretation

  • Measures the killing power (virulence) of a disease.

  • Reflects the quality of case management – a high CFR in cholera or dengue suggests delayed or poor treatment.
  • Used mainly for acute infectious diseases and in outbreak reports. Examples – rabies has a CFR of nearly 100% once symptoms appear; cholera with prompt rehydration is below 1%. It is a ratio (proportion), not a true rate, because time is not in the denominator.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Introduction to Epidemiology – Epidemiological Approaches and Processes
question: What are relative risk and odds ratio?
answer_html:
Both measure the strength of association between an exposure and a disease. Relative risk (RR) – used in cohort studies:

  • RR = Incidence among the exposed ÷ Incidence among the non-exposed.

  • Example – if lung cancer incidence is 1.2 per 1,000 among smokers and 0.1 per 1,000 among non-smokers, RR = 12, meaning smokers are 12 times more likely to develop lung cancer. Odds ratio (OR) – used in case-control studies, where incidence cannot be calculated:

  • From a 2 × 2 table (a = exposed cases, b = exposed controls, c = non-exposed cases, d = non-exposed controls), OR = ad ÷ bc.

  • It is a good estimate of the relative risk when the disease is rare. Interpretation – a value of 1 means no association; more than 1 means positive association (risk factor); less than 1 means a protective effect.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: (a) Explain the evolution, goals and organisation of the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP). (4 marks) (b) Describe the strategies of NTEP under the pillars Detect, Treat, Prevent and Build, with recent initiatives. (7 marks) (c) Explain the role of the community health nurse in TB elimination. (4 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Evolution, goals and organisation (4 marks) Evolution

  • 1962 – National TB Programme (NTP) – District TB Centres, BCG vaccination and domiciliary treatment; limited by long, unsupervised regimens and poor cure rates.
  • 1997 – Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) – adopted the DOTS strategy (political commitment, diagnosis by sputum microscopy, directly observed short-course chemotherapy, uninterrupted drug supply, and recording and reporting); covered the whole country by 2006.
  • 2012 – TB made a notifiable disease; programmatic management of drug-resistant TB expanded; molecular tests (CBNAAT) introduced.
  • 2017 – National Strategic Plan (NSP) for TB Elimination 2017–25 with the four pillars "Detect – Treat – Prevent – Build"; daily fixed-dose combination regimens.
  • 2018 – Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (nutritional support); the Prime Minister announced the goal of ending TB in India by 2025.
  • January 2020 – RNTCP renamed the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP); NSP 2020–25 refreshed the plan.
  • 2022 – Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (Ni-kshay Mitras); December 2024 – the intensified TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan.

Goals

  • In line with SDG target 3.3 and the WHO End TB Strategy, to end the TB epidemic – large reductions in incidence and deaths compared with 2015 and no TB-affected family facing catastrophic costs.
  • India's own target of ending TB by 2025 (incidence of 44 per lakh) was not achieved; work continues towards the 2030 global target.

Burden and progress

  • India accounts for about one-quarter of the world's TB cases.
  • Estimated incidence fell by 21%, from 237 per lakh in 2015 to 187 per lakh in 2024 (WHO Global TB Report 2025).
  • The WHO Global TB Report 2026 recorded a 38% fall in TB mortality (28 to 18 per lakh, 2015–2025) and a 94% treatment success rate for drug-sensitive TB.

Organisation

  • National – Central TB Division (MoHFW), with National Reference Laboratories and the National TB Elimination Board/Task Forces.
  • State – State TB Cell headed by the State TB Officer; Intermediate Reference Laboratories (culture and drug susceptibility testing).
  • District – District TB Centre with the District TB Officer.
  • Sub-district – TB Units with a Senior Treatment Supervisor and Senior TB Laboratory Supervisor; designated microscopy centres and NAAT (CBNAAT/Truenat) sites.
  • Peripheral – PHCs, Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, sub-centres, ASHAs and community treatment supporters, along with private providers.

(b) Strategies – Detect, Treat, Prevent, Build (7 marks) 1. DETECT – find every person with TB early

  • Passive case finding – every person with presumptive TB (cough for 2 weeks or more, fever, weight loss, night sweats, haemoptysis, or any symptom in a vulnerable person) attending any facility, including AAMs, is tested.
  • Active case finding (ACF) – house-to-house or camp screening of vulnerable populations: slum dwellers, tribal and hard-to-reach groups, migrants, prisoners, people living with HIV, persons with diabetes, malnourished people, smokers, alcohol users, the elderly and household contacts. Vulnerability mapping of villages and wards, screening with handheld digital chest X-ray and artificial intelligence (AI) tools.
  • Upfront molecular testing – NAAT (CBNAAT, Truenat) with detection of rifampicin resistance; universal drug susceptibility testing of every diagnosed patient; sputum collection and transport from peripheral facilities.
  • Private sector engagement – mandatory notification by all providers, laboratories and chemists; Patient Provider Support Agencies (PPSA); incentives for notification.
  • Ni-kshay – the case-based web and mobile portal for notification, tracking and payments.

2. TREAT – successful treatment for every patient

  • Free, quality-assured drugs for all patients, public or private – daily fixed-dose combinations by weight band for drug-sensitive TB, and shorter all-oral regimens (such as the 6-month BPaLM regimen) for drug-resistant TB.
  • Adherence support – community treatment supporters, family members, ASHAs; digital adherence technologies; counselling at each visit.
  • Patient support – Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (direct benefit transfer for nutrition), Ni-kshay Mitras who adopt patients and provide food baskets, differentiated care for patients at high risk of severe illness, and management of comorbidities (HIV, diabetes, undernutrition, tobacco and alcohol use).
  • Follow-up – sputum and clinical follow-up during and after treatment; tracking of outcomes on Ni-kshay.

3. PREVENT – stop new infections and disease

  • TB preventive treatment (TPT) for household contacts and people living with HIV, after ruling out active TB.
  • BCG vaccination at birth under UIP.
  • Airborne infection control in health facilities and homes – cough etiquette, ventilation, early diagnosis and treatment.
  • Action on social determinants – nutrition, housing, tobacco control, diabetes control and poverty reduction through convergence with other departments.

4. BUILD – strengthen systems and partnerships

  • Policy and legal measures (notification, regulation of drug sales), human resources and training, laboratory networks, research (ICMR) and digital tools (Ni-kshay, AI-based screening).
  • Community engagement – TB Champions (survivors), TB forums, Jan Bhagidari (people's participation), corporate and NGO partnerships.
  • TB Mukt Panchayat – Gram Panchayats meeting set criteria are certified TB-free; over 46,000 Panchayats were certified for 2024.

Recent initiatives

  • Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (2022) – Ni-kshay Mitras (individuals, institutions, companies) give nutritional, diagnostic and vocational support to patients and families.
  • TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan – a 100-day intensified campaign launched on 7 December 2024 in 347 high-priority districts, later extended to all districts; its next 100-day phase began on World TB Day, 24 March 2026, with the TB Mukt Bharat App and the TB Mukt Urban Ward Initiative.
  • Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana – support of ₹1,000 per month during treatment.

Indicators used – case notification rate, proportion bacteriologically confirmed, coverage of drug-susceptibility testing, treatment success rate, TPT coverage, Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana coverage and the number of TB Mukt Panchayats.

(c) Role of the community health nurse in TB elimination (4 marks)

  1. Case finding – screen for TB symptoms during home visits, ANC, NCD screening (the CBAC form includes TB symptoms), school health and camps; prepare lists of vulnerable households with ASHAs.
  2. Specimen collection and referral – teach correct sputum collection (deep cough, not saliva; spot and early morning samples), label and transport samples, refer for NAAT and chest X-ray.
  3. Notification and records – ensure every case is notified on Ni-kshay; maintain treatment cards and registers.
  4. Treatment support – counsel the patient and family about the disease, duration and importance of completing treatment; identify a treatment supporter; follow up missed doses immediately.
  5. Monitoring – recognise side effects (jaundice, vomiting, visual problems, tingling, rash) and refer; arrange follow-up tests; trace patients who interrupt treatment.
  6. Social support – help with bank details for Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana; link patients with Ni-kshay Mitras and schemes; give nutrition advice.
  7. Prevention – screen all household contacts, arrange TPT and supervise adherence; teach cough etiquette and ventilation; ensure BCG for newborns; screen for diabetes and HIV.
  8. Health education and stigma reduction – correct myths ("TB is a curse", "TB cannot be cured"), stress confidentiality and dignity; involve TB Champions.
  9. Community mobilisation – support TB Mukt Panchayat activities, World TB Day (24 March) events and campaigns; coordinate with private practitioners and chemists for referral and notification.
  10. Infection control at the sub-centre/AAM and in homes.

Nursing importance

  • Most TB care now happens in the community; the nurse and ASHA are the link that turns a diagnosis into a cure – through early detection, adherence support, contact care and social support.

Conclusion NTEP evolved from the National TB Programme (1962) and RNTCP with DOTS (1997) to the National TB Elimination Programme (2020), aiming to end TB in line with the SDGs. Its strategies are organised under Detect (active case finding, upfront NAAT, notification and private sector engagement), Treat (free drugs, adherence and nutritional support), Prevent (TPT, BCG, infection control, social determinants) and Build (policy, systems, digital tools and community engagement), strengthened by the PM TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan campaigns and TB Mukt Panchayats. The community health nurse finds cases, supports treatment, prevents spread and mobilises the community.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: (a) List the diseases covered under the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC) with their vectors. (3 marks) (b) Explain the strategies of the programme – surveillance, case management and integrated vector management. (7 marks) (c) Describe the malaria elimination framework and the elimination goals for lymphatic filariasis and kala-azar. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Integrated vector management under NCVBDC
labels: environmental management and source reduction (removing stagnant water

answer_html:
(a) Diseases and vectors (3 marks) The National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC) – formerly the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP, 2003), which merged the earlier malaria, filaria and kala-azar programmes – works under the National Health Mission for the prevention and control of six vector-borne diseases:

  1. Malaria – female Anopheles mosquitoes: An. culicifacies (main rural vector), An. stephensi (urban – breeds in overhead tanks and construction sites), An. fluviatilis (hill and forest areas), An. minimus and An. dirus (north-east). They bite at night and breed in clean, stagnant water. Forested tribal districts such as Gadchiroli in Maharashtra carry a high burden.
  2. Dengue – Aedes aegypti (and Ae. albopictus) – day-biting mosquitoes breeding in clean water in containers (coolers, tyres, pots, flower vases, discarded items).
  3. Chikungunya – Aedes mosquitoes.
  4. Lymphatic filariasis – Culex quinquefasciatus (for Wuchereria bancrofti; breeds in dirty, polluted water – drains, cesspits) and Mansonia (for Brugia malayi; associated with aquatic plants).
  5. Japanese encephalitis (JE) – Culex tritaeniorhynchus and the Culex vishnui group, breeding in paddy fields; pigs act as amplifying hosts and ardeid (water) birds as reservoirs.
  6. Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) – the sandfly Phlebotomus argentipes, breeding in cracks of mud walls and damp, organic soil.

(b) Strategies of the programme (7 marks) 1. Disease surveillance and early detection

  • Fever surveillance – active (ASHAs and MPWs visit households regularly to find fever cases) and passive (fever cases at health facilities); every fever case in endemic areas is tested by blood smear or rapid diagnostic test (RDT).
  • Sentinel surveillance hospitals and apex referral laboratories for dengue (NS1 antigen and IgM ELISA) and chikungunya; sentinel sites for JE and acute encephalitis syndrome (AES).
  • Night blood surveys (between 8.30 pm and midnight, because microfilariae circulate at night) and transmission assessment surveys (TAS) for filariasis.
  • rK39 rapid test and active case search for kala-azar and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL).
  • Entomological surveillance – mosquito density and larval indices (house index, container index, Breteau index) to predict outbreaks.
  • Reporting through IHIP; outbreak response by rapid response teams.

2. Early diagnosis and complete treatment (case management)

  • Malaria – diagnosis within 24 hours of fever and prompt, complete treatment as per national drug policy (chloroquine and 14-day primaquine for P. vivax; artemisinin-based combination therapy with single-dose primaquine for P. falciparum); referral of severe malaria.
  • Dengue and chikungunya – no specific antiviral drug; early recognition of warning signs, careful fluid management, paracetamol for fever and avoidance of NSAIDs; referral of severe cases.
  • JE/AES – early referral and supportive intensive care.
  • Kala-azar – single-dose liposomal amphotericin B, treatment of PKDL.
  • Lymphatic filariasis – morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) – lymphoedema care (washing, drying, skin care, exercise, elevation) and hydrocele surgery.

3. Integrated vector management (IVM) – the rational use of several methods together, based on local evidence:

  • Chemical control – indoor residual spraying (IRS) with insecticides (synthetic pyrethroids, malathion) in high-risk malaria and kala-azar areas; anti-larval chemicals (e.g. temephos) in water containers that cannot be emptied; space spraying (fogging) only during outbreaks.
  • Biological control – larvivorous fish (Gambusia, guppy) in tanks, ponds, wells and fountains; biolarvicides such as Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti).
  • Environmental management and source reduction – removing stagnant water, filling ditches, cleaning drains, covering water tanks, emptying coolers and containers once a week ("dry day"), proper disposal of tyres and junk, intermittent irrigation in paddy fields.
  • Personal protection – long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) distributed free in high-endemic areas, repellents, full-sleeved clothing, wire-mesh screens.
  • Legal measures – municipal by-laws against mosquito breeding in buildings and construction sites.

4. Mass drug administration (MDA) for filariasis

  • Annual single-dose MDA to the eligible population in endemic districts – DEC plus albendazole (DA) or the triple-drug regimen ivermectin, DEC and albendazole (IDA) – swallowed in front of the drug administrator; children under 2 years, pregnant women and the seriously ill are excluded.

5. JE vaccination – under UIP in endemic districts (two doses at 9–12 months and 16–24 months), and adult vaccination campaigns in some high-risk districts.

6. Behaviour change communication and community participation

  • World Malaria Day (25 April), National Dengue Day (16 May), Anti-Malaria Month (June) and Anti-Dengue Month (July); involvement of Panchayats, urban local bodies, schools, SHGs and NGOs.
  • Intersectoral action with municipal bodies, water supply, agriculture, education and tribal welfare departments.

7. Capacity building, monitoring and research – training of health staff, supervision, and support from research institutes (e.g. ICMR–National Institute of Malaria Research, Vector Control Research Centre).

(c) Malaria elimination framework and elimination goals (5 marks) Malaria

  • National Framework for Malaria Elimination (NFME) 2016–2030 – vision of a malaria-free India: eliminate malaria (zero indigenous cases) throughout the country by 2030 and maintain malaria-free status.
  • The National Strategic Plan for Malaria Elimination 2023–27 aims at zero indigenous cases by 2027, followed by certification of elimination by 2030.
  • Annual parasite incidence (API) = (number of confirmed malaria cases in a year ÷ total population) × 1,000 – used to classify areas:
    • Category 0 – no indigenous cases; prevention of re-establishment phase.
    • Category 1 – API below 1 in the state and all its districts; elimination phase.
    • Category 2 – state API below 1 but some districts with API of 1 or more; pre-elimination phase.
    • Category 3 – state API of 1 or more; intensified control phase.
  • Key elimination strategies – case-based surveillance (every case investigated and classified as indigenous or imported), focus investigation and response, complete radical treatment, vector control in foci, special attention to forest, tribal, mining and border areas and to migrants.

Lymphatic filariasis

  • India aims to eliminate lymphatic filariasis as a public health problem by 2027, ahead of the global target of 2030.
  • Strategy – MDA to interrupt transmission (until microfilaria rate falls below 1% and districts pass the transmission assessment survey), plus MMDP for people with lymphoedema and hydrocele.

Kala-azar

  • Elimination target – fewer than 1 case per 10,000 population at block (sub-district) level in the endemic states (Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh).
  • India achieved this target in all endemic blocks in 2023 and sustained it in 2024; the target must be maintained for three consecutive years for WHO validation.
  • Strategy – early case detection (rK39), single-dose liposomal amphotericin B, IRS with synthetic pyrethroids, treatment of PKDL and HIV–kala-azar co-infection, and community awareness.

Nursing importance

  • Vector-borne diseases are prevented mostly by community action – source reduction, LLIN use, prompt testing of fever and complete treatment – which the community health nurse organises with ASHAs and Panchayats.

Conclusion NCVBDC addresses malaria, dengue, chikungunya, lymphatic filariasis, JE and kala-azar, which are spread by Anopheles, Aedes, Culex/Mansonia mosquitoes and sandflies. Its strategies are surveillance and early detection, early diagnosis and complete treatment, integrated vector management, MDA for filariasis, JE vaccination, behaviour change communication and intersectoral action. India aims to eliminate malaria (zero indigenous cases by 2027, elimination by 2030) and filariasis (by 2027), and has reached the kala-azar elimination threshold in all endemic blocks.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: (a) Explain the epidemiological determinants of acute diarrhoeal diseases and cholera. (5 marks) (b) Describe the prevention and control of diarrhoeal diseases in the community, including the STOP Diarrhoea Campaign. (7 marks) (c) Explain the role of the community health nurse. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: F-diagram of faeco-oral transmission
labels: all leading to a new host; barriers – safe excreta disposal (primary barrier)
hand washing and food hygiene (secondary barriers)

answer_html:
(a) Epidemiological determinants (5 marks) Introduction

  • Diarrhoea is the passage of three or more loose or watery stools in 24 hours (or more frequent than normal for the individual).
  • Acute diarrhoeal diseases remain one of the leading causes of death and malnutrition among children under five in India, especially during the summer and monsoon months.
  • Almost all these deaths are preventable with ORS, zinc, safe water, sanitation and hygiene.
  • Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae, characterised by profuse "rice-water" stools, vomiting and rapid dehydration; untreated it can kill within hours.

1. Agent factors

  • Viruses – rotavirus (the commonest cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants), norovirus, adenovirus.
  • Bacteria – Escherichia coli (enterotoxigenic, enteropathogenic), Shigella (dysentery), Salmonella, Campylobacter, Vibrio cholerae.
  • Parasites – Giardia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium.
  • Cholera agent – V. cholerae serogroup O1 (biotypes classical and El Tor, serotypes Ogawa and Inaba) and O139 (Bengal); a large infective dose is needed, but it is lower in people with low gastric acidity.
  • Reservoir – humans: cases and carriers (incubatory, convalescent, healthy/contact and occasionally chronic carriers). Carriers and mild cases spread infection unnoticed. Brackish water and estuaries may also harbour vibrios.
  • Incubation period of cholera – a few hours to 5 days, usually 1–2 days.
  • Period of communicability – as long as organisms are excreted, usually 7–14 days.

2. Mode of transmission – faeco-oral route ("F-diagram")

  • Water-borne – the most important route; contaminated wells, ponds, broken pipelines leaking near drains, stored water handled with dirty hands.
  • Food-borne – contaminated food, raw vegetables and fruits, seafood, street food, ice and milk.
  • Direct contact – unclean hands ("fingers") – in families and institutions.
  • Flies – carrying faecal matter to food.

3. Host factors

  • Age – highest incidence at 6–24 months (start of complementary feeding, crawling, waning maternal antibodies).
  • Malnutrition and vitamin A and zinc deficiency increase severity and duration; diarrhoea in turn worsens malnutrition (a vicious cycle).
  • Lack of exclusive breastfeeding and use of feeding bottles.
  • Low immunity – measles, HIV, other illnesses; low gastric acidity.
  • Behaviour – no hand washing with soap, open defecation, poor food handling; low maternal education.
  • In cholera, persons with blood group O tend to have more severe illness.

4. Environmental factors

  • Unsafe drinking water and lack of household water treatment.
  • Open defecation and unsafe disposal of children's faeces; poor drainage.
  • Overcrowding, slums and poverty; poor housing.
  • Season – peaks in summer and the rainy season; outbreaks after floods, at fairs and pilgrimages (melas) and in disaster relief camps.
  • Flies and poor food hygiene.
  • India, particularly the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta, has long been considered an endemic home of cholera.

(b) Prevention and control in the community (7 marks) 1. Early and correct case management

  • ORS and zinc – low-osmolarity ORS to prevent and treat dehydration, plus zinc for 14 days (10 mg daily for infants 2–6 months, 20 mg daily for children above 6 months); continued feeding and breastfeeding; increased fluids.
  • Assessment of dehydration and prompt referral of severe dehydration for IV fluids.
  • Antibiotics only when indicated – dysentery (blood in stool), suspected cholera with severe dehydration – as per protocol.
  • ORS-zinc corners at health facilities and Anganwadis; ORS depots during outbreaks.

2. Safe drinking water

  • Protection of water sources; regular chlorination of wells and tanks; household treatment (boiling, chlorine tablets, filtration); safe storage in narrow-mouthed, covered vessels with a ladle.
  • Water quality testing (H₂S strip tests, field test kits) and piped water supply under the Jal Jeevan Mission.

3. Sanitation

  • Use of sanitary latrines by all; safe disposal of children's faeces; ODF Plus villages under the Swachh Bharat Mission; proper drainage and solid waste disposal.

4. Personal and food hygiene

  • Hand washing with soap at critical times – after defecation, after cleaning a child's bottom, before cooking, eating and feeding a child.
  • Food hygiene – eat freshly cooked hot food, wash fruits and vegetables with safe water, protect food from flies, avoid cut fruits and street food during outbreaks; medical examination and training of food handlers.

5. Improving host resistance

  • Exclusive breastfeeding for six months and appropriate complementary feeding.
  • Vitamin A supplementation (9 months to 5 years) and treatment of malnutrition.
  • Immunisation – rotavirus vaccine under UIP (at 6, 10 and 14 weeks) and measles-rubella vaccine; oral cholera vaccine (two doses) for high-risk populations and outbreak response.

6. Surveillance and outbreak control

  • Weekly reporting of acute diarrhoeal disease through IHIP; immediate reporting of clusters or any suspected cholera case.
  • Outbreak response – verification, line listing, stool culture, identification of the source (water/food), disinfection of water sources, chlorine tablets to households, health education and active case search.

7. STOP Diarrhoea Campaign
