  • Builds on the Intensified Diarrhoea Control Fortnight (IDCF), held every year since 2014; from 2024 it was expanded into a two-month STOP Diarrhoea Campaign during the summer–monsoon season (roughly June/July to August).
  • Goal – zero child deaths due to childhood diarrhoea.
  • Activities:
    • Prepositioning of ORS packets and zinc tablets by ASHAs in every household with a child under five, with demonstration of ORS preparation.
    • ORS-zinc corners at all health facilities and Anganwadi centres.
    • Identification and management of children with diarrhoea and dehydration, and referral of severe cases.
    • Intensive IEC/BCC on hand washing, safe water, sanitation and feeding during diarrhoea.
    • Convergence with water and sanitation, women and child development and education departments – cleanliness drives, chlorination and school activities.
  • Slogan used in 2025: "Diarrhoea ki Roktham, Safai aur ORS se rakhein apna dhyaan".

8. Health education – the meaning of dehydration and danger signs, ORS preparation, continued feeding, hand washing and toilet use; myths such as stopping food or breastfeeding during diarrhoea.

(c) Role of the community health nurse (3 marks)

  • Case finding and care – identify children with diarrhoea during home visits; assess dehydration; give ORS and zinc; teach mothers to prepare ORS (one packet in one litre of safe water) and give it by spoon; refer danger signs (lethargy, unable to drink, blood in stool, sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch).
  • Prevention – demonstrate hand washing; promote breastfeeding, toilet use and safe water; give vitamin A and rotavirus vaccine; chlorinate wells and distribute chlorine tablets.
  • Campaign implementation – supervise ASHAs in prepositioning ORS-zinc, set up ORS-zinc corners, conduct IEC sessions in schools and Anganwadis.
  • Surveillance and outbreak response – report through IHIP, collect stool samples (Cary-Blair transport medium for cholera), line list cases, trace the source, coordinate with the water supply department and Panchayat.
  • Records and follow-up – registers, follow-up of treated children for nutrition and growth.

Nursing importance

  • Every diarrhoea death is a missed opportunity – the community health nurse prevents most of them with simple tools: ORS, zinc, hand washing, safe water and toilets.

Conclusion Acute diarrhoeal diseases and cholera are caused by viruses (especially rotavirus), bacteria (including V. cholerae O1 and O139) and parasites, spread by the faeco-oral route, and are favoured by malnutrition, lack of breastfeeding, unsafe water, open defecation, poor hygiene, overcrowding, summer–monsoon seasons and floods. They are controlled by early ORS-zinc treatment, safe water, sanitation, hand washing, food hygiene, breastfeeding, vitamin A, rotavirus and cholera vaccines, surveillance, outbreak response and the annual STOP Diarrhoea Campaign, with the community health nurse at the centre of these efforts.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: Explain the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) and the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP).
answer_html:
Introduction The Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) was launched in November 2004 (initially with World Bank support) to strengthen surveillance of epidemic-prone diseases in India. It is run by the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), Delhi, and continues under the National Health Mission.

Objectives

  • To strengthen and maintain a decentralised, laboratory-based, IT-enabled disease surveillance system for epidemic-prone diseases.
  • To monitor disease trends and to detect and respond to outbreaks in the early rising phase through trained Rapid Response Teams (RRTs).

Organisation

  • Central Surveillance Unit (CSU) at NCDC, Delhi.
  • State Surveillance Units (SSU) in every state.
  • District Surveillance Units (DSU) in every district, each headed by a District Surveillance Officer, with an epidemiologist, data manager and a district public health laboratory.
  • Reporting units – sub-centres/AAMs, PHCs, CHCs, hospitals (government and private), medical colleges and laboratories.

Three levels of case definitions and reporting formats

  1. S form (Syndromic) – filled by health workers (ANMs, MPWs, CHOs) for "suspected" cases based on syndromes, e.g. fever, fever with rash, acute flaccid paralysis, acute diarrhoea, jaundice, unusual events.
  2. P form (Presumptive) – filled by medical officers and clinicians for "probable" cases diagnosed clinically.
  3. L form (Laboratory) – filled by laboratories for confirmed cases.

Reporting system

  • Weekly reporting (week from Monday to Sunday) of cases and deaths, including "zero reporting" when no cases occur.
  • Immediate reporting of early warning signals – any unusual increase in cases, clustering, deaths or a new disease – to the DSU so that the Rapid Response Team can investigate and control the outbreak.
  • Media scanning and verification cell – detects outbreaks reported in newspapers and media and verifies them.
  • Weekly outbreak reports are compiled and shared nationally.

Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP)

  • Launched on 5 April 2021, IHIP is the web- and mobile-based, near real-time digital platform that replaced the earlier IDSP portal.
  • Data are entered by health workers, clinicians and laboratories in S, P and L forms at the point of care, with geo-tagging and automatic analysis, alerts and maps; it allows case-based tracking and faster response.

Role of the nurse

  • Fill and send the S form every week accurately and on time (including zero reporting); report unusual events immediately.
  • Detect clusters during home visits and inform the medical officer and DSU.
  • Collect and transport samples properly; assist the RRT in house-to-house surveys, line listing and control measures.
  • Educate the community about early reporting of illness.

Conclusion IDSP (2004) built a decentralised surveillance network of central, state and district units that collects syndromic (S), presumptive (P) and laboratory (L) data weekly and responds to early warning signals through Rapid Response Teams. Since 2021, IHIP has made this surveillance digital and near real-time.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: Explain the cold chain system in India and the responsibilities of the health worker in maintaining it.

diagram.caption: Cold chain network for UIP vaccines
labels: manufacturer – Government Medical Store Depots/primary stores – state vaccine stores (walk-in coolers and freezers) – regional/divisional stores – district vaccine stores (ILRs and deep freezers) – PHC/CHC cold chain points – vaccine carriers to session sites at sub-centres

answer_html:
Definition The cold chain is the system of people, equipment and procedures that keeps vaccines at the recommended temperature from the point of manufacture to the point of use (the beneficiary). Vaccines lose potency permanently when exposed to heat or freezing, and lost potency cannot be restored.

Components

  1. Personnel – vaccine and cold chain managers, cold chain handlers, cold chain technicians, ANMs and other vaccinators.
  2. Equipment – for storage, transport and temperature monitoring.
  3. Procedures – vaccine logistics (forecasting, indenting, distribution), temperature recording and maintenance.

The cold chain network in India

  • Manufacturer → Government Medical Store Depots / primary vaccine stores → state vaccine stores → regional or divisional stores → district vaccine stores → PHC/CHC/urban PHC cold chain points (the "last cold chain point") → session sites (sub-centre, AAM, Anganwadi, outreach), reached by alternate vaccine delivery on the session day.
  • Large stores use walk-in coolers (WIC) and walk-in freezers (WIF); districts and PHCs use ice-lined refrigerators (ILRs) and deep freezers; solar direct-drive refrigerators are used where electricity is unreliable.
  • Transport – refrigerated vans, cold boxes (between stores and in emergencies) and vaccine carriers with conditioned ice packs (to session sites).

Temperature and storage

  • At the PHC level, all UIP vaccines are stored at +2 °C to +8 °C in the ILR; deep freezers are used to freeze ice packs.
  • Vaccines are kept in the ILR baskets – freeze-sensitive vaccines (e.g. pentavalent, hepatitis B, Td, PCV, IPV) are kept in the upper part away from the coldest bottom, while vaccines not harmed by freezing can go lower; boxes are spaced for air circulation.
  • "Earliest expiry, first out" (EEFO) and VVM status guide which vials are used first; returned open vials under the open vial policy are used first in the next session.
  • Diluents are stored with their vaccines or cooled for at least 24 hours before reconstitution so that they are at the same temperature as the vaccine.
  • Nothing else (food, drinks, drugs) is kept in the ILR.

Temperature monitoring and digital systems

  • Temperature is recorded twice daily (morning and evening) in the log book; alarms and temperature loggers flag excursions.
  • eVIN (electronic Vaccine Intelligence Network) gives real-time information on vaccine stocks and storage temperatures at all cold chain points.
  • U-WIN records every vaccination digitally for each beneficiary.

At the session site

  • The vaccine carrier is packed with four conditioned ice packs (frozen packs left at room temperature until ice starts to melt, to prevent freezing of vaccines), with vaccines kept in a polythene bag and covered by the foam pad.
  • The carrier is kept in the shade and opened as little as possible; opened vials are kept in the slits of the foam pad.
  • At the end of the session, usable opened vials (open vial policy) and unopened vials are returned to the cold chain point the same day.

Cold chain breaks and contingency

  • During power failure or equipment breakdown, keep the ILR closed and, if needed, shift vaccines in cold boxes to the nearest working cold chain point as per the contingency plan.
  • Record and report every temperature excursion; check VVMs and do the shake test if freezing is suspected; do not use damaged vaccines.

Responsibilities of the health worker

  • Maintain the ILR and deep freezer properly; record temperatures twice daily; defrost deep freezers and keep equipment clean.
  • Indent vaccines and logistics in time; keep stock registers; follow EEFO and VVM rules.
  • Pack vaccine carriers correctly; protect vaccines from sun, heat and freezing; return vials the same day.
  • Report breakdowns to the cold chain technician; follow the contingency plan.
  • Record each vaccination on U-WIN and in registers.

Conclusion The cold chain links the manufacturer to the child through a network of stores, ILRs, deep freezers, cold boxes and vaccine carriers that keep vaccines at +2 °C to +8 °C. Careful storage, temperature monitoring through log books and eVIN, correct packing at session sites, contingency planning and timely reporting by the health worker keep vaccines potent.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: Explain the role of the nurse in the prevention and control of vector-borne diseases.
answer_html:
Introduction Vector-borne diseases – malaria, dengue, chikungunya, lymphatic filariasis, Japanese encephalitis and kala-azar – are largely preventable by controlling vectors and by early diagnosis and treatment. The community health nurse, with ASHAs, MPWs and the community, plays a key role.

1. Health education and behaviour change

  • Explain how each disease spreads and where vectors breed:
    • Aedes – clean water in coolers, tyres, pots, flower vases, fridge trays and overhead tanks.
    • Anopheles – clean, stagnant water in ponds, paddy fields, wells and construction sites.
    • Culex – dirty water in drains and cesspits.
  • Promote personal protection – sleeping under LLINs every night, mosquito repellents, full-sleeved clothing, screens on doors and windows.
  • Teach that fever must be tested early; discourage self-medication with painkillers in dengue season.

2. Source reduction and vector control

  • Organise a weekly "dry day" – emptying, scrubbing and drying coolers and containers; covering water tanks; disposing of tyres and junk.
  • Lead cleanliness and source reduction drives with Panchayats, schools, SHGs and youth clubs; introduce larvivorous fish in ponds and wells; arrange anti-larval measures where needed.
  • Support IRS rounds – inform households in advance, ask them not to wash or re-plaster sprayed walls, and report refusals.
  • Conduct larval surveys with ASHAs – house index, container index and Breteau index – and act on high indices.

3. Surveillance and early diagnosis

  • Active fever surveillance in households; prepare blood smears or use RDTs for malaria; send samples for dengue testing as per protocol; report through IHIP.
  • Detect clusters of fever, encephalitis or deaths and report immediately.

4. Treatment and care

  • Give complete treatment for malaria as per national drug policy and ensure the 14-day primaquine course in P. vivax malaria.
  • In dengue – teach about warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, lethargy, cold extremities), encourage oral fluids, paracetamol only, and refer early.
  • Early referral of AES/JE cases and kala-azar suspects.

5. Filariasis elimination

  • Distribute MDA drugs and ensure that they are swallowed in front of her; reassure about mild side effects (fever, nausea, itching – often a sign that worms are being killed).
  • Teach lymphoedema care (daily washing and drying, skin and nail care, exercises, elevation) and refer hydrocele cases for surgery.

6. Immunisation – JE vaccination of children (and adults in campaigns) in endemic districts.

7. Community mobilisation and coordination – observe World Malaria Day, National Dengue Day, Anti-Malaria Month and Anti-Dengue Month; coordinate with municipal bodies for drainage and garbage removal.

8. Records and reporting – fever registers, slide and RDT records, treatment cards, MDA records and outbreak reports.

Conclusion The nurse prevents and controls vector-borne diseases by educating the community, leading source reduction and personal protection, supporting vector control, finding and testing fever cases, ensuring complete treatment, supporting MDA and lymphoedema care, vaccinating against JE, mobilising the community and keeping accurate records.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: Explain the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP).
answer_html:
Introduction

  • Leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium leprae, remains a public health concern in India, which still reports more than half of the world's new cases.
  • 1955 – National Leprosy Control Programme.
  • 1983 – became the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) after the introduction of multidrug therapy (MDT).
  • 2005 – India achieved elimination of leprosy as a public health problem at the national level (prevalence below 1 per 10,000), but new cases, including in children, show that transmission continues.

Current goal – National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023–27

  • Launched on 30 January 2023, it aims at zero transmission of leprosy by 2027 (ahead of the SDG 2030 target), together with zero disability among new cases (especially children) and zero stigma and discrimination.

Strategies and components

  1. Early case detection
    • Leprosy Case Detection Campaign (LCDC) – house-to-house search by trained ASHA and male volunteer pairs in high-endemic districts.
    • Focused leprosy campaigns in hotspot areas and special plans for hard-to-reach areas.
    • ASHA-based surveillance for leprosy suspects throughout the year.
    • Screening of children through RBSK and school health; contact screening of household and neighbourhood contacts.
  2. Treatment with MDT
    • Free MDT for all patients; since 1 April 2025, a uniform three-drug regimen (rifampicin, clofazimine and dapsone) is used for both paucibacillary (6 months) and multibacillary (12 months) cases under the revised classification.
  3. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) – a single dose of rifampicin for eligible contacts of new cases to reduce their risk of developing leprosy.
  4. Disability prevention and medical rehabilitation (DPMR)
    • Early detection and management of reactions and neuritis.
    • Self-care training for anaesthetic hands and feet, microcellular rubber (MCR) footwear, aids and appliances.
    • Reconstructive surgery for deformities.
  5. Reducing stigma and discrimination – IEC through the SPARSH Leprosy Awareness Campaign launched on Anti-Leprosy Day (30 January); interpersonal communication; repeal of discriminatory laws; involvement of persons affected by leprosy.
  6. Information system – case-based digital tracking through the Nikusth portal.
  7. Capacity building, monitoring and research.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Identify suspects (pale or reddish patches with loss of sensation, thickened nerves, weakness of hands or feet) during home visits and school health; refer for diagnosis.
  • Ensure regular intake of MDT and completion; monitor for reactions and drug side effects.
  • Screen contacts and support PEP; teach self-care of hands, feet and eyes; prevent ulcers and deformities.
  • Counsel patients and families; fight stigma; link them with social welfare schemes and disability certification.
  • Maintain records and report cases on time.

Conclusion NLEP has moved from control (1955) and MDT-based elimination as a public health problem (2005) to the goal of zero transmission by 2027 under the NSP and Roadmap 2023–27. Its key strategies are active case detection, a uniform three-drug MDT since April 2025, single-dose rifampicin PEP for contacts, disability prevention and rehabilitation, stigma reduction and digital tracking.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: Explain the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP).
answer_html:
Introduction

  • Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, D and E) is a major public health problem in India.
  • Hepatitis A and E spread by the faeco-oral route and cause outbreaks.
  • Hepatitis B and C spread through blood, unsafe injections, sexual contact and from mother to child, and cause chronic liver disease, cirrhosis and liver cancer.
  • The National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP) was launched on 28 July 2018 (World Hepatitis Day) under the National Health Mission.

Goal

  • To combat hepatitis and achieve the elimination of hepatitis C as a public health threat by 2030 (in line with SDG target 3.3).
  • To achieve a significant reduction in infected people, morbidity and mortality due to hepatitis B and C.
  • To reduce the risk, morbidity and mortality due to hepatitis A and E.

Objectives

  • Enhance community awareness and promote preventive measures.
  • Provide early diagnosis and management of viral hepatitis at all levels of health care.
  • Develop standard diagnostic and treatment protocols.
  • Strengthen surveillance, laboratories and capacity for prevention and management.

Components 1. Preventive component

  • Hepatitis B vaccination – birth dose within 24 hours of delivery (especially institutional deliveries), followed by pentavalent vaccine under UIP; vaccination of health-care workers and high-risk groups.
  • Safe injection practices and injection safety; safe blood transfusion (screening of donated blood).
  • Safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene to prevent hepatitis A and E.

  • Elimination of vertical transmission – screening of pregnant women for hepatitis B and giving the birth dose (and hepatitis B immunoglobulin where indicated) to newborns of positive mothers. 2. Diagnosis and treatment

  • Free screening and diagnosis (rapid tests, ELISA, viral load testing).

  • Free treatment through Model Treatment Centres (in medical colleges and large hospitals) and Treatment Centres (district hospitals) – direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C (a 12-week course cures most patients) and long-term antivirals (e.g. tenofovir) for eligible patients with chronic hepatitis B; management of acute liver failure. 3. Awareness and IEC – World Hepatitis Day activities, messages on safe injections, safe sex, avoiding sharing razors and needles, and safe water. 4. Surveillance, training, monitoring and research.

Role of the nurse

  • Give the hepatitis B birth dose to every newborn and complete the vaccination series; ensure her own vaccination.
  • Follow safe injection and infection-control practices and safe disposal of sharps.
  • Screen pregnant women and high-risk groups as per protocol; refer positives to treatment centres; support adherence to antiviral treatment.
  • Educate the community about modes of spread, prevention, and the need to avoid stigma; promote safe water and sanitation.
  • Report outbreaks of jaundice through IHIP.

Conclusion NVHCP (2018) works to eliminate hepatitis C and reduce the burden of hepatitis B, A and E through prevention (vaccination including the birth dose, safe injections, safe blood, sanitation, elimination of vertical transmission), free diagnosis and treatment at model and district treatment centres, awareness, surveillance and training.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: Explain zoonoses and the One Health approach.
tags: National Institute of One Health Nagpur
answer_html:
Definition Zoonoses are diseases and infections that are naturally transmitted between vertebrate animals and humans. About 60% of known human infectious diseases and roughly three-quarters of emerging infections (e.g. Nipah, avian influenza) are zoonotic.

Classification by type of agent (with examples relevant to India)

  • Bacterial – leptospirosis (rats, cattle – outbreaks after floods and in paddy farmers in Maharashtra, Kerala and Gujarat), brucellosis, anthrax, plague, bovine tuberculosis, salmonellosis.
  • Viral – rabies (dogs are the source of the great majority of human cases), Japanese encephalitis (pigs, birds), Kyasanur forest disease ("monkey fever", Karnataka), Nipah virus (fruit bats, Kerala), avian influenza (poultry), Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever.
  • Rickettsial – scrub typhus (chiggers/mites from rodents), Q fever.
  • Parasitic – hydatid disease (dogs), taeniasis and cysticercosis (pigs), toxoplasmosis (cats), kala-azar (animal reservoirs in some regions).
  • Fungal – ringworm from animals.

Modes of spread – animal bites and scratches (rabies), contact with animal urine or tissues (leptospirosis, anthrax), vectors (JE, KFD, plague, scrub typhus), consumption of contaminated milk, meat or food (brucellosis, taeniasis), and inhalation (avian influenza).

Prevention and control

  1. Control in animals – vaccination of dogs and livestock, animal birth control for stray dogs, culling of infected birds in avian influenza, deworming of dogs.
  2. Food safety – meat inspection, pasteurisation or boiling of milk, proper cooking of meat.
  3. Environmental measures – rodent control, safe disposal of carcasses and slaughterhouse waste, vector control.
  4. Personal protection – boots and gloves for farmers and sewage workers, protective clothing for veterinary and abattoir workers.
  5. Human vaccination and prophylaxis – rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (and pre-exposure for high-risk groups), JE vaccine, doxycycline prophylaxis in leptospirosis outbreaks where advised.
  6. Surveillance – joint human and animal surveillance and outbreak response.

One Health approach

  • One Health recognises that the health of people, animals and the environment is closely linked, and calls for collaboration between human health, veterinary, agriculture, wildlife and environment sectors to prevent, detect and respond to health threats – especially zoonoses, antimicrobial resistance and food safety.
  • Globally it is promoted by the quadripartite of WHO, FAO, WOAH (World Organisation for Animal Health) and UNEP.
  • In India
    • The National One Health Mission coordinates human, animal and environmental health for integrated disease control and pandemic preparedness, anchored by the National Institute of One Health, Nagpur.
    • NCDC runs programmes for zoonoses and supports joint outbreak response.
    • The National Action Plan for dog-mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE) aims at zero human rabies deaths by 2030.

Role of the nurse

  • Educate people on washing animal-bite wounds with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seeking PEP immediately; ensure completion of the vaccine schedule.
  • Teach farmers and workers about protective footwear and gloves, safe handling of animals and boiling of milk.
  • Report clusters of unusual fever, encephalitis or animal deaths; support rodent and vector control.
  • Work with veterinary staff and Panchayats in a One Health spirit.

Conclusion Zoonoses are infections shared between animals and humans – bacterial (leptospirosis, brucellosis, anthrax), viral (rabies, JE, KFD, Nipah, avian influenza), rickettsial (scrub typhus), parasitic and fungal. They are controlled by action in animals, food safety, environmental measures, personal protection, vaccination and joint surveillance – the essence of the One Health approach, which India promotes through the National One Health Mission anchored at Nagpur.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: Differentiate between reproductive tract infections (RTIs) and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Add a note on syndromic management.
answer_html:
Reproductive tract infections (RTIs) are infections of the genital tract in women and men. They are of three types:

  • Endogenous – overgrowth of organisms normally present (bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis).
  • Iatrogenic – after unsafe abortion, delivery or IUCD insertion.
  • Sexually transmitted. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections spread mainly through sexual contact – syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, chancroid, trichomoniasis, genital herpes, genital warts (HPV), HIV and hepatitis B. Thus all STIs are RTIs, but not all RTIs are sexually transmitted. Syndromic management – treatment based on the syndrome (urethral discharge, vaginal discharge, genital ulcer, lower abdominal pain, inguinal bubo) without waiting for laboratory tests, using colour-coded pre-packed kits (kits 1–7) at Suraksha clinics under NACP, with partner treatment, condom promotion and counselling.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What is the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana?
answer_html:
The Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (NPY) is a nutritional support scheme for TB patients under the National TB Elimination Programme, started in April 2018.

  • Every notified TB patient (public or private sector) receives cash support by direct benefit transfer (DBT) into a bank account for the entire duration of treatment; the amount is now ₹1,000 per month.
  • The patient must be registered on Ni-kshay with bank details. Purpose – TB and undernutrition worsen each other; better nutrition improves treatment success and reduces deaths, and the support reduces the financial burden on families. The nurse helps patients enrol, gives dietary advice and links them with Ni-kshay Mitras for food baskets.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What are long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs)?
answer_html:
Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) are mosquito nets factory-treated with a synthetic pyrethroid insecticide that is incorporated into or bound onto the fibres, so that the insecticide remains effective for about three years or at least 20 washes without re-treatment. Uses

  • Protect sleepers from night-biting Anopheles mosquitoes (malaria) and other vectors; they kill or repel mosquitoes touching the net.
  • When most of the community uses them, they also reduce the vector population (mass effect).
  • Distributed free under NCVBDC in high malaria-endemic areas, giving priority to pregnant women and children. Correct use and care – hang every night and tuck the edges under the mattress; wash gently with ordinary soap in cold water not more than every three months; dry in the shade, not in direct sunlight; repair holes.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What is the open vial policy?
answer_html: The open vial policy (OVP) allows partially used multi-dose vials of certain vaccines to be reused in subsequent sessions for up to 4 weeks (28 days) after opening, which reduces vaccine wastage (MoHFW revised guidelines, 2015). Applicable to – liquid vaccines such as DPT, TT/Td, hepatitis B, OPV, pentavalent and IPV (and PCV as per later guidance). Not applicable to – reconstituted vaccines – BCG, measles/MR and JE – which are discarded at the end of the session or 4 hours after reconstitution, whichever is earlier. Conditions – the expiry date has not passed; the VVM has not reached the discard point; vials have been stored at +2 °C to +8 °C and not submerged in water; aseptic technique was used; the date and time of opening are written on the vial.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What is TB preventive treatment (TPT)?
answer_html:
TB preventive treatment (TPT) is the treatment of TB infection (latent TB) in people at high risk, to prevent progression to active TB disease. Who is eligible (NTEP)

  • People living with HIV.
  • Household contacts of pulmonary TB patients – all ages, after active TB has been ruled out.

  • Other high-risk groups – people on dialysis, anti-TNF treatment or preparing for organ transplant, and those with silicosis. Regimens

  • 6H – daily isoniazid for 6 months.

  • 3HP – weekly isoniazid and rifapentine for 12 weeks (age 2 years and above).
  • Levofloxacin-based TPT for contacts of drug-resistant TB, as per guidelines. Before TPT, active TB must be excluded by symptom screening (and chest X-ray where available); adherence and side effects are monitored and recorded on Ni-kshay.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What is NAPRE?
tags: National Action Plan for dog-mediated Rabies Elimination
answer_html:
The National Action Plan for dog-mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE) was launched on World Rabies Day, 28 September 2021, by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying.

  • Goal – zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030 ("Zero by 30").

  • Approach – One Health – joint work by the human health, veterinary and local government sectors under the National Rabies Control Programme. Key strategies

  • Free and timely post-exposure prophylaxis (wound washing, anti-rabies vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin) at all health facilities.

  • Mass dog vaccination and animal birth control.
  • Surveillance and reporting of human rabies cases and animal bites; awareness campaigns in schools and communities.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Non-communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: (a) List the national health programmes for non-communicable diseases in India. (3 marks) (b) Explain the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD) – objectives, components and strategies. (8 marks) (c) Describe the role of the community health nurse in NCD control. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: NP-NCD continuum of care
labels: ASHA enumerates all persons aged 30+ and fills CBAC – screening at Ayushman Arogya Mandir (BP
breast and cervical examination) – confirmation and treatment initiation at PHC – NCD clinic at CHC/district hospital – tertiary care – follow-up
monthly drugs and lifestyle counselling back at the AAM
with teleconsultation and the National NCD Portal linking all levels

answer_html:
(a) National programmes for NCDs (3 marks)

  • National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD) – earlier NPCDCS (2010); covers hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, stroke, common cancers, chronic kidney disease, COPD and related conditions.
  • National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI) – started in 1976.
  • National Programme for Prevention and Control of Deafness (NPPCD) – 2006.
  • National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) – 1982, with the District Mental Health Programme and Tele-MANAS.
  • National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP) – 2007–08.
  • National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP) – the goitre programme of 1962, renamed in 1992.
  • National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE) – 2010.
  • National Programme for Palliative Care (NPPC) – 2012.
  • National Oral Health Programme (NOHP).
  • National Programme for Prevention and Control of Fluorosis (NPPCF).
  • Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme – 2016.
  • National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health (NPCCHH) – 2019.
  • National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission – 2023.
  • National Programme for Prevention and Management of Burn Injuries.

(b) NP-NCD (8 marks) Introduction

  • NCDs – cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, cancers and chronic respiratory diseases – now cause about two-thirds of all deaths in India, many of them premature (below 70 years).
  • They share common modifiable risk factors – tobacco use, unhealthy diet (high salt, sugar and fat; low fruits and vegetables), physical inactivity, harmful use of alcohol and air pollution – which lead to raised blood pressure, blood sugar and lipids, and obesity.
  • The National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS) was launched in 2010; it was renamed NP-NCD in 2023 and is implemented under the National Health Mission.

Objectives

  1. Prevent and control common NCDs through behaviour and lifestyle changes.
  2. Provide early diagnosis and management of common NCDs.
  3. Build capacity at various levels of health care for prevention, diagnosis and treatment.
  4. Train human resources within the public health system.
  5. Establish and develop capacity for palliative and rehabilitative care.

Components and strategies 1. Health promotion and prevention

  • IEC/BCC on healthy diet (less salt, sugar and oil), physical activity, yoga, avoiding tobacco and alcohol, and stress management – through mass media, health days and wellness sessions at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
  • Convergence with Fit India, Eat Right India, school health and the National Tobacco Control Programme.

2. Population-based screening (PBS) at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs

  • Enumeration of every person aged 30 years and above by the ASHA, who fills the Community Based Assessment Checklist (CBAC) for risk scoring and early symptoms.
  • Screening of everyone aged 30+ for the five common NCDs:
    • Hypertension – blood pressure measurement.
    • Diabetes – capillary blood glucose.
    • Oral cancer – oral visual examination.
    • Breast cancer – clinical breast examination in women.
    • Cervical cancer – VIA in women aged 30–65.
  • Screening is repeated every year for hypertension and diabetes and every five years for cancers.
  • Screen-positive persons are referred to the PHC medical officer for confirmation and treatment initiation.
  • Expanded package – screening is extending to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma, chronic kidney disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and recognition and referral of stroke and STEMI (heart attack).

3. Opportunistic screening at all health facilities (PHCs, CHCs and hospitals).

4. NCD clinics and higher-level care

  • NCD clinics at CHCs and district hospitals for diagnosis, management and counselling.
  • District NCD Cells for planning and monitoring.
  • Cardiac care units, day-care chemotherapy centres and stroke and STEMI management at district level, linked to tertiary cancer care centres and medical colleges.

5. Free drugs and diagnostics – under the Free Drugs and Free Diagnostics Service Initiatives; follow-up medicines dispensed monthly at AAMs close to the patient's home.

6. Standard treatment workflows/protocols – simple, drug- and dose-specific protocols (e.g. state hypertension protocols developed with the India Hypertension Control Initiative) that CHOs and medical officers follow.

7. Teleconsultation (e-Sanjeevani) linking AAMs with PHC doctors and specialists.

8. National NCD Portal – a digital, individual-wise record of screening, diagnosis, treatment and follow-up, used for monitoring at every level.

9. 75/25 initiative

  • Launched on World Hypertension Day, 17 May 2023, to bring 75 million people with hypertension and diabetes under standard care by December 2025.
  • By March 2025, about 42 million people were on treatment for hypertension and 25 million for diabetes (nearly 90% of the target).
  • A nationwide campaign from 20 February to 31 March 2025 aimed at screening every person aged 30 years and above.

10. Capacity building, monitoring, research and inter-sectoral action – with ministries of education, sports, food safety, urban development and agriculture.

(c) Role of the community health nurse (4 marks)

  1. Community enumeration and risk assessment – supervise ASHAs in listing all persons aged 30+ and filling the CBAC; prioritise those with high scores.
  2. Screening at the AAM and in camps – measure BP correctly, check blood glucose, examine the mouth, perform clinical breast examination and VIA (when trained); record findings.
  3. Referral and confirmation – refer screen-positives to the medical officer; use teleconsultation.
  4. Treatment support and follow-up
    • Dispense monthly medicines as prescribed and follow the standard treatment workflow.
    • Monitor BP and blood sugar; check adherence; recognise complications and refer.
    • Trace patients who miss follow-up.
  5. Lifestyle counselling – reduce salt to less than one teaspoon (5 g) a day, cut down oil and sugar, eat more fruits, vegetables and millets, walk or exercise at least 150 minutes a week, keep a healthy weight, quit tobacco and alcohol, sleep well and manage stress (yoga, meditation).
  6. Health promotion events – World Cancer Day (4 February), World No Tobacco Day (31 May), World Hypertension Day (17 May), World Heart Day (29 September), World Stroke Day (29 October), World Diabetes Day (14 November); wellness sessions and school activities.
  7. Special care – foot care education for diabetics, eye check-up referral, home visits to bedridden patients, palliative and rehabilitative support.
  8. Records and reporting – NCD registers, patient-held cards and entries on the National NCD Portal.
  9. Coordination with ASHAs, MPWs, Anganwadi workers, schools, SHGs and Panchayats for community action against tobacco and for healthy environments.

Nursing importance

  • NCDs are lifelong conditions; the nurse at the AAM provides the continuity – screening, monthly follow-up, adherence support and lifestyle counselling – that prevents strokes, heart attacks, kidney failure and late-stage cancers.

Conclusion India has a set of programmes for NCDs – NP-NCD, NPCBVI, NPPCD, NMHP, NTCP, NIDDCP, NPHCE, NPPC, NOHP, NPPCF, the dialysis programme, NPCCHH and the sickle cell mission. NP-NCD (NPCDCS from 2010, renamed in 2023) aims to prevent and control NCDs through health promotion, population-based screening of everyone aged 30+ at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, opportunistic screening, NCD clinics, free drugs and diagnostics, standard protocols, teleconsultation, the National NCD Portal and the 75/25 initiative. The community health nurse leads enumeration, screening, referral, follow-up, counselling and record keeping.

question: (a) Explain the burden and health effects of tobacco use in India. (3 marks) (b) Describe the National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP) and the main provisions of COTPA, 2003. (7 marks) (c) Explain the methods of tobacco cessation and the role of the nurse. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Brief tobacco cessation intervention
labels: Ask about tobacco use at every visit – Advise to quit – Assess willingness – if willing
quitline) and Arrange follow-up; if not willing

answer_html:
(a) Burden and health effects (3 marks) Burden (Global Adult Tobacco Survey-2, 2016–17)

  • 28.6% of adults aged 15 years and above (about 26.7 crore people) use tobacco in some form – 42.4% of men and 14.2% of women.
  • 21.4% use smokeless tobacco and 10.7% smoke; bidis are the commonest smoked product.
  • Among school students aged 13–15 years, 8.5% use some form of tobacco (Global Youth Tobacco Survey-4, 2019).
  • Smoking and second-hand smoke kill about 1.2 million Indians every year, and India carries most of the world's burden of smokeless tobacco use.

Forms – smoked: bidi, cigarette, hookah, chillum; smokeless: khaini, gutkha, zarda, mawa, betel quid with tobacco, mishri, gul and tobacco toothpaste.

Health effects

  • Cancers – mouth, tongue, throat, larynx, lung, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, bladder and cervix; most oral cancers in India are linked to smokeless tobacco.
  • Cardiovascular diseases – coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension.
  • Respiratory diseases – COPD, asthma attacks, and higher risk of tuberculosis and poor TB outcomes.
  • Reproductive effects – infertility, low birth weight, stillbirth, preterm birth and sudden infant death.
  • Oral problems – oral submucous fibrosis, leukoplakia, gum disease, tooth loss.
  • Second-hand smoke harms non-smokers, especially children (pneumonia, asthma, ear infections).
  • Economic loss – spending on tobacco and treatment pushes families into poverty.

(b) National Tobacco Control Programme and COTPA, 2003 (7 marks) NTCP – launched in 2007–08 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, implemented under the National Health Mission.

Objectives

  1. Create awareness about the harmful effects of tobacco use.
  2. Reduce the production and supply of tobacco products.
  3. Ensure effective implementation of COTPA, 2003 and related laws.
  4. Help people quit tobacco through cessation services.
  5. Facilitate implementation of strategies for prevention and control advocated by the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), which India ratified in 2004.

Structure and components

  • National Tobacco Control Cell at the Ministry; State Tobacco Control Cells; District Tobacco Control Cells with a nodal officer, consultant, psychologist or social worker.
  • Training of health and social workers, teachers, police and enforcement officers.
  • School programmes – tobacco-free educational institution guidelines.
  • IEC and mass media – television, radio, cinema and social-media campaigns; World No Tobacco Day (31 May).
  • Enforcement – tobacco control squads, fines and monitoring of COTPA compliance.
  • Tobacco Cessation Centres (TCCs) at district hospitals; the National Tobacco Quitline Service; integration of cessation into Ayushman Arogya Mandirs and NCD clinics.
  • Surveillance and research – GATS and GYTS surveys, tobacco product testing laboratories.

Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA), 2003 – main provisions

  • Section 4 – prohibition of smoking in public places (hospitals, offices, educational institutions, public transport, restaurants, cinemas); "No Smoking" signboards must be displayed.
  • Section 5 – ban on direct and indirect advertising, promotion and sponsorship of tobacco products.
  • Section 6(a) – no sale of tobacco products to persons below 18 years.
  • Section 6(b) – no sale within 100 yards of educational institutions.
  • Section 7 – mandatory pictorial and text health warnings on all tobacco packs (covering 85% of the main display area), along with the quitline number.
  • Violations are punishable with fines and imprisonment.

Other legal measures – the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019 bans the production, import, sale and advertisement of e-cigarettes; food safety regulations prohibit tobacco and nicotine in food products, the basis for state bans on gutkha and pan masala containing tobacco; high taxes on tobacco products.

MPOWER measures (WHO) – the basis of tobacco control policy:

  • Monitor tobacco use and prevention policies.
  • Protect people from tobacco smoke.
  • Offer help to quit.
  • Warn about the dangers of tobacco.
  • Enforce bans on advertising, promotion and sponsorship.
  • Raise taxes on tobacco.

(c) Tobacco cessation and the role of the nurse (5 marks) Methods of tobacco cessation

  1. Brief advice using the 5 As (for every tobacco user, at every contact)
    • Ask about tobacco use and record it.
    • Advise clearly and personally to quit ("Quitting tobacco is the most important thing you can do for your health").
    • Assess willingness to quit.
    • Assist – set a quit date, give counselling, suggest coping skills and medicines, refer to the quitline or a TCC.
    • Arrange follow-up – the first week after the quit date is crucial.
  2. Motivational counselling using the 5 Rs for those not yet willing to quit
    • Relevance – why quitting matters to the person (family, money, children).
    • Risks – of continued use (cancer, heart attack).
    • Rewards – of quitting (better health, savings, better breath and taste).
    • Roadblocks – barriers and how to overcome them.
    • Repetition – repeat at every visit.
  3. Behavioural support – identifying triggers, avoiding situations linked with tobacco, family support, the 4 Ds for cravings – Delay, Deep breathing, Drink water, Do something else.
  4. Pharmacotherapy (at TCCs or under medical advice) – nicotine replacement therapy (gum, patch, lozenges), bupropion and varenicline.
  5. Quitline and digital support
    • National Tobacco Quitline – 1800-112-356 (toll-free), printed on every tobacco pack.
    • mCessation – a missed call to 011-22901701 registers the user for text-message support.
  6. Managing withdrawal – irritability, restlessness, poor concentration, sleep disturbance, increased appetite and weight gain usually settle within a few weeks; regular meals, exercise and fruits help.

Role of the nurse

  • Ask every client about tobacco use – at the AAM, ANC clinic, TB and NCD clinics, home visits and school health; give brief advice.
  • Counsel pregnant women, TB patients, diabetics and people with hypertension as priority groups; involve family members.
  • Refer to TCCs, NCD clinics and the quitline; follow up quitters and prevent relapse.
  • Prevent initiation – educate adolescents and school children; help schools and villages become tobacco-free; correct myths (e.g. that tobacco aids digestion or relieves toothache).
  • Support enforcement – promote "No Smoking" signs at the health centre, report sale of tobacco near schools and to minors.
  • Screen for oral pre-cancerous lesions (white or red patches, restricted mouth opening) and refer.
  • Be a role model – never use tobacco, and keep the health facility tobacco-free.

Nursing importance

  • Tobacco is the single largest preventable cause of NCD deaths; even a brief, repeated message from a nurse doubles a person's chance of quitting.

Conclusion Tobacco – both smoked and smokeless – is used by more than a quarter of Indian adults and causes cancers, heart and lung disease, TB and harm in pregnancy. NTCP (2007–08) works through awareness, enforcement of COTPA 2003 (no smoking in public places, no advertising, no sale to minors or near schools, pictorial warnings), the e-cigarette ban, school programmes, MPOWER measures and cessation services. Nurses help users quit with the 5 As and 5 Rs, behavioural support, nicotine replacement, the quitline (1800-112-356) and mCessation, and prevent young people from starting.

question: (a) Explain the magnitude and risk factors of road traffic accidents in India. (5 marks) (b) Describe the prevention of road traffic injuries, including legal measures. (6 marks) (c) Explain the trauma care system on highways and the role of the nurse. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Haddon matrix applied to road traffic injuries
labels: crash and post-crash phases; columns – human (training
speed; helmets and seat belts; first aid)
crash-worthiness; fire risk) and environment (road design
lighting; crash barriers; ambulance and trauma care access)

answer_html:
(a) Magnitude and risk factors (5 marks) Magnitude

  • Worldwide, road traffic crashes kill about 1.19 million people every year and are the leading cause of death among children and young people aged 5–29; SDG target 3.6 aims to halve road traffic deaths by 2030.
  • In India, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways report "Road Accidents in India 2023" recorded 4,80,583 road accidents, 1,72,890 deaths and 4,62,825 injured persons – about 55 accidents and 20 deaths every hour.
  • Young adults aged 18–45 years made up about two-thirds of deaths, and people of working age (18–60 years) more than four-fifths – a huge economic and social loss.
  • Over-speeding accounted for about 68% of accidents and deaths.
  • Pedestrians (over 35,000 deaths) and two-wheeler riders are the most vulnerable road users.
  • Not wearing seat belts was linked to more than 16,000 deaths in 2023, and many two-wheeler deaths involve riders without helmets.

Risk factors – analysed as human, vehicle and environmental factors (agent–host–environment). 1. Human (host) factors

  • Over-speeding and rash or dangerous driving; overtaking wrongly; driving on the wrong side.
  • Drunken driving and drugs; drowsiness and fatigue (long-distance truck and bus drivers).
  • Use of mobile phones while driving; jumping red lights.
  • Non-use of helmets, seat belts and child restraints.
  • Inexperience and lack of training; young male drivers; underage driving.
  • Poor vision or hearing, epilepsy, diabetes with hypoglycaemia, the elderly.
  • Pedestrian behaviour – crossing at unsafe places, walking on highways at night.

  • Overloading of passengers and goods. 2. Vehicle (agent) factors

  • Defective brakes, tyres, steering and lights; poor maintenance.

  • Lack of safety features (airbags, anti-lock brakes, crash-worthy design).

  • Two-wheelers offer little protection; mixed traffic of heavy and light vehicles, animal carts and bicycles. 3. Environmental factors

  • Poor road design, sharp curves, potholes (thousands of crashes and over 2,000 deaths in 2023), unguarded level crossings, accident "black spots".

  • Lack of footpaths, pedestrian crossings, signals, signboards and street lighting; encroachments and stray cattle.
  • Weather – fog, rain, darkness.
  • Delay in rescue and lack of trauma care after the crash increases deaths.

(b) Prevention of road traffic injuries (6 marks) Haddon matrix – prevention is planned for each phase (pre-crash, crash and post-crash) and each factor (human, vehicle, environment).

The "4 Es" of road safety

  1. Education
    • Road safety education in schools and colleges; awareness campaigns (National Road Safety Month in January).
    • Driver training and testing; education of pedestrians and cyclists; messages against drink-driving and mobile-phone use.
  2. Enforcement (legal measures)
    • Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 – much higher penalties for over-speeding, drunken driving, driving without a licence, not wearing helmets or seat belts and dangerous driving.
    • Helmets are compulsory for riders and pillion riders (including children above four years) on two-wheelers; seat belts or child restraints for children in cars.
    • Penalties make guardians or owners liable for offences by juveniles.
    • Drink-driving limit – blood alcohol above 30 mg per 100 ml is an offence; breath-analyser checks.
    • Speed limits with speed cameras and electronic enforcement; regulation of driving hours for commercial drivers; fitness certificates for vehicles.
  3. Engineering
    • Road engineering – rectification of black spots, safe road design, divided highways, crash barriers, speed breakers and rumble strips, footpaths and pedestrian crossings, street lighting and signage.
    • Vehicle engineering – airbags, anti-lock brakes, better lights and crash-tested designs (Bharat NCAP star rating).
  4. Emergency care
    • Quick rescue, first aid at the scene, 108 ambulance transport and treatment within the "golden hour" – defined in the Motor Vehicles Act as the one hour after a traumatic injury during which prompt medical care is most likely to prevent death.

Protection of Good Samaritans – Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act (added in 2019) protects any person who helps a road accident victim from civil or criminal liability. They cannot be forced to disclose their identity or to stay at the hospital, and hospitals cannot demand payment before treatment.

Cashless Treatment of Road Accident Victims Scheme, 2025 – from 5 May 2025, any victim of a road accident involving a motor vehicle is entitled to cashless treatment up to ₹1.5 lakh for up to seven days at designated hospitals (stabilisation at other hospitals), implemented through the National Health Authority.

(c) Trauma care on highways and the role of the nurse (4 marks) Trauma care system

  • Pre-hospital care – emergency response through 112/108 ambulances (basic and advanced life support), highway patrol and ambulances on national highways; trained first responders among police, drivers, dhaba owners and villagers along highways.
  • Network of trauma care facilities – under the Ministry of Health's programme for trauma care on national highways, government hospitals along highways are developed as Level III (basic stabilisation – CHC/sub-district), Level II (district hospitals) and Level I (medical college/tertiary) trauma care facilities, with equipment, trained staff, blood banks and referral links, so that victims reach definitive care within the golden hour.
  • Hospital care – trauma teams, triage, emergency surgery, blood transfusion, ICU care and rehabilitation; data collection through trauma registries.

Role of the nurse

  • At the scene – ensure safety, call 108, assess airway, breathing and circulation, stop bleeding with pressure, immobilise the neck and spine, splint fractures, cover wounds and burns, keep the victim warm, and triage when there are many victims (treating the most serious first).
  • Safe transport – log-roll and move on a firm board, monitor vital signs and level of consciousness during transfer.
  • In the trauma unit – primary and secondary survey, IV access, fluids and blood, preparation for surgery, documentation for medico-legal records.
  • Community education – helmets, seat belts, child restraints, no drink-driving or mobile phones; first-aid training for community members, drivers and school students; inform people about Good Samaritan protection and the cashless scheme.
  • Rehabilitation and support – physiotherapy referral, disability certification, psychological support to victims and bereaved families.

Nursing importance

  • Most road traffic deaths are preventable – by safer behaviour before a crash and by quick, skilled care in the golden hour after it; the nurse contributes at both ends.

Conclusion Road traffic accidents killed over 1.72 lakh people in India in 2023, mostly young adults, and are driven by human factors (speeding, drink-driving, mobile phones, no helmets or seat belts), vehicle defects and unsafe roads. Prevention uses the Haddon matrix and the 4 Es – education, enforcement (MV Amendment Act 2019), engineering and emergency care – supported by Good Samaritan protection and the cashless treatment scheme. A tiered trauma care network on highways, quick ambulance transport and skilled nursing at the scene and in hospital save lives within the golden hour.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Non-communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: Explain the primary management, referral and follow-up of hypertension and diabetes at the Ayushman Arogya Mandir as per standard treatment protocols.
answer_html:
Introduction Under NP-NCD, people aged 30 years and above are screened at the Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM). Those found positive are confirmed and started on treatment by the PHC medical officer, and then followed up monthly at the AAM by the CHO/staff nurse using standard, drug- and dose-specific treatment protocols, so that care is close to home and consistent.

1. Hypertension Screening and diagnosis

  • Measure BP correctly – seated, rested for five minutes, correct cuff size, arm at heart level; take two readings.
  • BP of 140/90 mmHg or more is high:
    • 140–159/90–99 – recheck on another day; start treatment if still raised.
    • 160–179/100–109 – start treatment the same day.
    • 180/110 or more – start treatment and refer to the medical officer/specialist.
  • Baseline tests – haemoglobin, blood sugar, urine protein, serum creatinine where available.

Treatment protocol (example – Maharashtra state protocol developed with the India Hypertension Control Initiative)

  • Step 1 – amlodipine 5 mg daily with adherence counselling.
  • Step 2 – add telmisartan 40 mg.
  • Step 3 – increase telmisartan to 80 mg.
  • Step 4 – increase amlodipine to 10 mg.
  • Step 5 – add chlorthalidone 6.25 mg.
  • Step 6 – increase chlorthalidone to 12.5 mg.
  • At each step, BP is checked after 30 days and the next step is taken only if BP is still above target; if not controlled at the last step despite regular intake, the patient is referred.
  • Target BP is below 140/90 mmHg.
  • Special groups (pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, young patients, heart disease) are managed by the medical officer.

2. Diabetes

  • Screening – capillary random blood glucose; a value of 140 mg/dl or more is referred to the medical officer for confirmation (fasting and post-meal plasma glucose or HbA1c).
  • Treatment – lifestyle changes for all, with metformin as the first drug; a sulphonylurea such as glimepiride is added in steps as per protocol; insulin is started at higher facilities when needed.
  • Hypoglycaemia education – sweating, tremors, confusion – take sugar or glucose immediately and report.
  • Foot care – daily inspection, proper footwear, no walking barefoot; yearly eye and kidney check-ups.

3. Follow-up at the AAM

  • Monthly visit – check BP or blood sugar, weight and symptoms; dispense one month's medicines; record in the patient card and on the National NCD Portal.
  • Adherence counselling – explain that BP and diabetes are lifelong conditions, medicines must be taken daily even when the person feels well, and the doses are adjusted step by step.
  • Lifestyle advice
    • Salt less than one teaspoon a day.
    • Less fried food and sugar; more vegetables, fruits and whole grains.
    • At least 150 minutes of exercise a week; weight reduction.
    • No tobacco or alcohol; stress management through yoga.
  • Tracing defaulters through ASHAs; home delivery of medicines for the elderly and disabled where available.

4. Referral criteria

  • BP of 180/110 or more, or BP not controlled at the final protocol step.
  • Signs of target-organ damage – chest pain, breathlessness, swelling of feet, weakness of a limb, slurred speech, visual disturbance, decreased urine.
  • Pregnancy with high BP or high sugar.
  • Very high blood sugar or repeated hypoglycaemia; foot ulcer, infection or gangrene.
  • Suspected side effects of drugs (ankle swelling with amlodipine, dizziness, low potassium).

Conclusion At the AAM, hypertension and diabetes are screened, confirmed by the medical officer and managed with simple step-wise protocols – amlodipine, telmisartan and chlorthalidone for BP (target below 140/90), and metformin followed by glimepiride for diabetes – with monthly follow-up, adherence and lifestyle counselling, digital records and timely referral.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology

question: Explain the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission.
tags: National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission
answer_html:
Introduction

  • Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited haemoglobin disorder (autosomal recessive) that causes chronic anaemia, painful crises, infections, stroke, organ damage and early death.
  • In India it is common among tribal communities in central, western and southern states, including the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Gujarat.
  • The National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission was launched by the Prime Minister on 1 July 2023 at Shahdol, Madhya Pradesh, under the National Health Mission.

Goal – elimination of sickle cell disease as a public health problem by 2047, by preventing new births with the disease and ensuring quality care for those affected.

Target area and group

  • People aged 0–40 years in 17 high-prevalence states (mainly tribal districts), with an initial target of screening 7 crore people.

Strategies

  1. Universal screening – at all facilities from Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to district hospitals and in camps and schools, using point-of-care (solubility or rapid) tests, with confirmation by HPLC or electrophoresis where needed.
  2. Sickle cell (genetic status) cards – every screened person gets a card showing whether they are normal, a carrier (trait) or affected; the colour-coded cards help in premarital and preconception counselling ("two carriers should know their risk before marriage or pregnancy").
  3. Genetic counselling – explaining the 25% risk of an affected child when both parents are carriers; prenatal diagnosis where available.
  4. Management of patients
    • Registration and regular follow-up.
    • Hydroxyurea (included in the essential drugs list), folic acid, vaccination and penicillin prophylaxis for children.
    • Pain management, hydration and management of crises.
    • Blood transfusion when needed; referral for complications.
  5. Awareness – IEC in tribal areas, schools and through community leaders; World Sickle Cell Day (19 June).
  6. Integration with RBSK, ANC screening, RKSK and the National Health Mission; digital tracking through the sickle cell portal.

Progress – by June 2026, more than 7 crore people had been screened, over 20 lakh carriers and about 2.46 lakh persons with the disease identified, and over 4 crore sickle cell cards distributed.

Role of the nurse

  • Mobilise people for screening; perform point-of-care tests where trained; distribute and explain the cards.
  • Counsel carriers and couples; encourage premarital testing and ANC screening of pregnant women.
  • Teach patients and families about plenty of fluids, avoiding extreme heat, cold and dehydration, early treatment of fever, immunisation, regular hydroxyurea and folic acid, and warning signs (severe pain, breathlessness, pallor, swelling of abdomen, weakness of limbs).
  • Follow up registered patients; reduce stigma; maintain records.

Conclusion The National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) aims to eliminate SCD as a public health problem by 2047 through universal screening of people aged 0–40 in 17 high-prevalence states, genetic status cards, counselling, comprehensive care with hydroxyurea and awareness; the community health nurse is central to screening, counselling and follow-up.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology

question: Explain the National Programme for Palliative Care (NPPC) and community-based palliative care.
answer_html:
Introduction

  • Palliative care improves the quality of life of patients and families facing life-threatening or life-limiting illness by preventing and relieving suffering – pain and other physical, psychosocial and spiritual problems.
  • In India, many people with advanced cancer, HIV, heart, lung, liver or kidney failure, stroke, dementia and frailty in old age need palliative care, but few receive it, and access to oral morphine has been limited.

National Programme for Palliative Care (NPPC)

  • Launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2012; now implemented through the National Health Mission along with NP-NCD.
  • Palliative care is one of the expanded service packages at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.

Objectives

  1. Improve the capacity to provide palliative care at all levels – primary, secondary and tertiary – including home-based care.
  2. Refine legal and regulatory systems to improve access to opioids for medical use.
  3. Encourage attitudinal change among health professionals.
  4. Develop national standards for palliative care services.
  5. Promote community awareness and behaviour change.

Components

  • Palliative care units at district hospitals with trained doctors and nurses, and outpatient and inpatient services.
  • Home-based palliative care through teams from CHCs and PHCs, with AAM staff and ASHAs.
  • Training of doctors, nurses and community health workers; inclusion of palliative care in nursing and medical curricula.
  • Availability of essential drugs, especially oral morphine – the NDPS (Amendment) Act, 2014 created a category of "essential narcotic drugs" (such as morphine, fentanyl and methadone) with simpler licensing for recognised medical institutions.
  • IEC, monitoring and research.

Community-based palliative care – the Kerala model

  • Kerala developed India's best-known community model – the Neighbourhood Network in Palliative Care (NNPC), started in the early 2000s in Malappuram, in which trained community volunteers identify patients, visit homes, give emotional support and arrange services, working with doctors and nurses.
  • Kerala adopted a state palliative care policy in 2008; local self-government institutions support primary palliative care units with home-care nurses.
  • Principles – care in the patient's own home, involvement of family and neighbours, volunteers as the backbone, low cost, and linkage with health services.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Identify patients needing palliative care in the community (bedridden, advanced illness, elderly).
  • Home care – pain assessment and administration of oral morphine and other drugs as prescribed; management of symptoms (nausea, constipation, breathlessness, wounds, bedsores, lymphoedema); catheter and colostomy care; nutrition and hydration.
  • Teach and support caregivers – positioning, bathing, mouth care, feeding; prevention of caregiver burnout.
  • Psychosocial and spiritual support; counselling about prognosis and wishes; end-of-life and bereavement care.
  • Link families with schemes (pensions, disability certificates, PM-JAY), volunteers and NGOs; arrange equipment (air mattress, wheelchair).
  • Records and referral to palliative care units.

Conclusion NPPC (2012) aims to make palliative care available at all levels – from district palliative care units to home-based care through AAMs – with trained staff, better access to oral morphine after the NDPS amendment of 2014 and community awareness. Kerala's Neighbourhood Network shows how volunteers, families and nurses together can provide low-cost palliative care at home.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
