question: Explain the early recognition, first response and prevention of stroke and heart attack in the community.
answer_html:
Introduction

  • Heart attack (acute myocardial infarction) and stroke are the leading causes of death and disability among adults in India, often affecting people in their 40s and 50s.
  • Both are caused mainly by atherosclerosis and blood clots, and both are time-critical – "time is muscle" in heart attack and "time is brain" in stroke.
  • NP-NCD includes early recognition, referral and treatment of STEMI and stroke.

1. Early recognition Heart attack

  • Central chest pain, pressure or heaviness lasting more than 15–20 minutes, often spreading to the left arm, jaw, neck or back.
  • Sweating, breathlessness, nausea or vomiting, giddiness, fear.

  • Atypical presentation in women, the elderly and diabetics – breathlessness, fatigue, upper abdominal discomfort or "gas", without obvious chest pain. Stroke – "BE FAST"

  • Balance – sudden loss of balance or dizziness.

  • Eyes – sudden loss or blurring of vision.
  • Face – drooping of one side of the face.
  • Arm – weakness or numbness of an arm or leg (one side).
  • Speech – slurred speech or difficulty understanding.
  • Time – note the time of onset and call for help immediately.
  • Sudden severe headache, confusion or unconsciousness may also occur.

2. First response in the community

  • Call 108/112 immediately and arrange transport to the nearest facility that can treat heart attack or stroke; do not wait for symptoms to pass.
  • Keep the person at rest, loosen tight clothing, reassure.
  • Suspected heart attack – sit the person in a comfortable position; aspirin may be chewed as per the medical officer's protocol if not allergic.
  • Suspected stroke – give nothing by mouth (risk of choking), lay the person on the side if drowsy or vomiting, protect weak limbs.
  • If the person becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally – start hands-only CPR (hard, fast chest compressions in the centre of the chest) and use an AED if available.
  • Note the time of onset – treatment decisions depend on it.

3. Treatment windows and the health system

  • Heart attack (STEMI) – early ECG, and thrombolysis (e.g. tenecteplase) as early as possible, ideally within the first few hours of onset, at "spoke" hospitals (district hospitals/CHCs) linked by teleconsultation to "hub" hospitals that provide angioplasty – the hub-and-spoke model.
  • Ischaemic stroke – CT scan to rule out bleeding, then thrombolysis within 4.5 hours of onset at stroke-ready hospitals; stroke units and rehabilitation.

4. Prevention

  • Primary prevention – control of BP, blood sugar and cholesterol; quitting tobacco; healthy diet low in salt, sugar and saturated fat; regular physical activity; weight control; limiting alcohol; reducing air pollution exposure; regular NCD screening from 30 years.
  • Secondary prevention (after a first event) – regular antiplatelet drugs, statins and BP medicines as prescribed; diabetes control; cardiac and stroke rehabilitation (graded exercise, physiotherapy, speech therapy); adherence to follow-up.

Role of the nurse

  • Teach the community the warning signs and BE FAST, the 108 number and hands-only CPR.
  • Identify and control risk factors through screening and follow-up of people with hypertension and diabetes.
  • Ensure adherence to medicines after heart attack or stroke; support rehabilitation at home (positioning, exercises, prevention of bedsores and falls).
  • Counsel families on lifestyle change; observe World Heart Day (29 September) and World Stroke Day (29 October).

Conclusion Heart attack and stroke must be recognised early – chest pain and its atypical forms, and the BE FAST signs – and treated urgently by calling 108, giving correct first aid and CPR, and reaching facilities that can give thrombolysis or angioplasty within the time window. Control of BP, sugar, cholesterol and tobacco, and secondary prevention and rehabilitation, prevent first and repeat events.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Non-communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: Name any two non-communicable diseases and state their common risk factors.
answer_html:
Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are chronic diseases that are not passed from person to person; they usually develop slowly and last long. Examples

  1. Diabetes mellitus.
  2. Hypertension and other cardiovascular diseases (coronary heart disease, stroke). Others – cancers (oral, breast, cervical, lung), chronic respiratory diseases (COPD, asthma), chronic kidney disease and mental disorders. Common risk factors
  • Behavioural (modifiable) – tobacco use, unhealthy diet (high salt, sugar and fat; low fruits and vegetables), physical inactivity, harmful use of alcohol.
  • Metabolic – raised blood pressure, raised blood sugar, raised cholesterol, overweight and obesity.
  • Environmental – air pollution.
  • Non-modifiable – age, sex, family history.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Non-communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What is the 75/25 initiative?
answer_html:
The "75/25" initiative was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on World Hypertension Day, 17 May 2023, under NP-NCD.

  • Aim – to bring 75 million (7.5 crore) people with hypertension and diabetes under standard care by December 2025.
  • Approach – population-based screening of everyone aged 30 years and above at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, confirmation and treatment by protocol, monthly follow-up with free drugs, teleconsultation and tracking on the National NCD Portal.
  • Progress – by March 2025, about 42 million people were on treatment for hypertension and 25 million for diabetes, nearly 90% of the target. It is one of the largest NCD care expansions in primary health care in the world.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Non-communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What is the Community Based Assessment Checklist (CBAC)?
answer_html:
The Community Based Assessment Checklist (CBAC) is a simple form filled by the ASHA during home visits for every person aged 30 years and above under NP-NCD. Part A – risk score based on:

  • age;
  • tobacco use;
  • alcohol use;
  • waist circumference;
  • physical activity;
  • family history of hypertension, diabetes or heart disease. A score of more than 4 marks the person as higher risk and a priority for screening at the AAM, although everyone aged 30+ is screened. Part B – early symptoms suggestive of cancers, TB, chronic lung disease, leprosy and other conditions, so that the person can be referred promptly. Data are entered on the National NCD Portal and used to plan screening.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Non-communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What is VIA? Write its importance.
answer_html:
VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid) is a simple screening test for cervical cancer and pre-cancer.

  • After inserting a speculum, the cervix is painted with 3–5% acetic acid; after about one minute it is inspected in good light.

  • Dense white (acetowhite) areas near the squamocolumnar junction indicate a VIA-positive result (possible pre-cancerous lesion). Importance

  • Simple, cheap and gives an immediate result; can be done by trained nurses, CHOs and doctors at primary level.

  • Used under NP-NCD for women aged 30–65 years, once every five years.
  • Allows a "screen and treat" approach – VIA-positive women can be treated with thermal ablation or cryotherapy at the same or next visit, or referred for colposcopy and biopsy.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Non-communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What is the Haddon matrix?
answer_html:
The Haddon matrix (William Haddon Jr., 1970s) is a tool for planning injury prevention, especially for road traffic injuries. It is a grid with:

  • Rows – three phases: pre-event (pre-crash), event (crash) and post-event (post-crash).

  • Columns – factors: human (host), vehicle/equipment (agent) and environment (physical and social). Examples

  • Pre-crash – driver training and no drink-driving (human); good brakes and lights (vehicle); good roads and speed limits (environment).

  • Crash – helmets and seat belts (human); airbags (vehicle); crash barriers (environment).
  • Post-crash – first-aid skills (human); easy rescue from the vehicle (vehicle); quick ambulance and trauma care (environment). It shows that injuries are preventable at many points.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: Non-communicable Diseases and National Health Programmes
question: What is the Good Samaritan law?
answer_html:
A Good Samaritan is a person who, in good faith and without expecting reward, gives emergency help or first aid to a road accident victim or takes the victim to hospital.

  • The Supreme Court (2016) approved guidelines to protect such persons, and Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act (added by the 2019 Amendment) gives them legal protection. Main provisions

  • A Good Samaritan shall not be liable for any civil or criminal action for injury or death of the victim resulting from their help.

  • They cannot be forced to disclose their name or identity, to stay at the hospital, or to be a witness.
  • Hospitals cannot demand payment or deposit before giving emergency treatment. The law encourages bystanders to help within the golden hour and so saves lives.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: School Health Services
question: (a) Define school health services and state their objectives. (3 marks) (b) Describe the components of school health services. (8 marks) (c) Explain the role of the school health nurse. (4 marks)
tags: Ayushman Bharat School Health and Wellness Programme

diagram.caption: Components of school health services
labels: screening) – remedial measures and follow-up – prevention of communicable diseases – healthful school environment – nutritional services – first aid and emergency care – mental
dental and eye health – health education – education of children with special needs – school health records

answer_html:
(a) Definition and objectives (3 marks) Definition

  • School health services are the organised health services provided to school children and school personnel to promote and protect their health, detect and correct health problems early, and provide a healthy school environment and health education.
  • They are an important part of the national health system, because school children make up a large part of the population and schools are an excellent platform to reach them and, through them, their families.

Importance

  • School age (6–18 years) is a period of rapid growth and learning, when healthy habits are formed.
  • Many health problems (malnutrition, anaemia, worms, poor vision, dental caries, hearing problems, learning difficulties) are common, often unnoticed, and affect attendance and learning.
  • Schools bring children together, which can spread infections but also allows easy screening and education.
  • Children carry health messages home – "a child is a messenger of health to the family".

Objectives

  1. Promotion of positive health and healthy habits.
  2. Prevention of diseases and injuries.
  3. Early diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of health problems.
  4. Awakening health consciousness in children through health education.
  5. Provision of a healthful school environment.
  6. Development of children into healthy, responsible citizens who contribute to their community.

(b) Components of school health services (8 marks) 1. Health appraisal of school children and staff

  • Periodic medical examination – at entry to school and then at regular intervals; it includes history, height, weight, BMI, vision, hearing, teeth, skin, haemoglobin and a general and systemic examination.
  • Under the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), mobile health teams visit government and government-aided schools (and Anganwadis) to screen children for the 4 Ds – defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays including disability – and refer them to District Early Intervention Centres (DEICs) and hospitals for free treatment.
  • Daily morning inspection by the class teacher for signs of illness (fever, rash, red eyes, cough, lice, skin infections, unusual behaviour).
  • Health examination of teachers and other staff, since an infected teacher (e.g. with TB) can infect many children.

2. Remedial measures and follow-up

  • Treatment of detected problems – spectacles for refractive errors, dental treatment, treatment of anaemia and worms, ear care, surgery for congenital defects (free under RBSK).
  • Follow-up to see that advice has been carried out; involvement of parents.

3. Prevention of communicable diseases

  • Immunisation – booster doses (e.g. Td at 10 and 16 years) and campaign vaccines (e.g. MR); keeping immunisation records.
  • Exclusion and readmission – children with infectious diseases (measles, chickenpox, mumps, conjunctivitis, scabies) stay at home until no longer infectious.
  • Safe water, sanitation and hand washing with soap; control of outbreaks.

4. Healthful school environment

  • Suitable site away from noise, traffic and dirty places; safe building with a boundary wall.
  • Classrooms with adequate space, natural lighting, ventilation and suitable furniture.
  • Safe drinking water, separate and clean toilets for girls and boys with water and hand-washing facilities, and facilities for menstrual hygiene.
  • Clean premises, safe disposal of waste, playground, and a hygienic kitchen and eating place.
  • A tobacco-free campus and safety from injuries and violence.

5. Nutritional services

  • PM POSHAN (mid-day meal) – hot cooked meals providing energy, protein and micronutrients; prevention of classroom hunger; improved attendance.
  • Weekly iron and folic acid supplementation (WIFS) and biannual deworming (National Deworming Day); vitamin A where indicated; nutrition education and school nutrition gardens.

6. First aid and emergency care

  • First-aid box in every school, trained teachers, emergency contact numbers, a link with the nearest health facility and ambulance; disaster preparedness.

7. Mental health

  • A supportive, non-threatening school climate; prevention of bullying, examination stress and substance use; early identification of behavioural, emotional and learning problems; counselling services and referral (Tele-MANAS).

8. Dental and eye health

  • Regular dental check-ups, tooth-brushing education and control of sweets; vision testing and provision of spectacles (school eye screening under NPCBVI).

9. Health education

  • Planned teaching of personal hygiene, nutrition, safety, prevention of diseases, physical activity and yoga, puberty and reproductive health, mental well-being and substance-use prevention.
  • The Ayushman Bharat School Health and Wellness Programme delivers this through two trained teachers in every school – the Health and Wellness Ambassadors – covering 11 themes.

10. Education of children with special needs

  • Early identification of children with visual, hearing, locomotor or intellectual disabilities and learning disorders; inclusive education; aids and appliances; referral.

11. School health records

  • A cumulative health record for each child – identification data, past history, immunisation, findings of examinations, treatment and follow-up – which moves with the child from class to class and school to school.

(c) Role of the school health nurse (4 marks)

  1. Planning and organisation – helps the school health committee to plan services, prepares the yearly calendar of activities and coordinates with the PHC, RBSK teams and parents.
  2. Health appraisal – assists in medical examination; measures height, weight and BMI; tests vision and hearing; checks haemoglobin; trains teachers in daily morning inspection.
  3. Follow-up and referral – visits homes of children with health problems, explains treatment to parents and checks that it is carried out.
  4. Prevention – organises immunisation, deworming and WIFS; isolates and excludes infectious cases; advises on control of outbreaks.
  5. Environmental sanitation – inspects water, toilets, kitchen and classrooms, and reports deficiencies.
  6. Health education – teaches children, teachers and parents; supports Health and Wellness Ambassadors and Messengers; organises health days and campaigns.
  7. First aid and emergency care – gives first aid, trains teachers and maintains first-aid boxes.
  8. Nutrition – monitors the quality and hygiene of mid-day meals and identifies malnourished children.
  9. Counselling – of adolescents on puberty, menstrual hygiene, stress, substance use and safety; identifies abuse and bullying and refers appropriately (POCSO reporting).
  10. Records and reports – maintains school health records and sends reports.

Health-promoting school (WHO concept) – a school that constantly strengthens its capacity as a healthy setting for living, learning and working. It has a written health policy, a safe physical and social environment, health education linked to life skills, access to health services, links with families and the community, and attention to the health of teachers and staff. School health services in India increasingly follow this whole-school approach, in which every teacher, parent and child has a part to play.

Nursing importance

  • The school health nurse links the school, the family and the health system – a healthy child learns better, and healthy habits learned at school last a lifetime.

Conclusion School health services are organised services that promote and protect the health of school children through health appraisal (medical examination, RBSK screening and daily inspection), remedial measures and follow-up, prevention of communicable diseases, a healthful school environment, nutritional services (PM POSHAN, WIFS, deworming), first aid, mental, dental and eye health, health education (AB-SHWP), care of children with special needs and school health records. The school health nurse plans, screens, follows up, prevents, educates, counsels and records.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: School Health Services
question: Explain the common health problems of school children and their prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction School children (6–18 years) suffer from many health problems that may not be serious enough to keep them in bed but affect growth, attendance and learning. Most are preventable or easily treatable if detected early.

Common health problems

  1. Malnutrition – stunting and thinness due to poor diet and repeated infections; at the same time, rising overweight and obesity from junk food and inactivity.
  2. Anaemia – due to iron deficiency, worms and poor diet, especially among adolescent girls; causes tiredness and poor concentration.
  3. Worm infestations – roundworm, hookworm and whipworm from soil contamination and poor hygiene.
  4. Dental problems – dental caries, gum disease and malocclusion.
  5. Eye problems – refractive errors (myopia increasing with screen use), squint, conjunctivitis, vitamin A deficiency.
  6. Ear problems – wax, ear discharge, hearing loss.
  7. Skin infections – scabies, pediculosis (lice), fungal infections, impetigo.
  8. Communicable diseases – diarrhoea, typhoid, hepatitis A, respiratory infections, measles, mumps, chickenpox, conjunctivitis, TB; sore throat leading to rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease.
  9. Injuries – falls, sports injuries, road accidents on the way to school, drowning, burns.
  10. Learning and behavioural problems – learning disabilities, ADHD, poor school performance, truancy.
  11. Mental health problems – examination stress, anxiety, depression, bullying, self-harm, internet and gaming overuse.
  12. Adolescent problems – menstrual problems and poor menstrual hygiene, early sexual activity, substance use (tobacco, alcohol, inhalants).
  13. Non-communicable disease risks – unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, high screen time, early hypertension and diabetes.
  14. Congenital and chronic conditions – heart disease, epilepsy, asthma, thalassaemia and sickle cell disease.

Prevention

  • Regular health check-ups and RBSK screening with treatment and follow-up.
  • Nutrition – PM POSHAN meals, WIFS, biannual deworming, nutrition education, limiting junk food in and around schools.
  • Hygiene – safe water, clean toilets, hand washing with soap, nail and hair care, menstrual hygiene facilities.
  • Immunisation as per schedule and campaigns.
  • Dental and eye care – tooth brushing, vision screening and spectacles, limited screen time and outdoor play.
  • Safe environment – injury prevention, road safety education, safe transport, anti-bullying policies.
  • Physical activity, yoga and sports every day.
  • Life skills and mental health promotion – counselling, teacher training, supportive school climate.
  • Health education of children and parents; early referral of children with chronic illnesses.

Conclusion School children commonly suffer from malnutrition (both under- and over-nutrition), anaemia, worms, dental, eye, ear and skin problems, communicable diseases, injuries, learning, behavioural and mental health problems and adolescent issues. Regular screening, good nutrition, hygiene, immunisation, a safe environment, physical activity, life-skills education and follow-up prevent most of them.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: School Health Services
question: Explain the Ayushman Bharat School Health and Wellness Programme.
answer_html:
Introduction

  • The School Health and Wellness Programme is the school component of Ayushman Bharat, jointly run by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of Education.
  • Its curriculum and the "School Health Ambassador" initiative were released on 12 February 2020.
  • It is implemented in government and government-aided schools, with priority to aspirational districts.
  • It adds a strong health promotion and prevention component to the screening and services already given in schools.

Objectives

  • To provide age-appropriate information about health and nutrition to children.
  • To promote healthy behaviours that they will follow throughout life.
  • To detect and treat diseases early through screening and referral.
  • To promote the use of safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools.
  • To promote yoga and meditation, and research on child health and wellness.

Key features

  1. Health and Wellness Ambassadors (HWAs) – two teachers in every school, preferably one male and one female, trained to conduct joyful, activity-based sessions for one hour every week (about 24 weeks a year).
  2. Health and Wellness Messengers – students (two from each class) who help in activities and carry messages to peers and families.
  3. Tuesday as Health and Wellness Day – schools may dedicate every Tuesday to these activities.
  4. 11 thematic areas (curriculum prepared with NCERT):
    • growing up healthy;
    • emotional well-being and mental health;
    • interpersonal relationships;
    • values and responsible citizenship;
    • gender equality;
    • nutrition, health and sanitation;
    • prevention and management of substance misuse;
    • promotion of a healthy lifestyle;
    • reproductive health and HIV prevention;
    • safety and security against violence and injuries;
    • promotion of safe use of the internet, media and social media.
  5. Services – health screening by RBSK teams, WIFS and deworming, provision of sanitary napkins, age-appropriate immunisation, and referral of children needing services to Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, Adolescent Friendly Health Clinics and DEICs.
  6. Convergence – with RBSK, RKSK, PM POSHAN, Fit India, Eat Right India and Swachh Vidyalaya.

Role of the nurse/CHO

  • Support and train HWAs; conduct sessions on health topics; organise screening, WIFS and deworming days; receive referred children at the AAM and follow them up; counsel adolescents; maintain records.

Conclusion The Ayushman Bharat School Health and Wellness Programme uses two trained teachers per school as Health and Wellness Ambassadors, supported by student Health and Wellness Messengers, to cover 11 health themes through weekly activities, along with screening, supplementation, sanitary napkins and referral – building lifelong healthy behaviours in school children.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: School Health Services
question: Explain the initiation and planning of school health services.
answer_html:
Introduction School health services succeed only when they are planned jointly by the school, the health department and the community, according to the needs of the children. The community health nurse often takes the lead in initiating and planning them.

Steps in initiation and planning

  1. Getting approval and support – meet the head teacher and management; obtain permission from education and health authorities; explain the purpose and benefits.
  2. Forming a school health committee – head teacher (chairperson), teachers (including the Health and Wellness Ambassadors), the school health nurse or CHO, medical officer of the PHC, parents' representatives (School Management Committee) and student representatives.
  3. Assessment of needs (situation analysis)
    • Survey of the school – number and age of children, enrolment and attendance, drop-outs.
    • Health status from previous records and screening (anaemia, malnutrition, vision, dental and skin problems).
    • School environment – building, classrooms, water, toilets, kitchen, playground, hazards.
    • Existing services and resources – first-aid box, health records, nearby health facilities, NGOs.
  4. Setting priorities and objectives – e.g. "reduce anaemia among girls of classes 6–12", "ensure all children have their vision tested this year", "make every toilet functional".
  5. Identifying resources – staff, time in the timetable, funds (school grants, NHM, Panchayat), equipment (weighing scale, height scale, vision chart, first-aid box), IEC materials.
  6. Preparing a plan of action and annual calendar
    • Health check-ups and RBSK visits.
    • Immunisation and deworming days; WIFS on fixed days.
    • Weekly health and wellness sessions.
    • Health days (World Health Day, Hand Washing Day, Anti-Tobacco Day, Nutrition Week).
    • Sanitation drives and first-aid training.
    • Parent meetings.
  7. Orientation and training of teachers, cooks and students (health messengers) for their roles.
  8. Implementation – carry out activities as per the calendar; involve parents; coordinate with the PHC/AAM for referral and treatment.
  9. Recording and reporting – maintain individual school health records and registers; send reports.
  10. Supervision and evaluation
    • Process indicators – number of children examined, sessions held.
    • Outcome indicators – reduction in anaemia, improvement in hygiene, attendance and learning.
    • Revise the plan every year.

Principles – needs-based planning, participation of teachers, parents and students, use of existing resources, integration with national programmes, continuity and follow-up.

Conclusion Initiation and planning of school health services involves obtaining support, forming a school health committee, assessing needs, setting priorities and objectives, mobilising resources, preparing an action plan and annual calendar, training staff, implementing with coordination, recording, and supervising and evaluating the programme every year.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: School Health Services
question: What is a school health record? List its contents.
answer_html:
A school health record is a cumulative record of the health of each child, started at admission and kept up to date throughout the school years; it moves with the child when changing class or school. Contents

  • Identification data – name, age, sex, class, parents' names, address, contact number.
  • Past history – illnesses, allergies, disabilities, family history.
  • Immunisation record.
  • Findings of periodic medical examinations – height, weight, BMI, vision, hearing, teeth, haemoglobin, skin, systemic findings.
  • Screening results (RBSK), treatment given, referrals and follow-up.
  • Absences due to illness; special needs; signatures of the examiner. Uses – continuity of care, follow-up, planning school health services and evaluating their impact.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: School Health Services
question: Who are Health and Wellness Ambassadors?
tags: Ayushman Bharat School Health and Wellness Programme
answer_html:
Health and Wellness Ambassadors (HWAs) are teachers trained under the Ayushman Bharat School Health and Wellness Programme to promote health in schools.

  • Two teachers in every government and government-aided school, preferably one male and one female, are selected (motivated teachers with good communication skills, often from science or physical education).
  • They conduct joyful, activity-based sessions for one hour every week on 11 themes such as growing up healthy, emotional well-being, nutrition and sanitation, substance misuse, reproductive health, safety against violence and injuries, and safe use of the internet.
  • They identify children needing help and link them with health services, working with student Health and Wellness Messengers.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: School Health Services
question: What is daily morning inspection in school health?
answer_html:
Daily morning inspection is a quick observation of every child by the class teacher at the start of the school day, to detect early signs of illness or neglect. Signs looked for

  • Unusual appearance – flushed face, fever, drowsiness, pallor.
  • Red or watery eyes; running nose, cough, sore throat.
  • Skin rashes, sores, scabies, lice; swelling of the face or neck (mumps).
  • Vomiting, diarrhoea; poor personal hygiene; injuries.
  • Unusual behaviour – withdrawal, sadness, irritability. Action – the child is separated if infectious, sent to the school health nurse or a health facility, and parents are informed. It helps in early detection of communicable diseases and other problems, and teaches hygiene habits.

subject: Community Health Nursing I including Environmental Science & Epidemiology
unit_title: School Health Services
question: List the standards of a healthful school environment.
answer_html:
Standards of a healthful school environment include:

  • Site – on high, well-drained land, away from noise, traffic, factories, markets and dirty places; fenced, with a playground.
  • Building – safe and strong, with an adequate number of rooms.
  • Classrooms
    • No more than about 40 children in a class, with at least 10 square feet of floor space per child.
    • Doors and windows equal to about one-fourth of the floor area, giving natural light (preferably from the left) and cross-ventilation.
  • Furniture – desks and chairs suited to the child's height.
  • Water and sanitation – safe drinking water; separate, clean toilets for girls and boys with hand-washing facilities and provision for menstrual hygiene.
  • Eating facilities – a clean kitchen and dining space for mid-day meals.
  • Safe waste disposal, cleanliness, first-aid facilities and a tobacco-free, violence-free campus.
